Property Types and Classifications 2+1 / 4+1 System In Singapore real estate listings, this numbering system indicates the number of bedrooms plus a domestic helper's room. For example, "2+1" means 2 bedrooms plus a helper's room, while "4+1" denotes 4 bedrooms plus a helper's room[8]. Air Con or A/C Refers to air conditioning, a standard feature in Singapore properties due to the tropical climate. Often specified in property listings with details about the number of units or type of system[8]. Black and White Houses Houses in Singapore with a history dating back centuries, representing the traditional bungalow-style residences that provide insights into the city's colonial past. Made famous due to Ridout issue in Singapore. These striking government-owned historical bungalows with colonial roots are heritage protected and available for foreigners to rent via an auction process. BR (Bedroom) Abbreviation commonly used in property listings to indicate the number of bedrooms in a property. B/S (Bomb Shelter) A mandatory feature in newer HDB flats and some private properties, designed as a reinforced space that can be used as storage or utility room during normal times. BTO (Build-To-Order) A category of newly constructed flats by the Housing and Development Board (HDB), where construction begins only when a certain percentage of units have been booked by eligible buyers. Also the term made famous by "Wanna to BTO Together ?" Bungalow Expensive properties in Singapore, often spanning 2 to 3 stories, undergoing renovations to meet evolving needs and preferences. These standalone houses typically sit on larger land plots and represent the most exclusive form of landed property in Singapore. Cluster House A hybrid property type that combines the privacy and space of landed property with the convenience of condominium facilities. Cluster housing developments feature landed properties (bungalows, semi-detached or terrace houses) with shared amenities like pools, playgrounds, and gyms. These strata-titled landed properties are located within gated communities. Community Care Apartment Senior-friendly housing with specific amenities designed to support aging in place, including healthcare services and communal facilities. Condo (Condominium) A housing type where a portion of real estate is individually owned, with access to shared facilities. In Singapore and Malaysia, condos specifically refer to residential buildings with luxury facilities such as security guards, swimming pools, or tennis courts. Condominium Complex Refers to the entire development comprising individually owned residential units and shared facilities such as swimming pools, gyms, and security services[5]. Corner Terrace House A terrace house located at the end of a row, typically offering more land area and windows on three sides instead of just the front and back. Cul-de-sac House A property located on a dead-end street that typically forms a circular area for turning around. These properties often command premium prices due to reduced traffic and increased privacy. Executive Condominium (EC) A public-private housing hybrid introduced in the 1990s, physically resembling private condominiums in style and facilities. ECs are aimed at the "sandwich class" - households with higher incomes that don't qualify for public housing but find private property too expensive. They follow public housing regulations including a 5-year Minimum Occupation Period (MOP) before resale, and after 10 years transform into private condominiums that can be sold on the open market to foreigners. Read more about ECs on PatkoProperty. Executive Flat An HDB flat with distinctive features, including 3 bedrooms, generally larger than standard HDB units and often featuring additional amenities. HDB (Housing & Development Board) The public housing authority in Singapore tasked with planning and developing housing estates. HDB flats house over 80% of Singapore's resident population. Heartlands Areas where the majority of Singaporeans, especially the middle and working classes, reside, often located in HDB estates outside the central business district. Jumbo Flat A combination of two adjacent flats, typically created by combining a 3-room and a 4-room flat, resulting in a significantly larger living space. Land-titled Property Property that sits within its own land boundaries, as opposed to strata-titled properties. Level 1 In Singapore, this refers to the ground floor of a building. The numbering system starts with 1 rather than 0 or G as in some other countries. Maisonette Two-story buildings comprising bedrooms, wardrobes, kitchens, and bathrooms, similar to flats on two floors. These were built by HDB primarily in the 1980s and 1990s. In private properties, maisonettes typically have bedrooms and main bathroom upstairs. Prime Residential Districts (District 9, 10, and 11) Formerly prominent residential areas for expatriates, no longer in official use but recognized for luxury properties. District 9 includes Orchard Road and Cairnhill, District 10 covers Bukit Timah and Holland, and District 11 encompasses Thomson and Newton. Hot developments here include Watten House and 32 Gilstead. Private Apartment Units in a non-public development with fewer communal facilities than a condominium, typically in buildings with less than 50 units. Semi-Detached House (Semi or Semi-D) Two houses connected by a common wall, a suitable option for those seeking camaraderie and amicable relations with neighbors. Shophouse Property that used to be a traditional shop selling spices or trading goods with residential space above. Many of these properties are now on conservation lists, representing important cultural heritage. They typically feature distinctive architectural elements including five-foot ways (covered walkways). Shophouses are now a huge importance of the asset progression. State-titled Property An apartment in a building where some areas are common or shared among residents. Straits Architecture Commonly known as the Chinese doll's house, it comprises shops on the ground floor and residential apartments above, often spanning up to three storeys. These shophouses are culturally significant in Singapore's architectural heritage. Terrace House (Terr) A row of linked houses, often featuring gardens. These landed properties share walls with neighboring units on both sides, except for corner units. Walk-Up Apartment Apartments in a building with five floors or fewer, where upper-floor access is available solely by staircase, without elevators. Geographic and Market Regions Core Central Region (CCR) Prime areas comprising luxury neighborhoods such as Orchard, Bukit Timah, and Marina Bay. The CCR is synonymous with high-end living and investment properties, particularly attractive to affluent buyers. Read about the 3 Regions in Singapore. Rest of Central Region (RCR) The area surrounding the CCR, featuring a mix of private and public housing at more moderate price points than the CCR. Outside Central Region (OCR) Suburban areas of Singapore outside the central regions, typically featuring more affordable housing options while still maintaining good connectivity to the city center. Ownership Types and Regulations Agreement of Sale The basic contract of sale and purchase between a willing seller and buyer. No matter what the parties have agreed to verbally, no contract exists until an agreement of sale is completed and signed by both parties[8]. Bankruptcy Search A search conducted by conveyancers to verify whether a buyer or borrower has been, is, or is on the verge of being declared bankrupt[1]. Certificate of Statutory Completion (CSC) Issued by the building authority, indicating legal completion of a building after obtaining the Temporary Occupation Permit. Decoupling Selling shares of a property to a single owner to acquire additional properties without incurring ABSD, a strategy used by married couples to optimize property ownership. Diplomatic Clause Allows a tenant to terminate the tenancy with advance notice only after the initial twelve months, with a written notice period or payment of rent in lieu. Very useful and important for expats. Very important when you do rental for "Ang Mo". En-bloc Sale Collective sales of individual units in a private residential or commercial building, often fetching a higher price than market value. This requires a minimum consensus among owners (80-90% depending on the property's age)[1]. Fixtures Personal property attached to the real estate, such as escalators, that becomes part of the property legally[1]. Freehold Tenure A form of land ownership where an estate is held indefinitely. There are not many freehold properties for sale in Singapore, making them generally more valuable. Joint Tenancy Treats owners as a single entity, with the right of survivorship. If one owner passes away, their share automatically transfers to the surviving owner(s)[1]. LDAU (Land Dealings Approval Unit) Approval required for foreigners to purchase landed property. Especially important in Sentosa too[1]. Lease Period A fixed time frame for which a lease agreement is in force. This is usually two or three years at an agreed rental rate and often comes with an option to renew for a further term[4]. Leasehold A tenure held by a lessee under a lease agreement. In Singapore, houses are sold in 99 years or 999 years leasehold terms. Most HDB flats are on 99-year leases[1]. Minimum Occupation Period (MOP) The duration a buyer of an HDB flat must reside in it before putting it up for resale. One of the most favourite topic about what you can or cannot do in MOP. Restricted / Non-restricted Property Property requiring or not requiring approval from the relevant authority for purchase, particularly relevant for foreign buyers[1]. Strata Ownership The sharing of common areas in a multi-level apartment block by some units, denoted by a title associated with townhouses, units, and blocks of flats[1]. Strata Title A title to a unit or lot on a plan of subdivision associated with townhouses, units, and blocks of flats, based on the horizontal and vertical subdivision of airspace[1]. Tenancy-in-Common Ownership Ownership where individuals are considered separate entities, each capable of passing their share to others according to their will[1]. Temporary Occupation Permit (TOP) Granted by the Commissioner of Building Control upon the completion of a construction project, allowing for occupancy before the issuance of the CSC[1]. Government Schemes and Programs Design, Build and Sell Scheme (DBSS) A housing program where private developers build and sell public housing units with design features similar to private condominiums[5]. Fresh Start Housing Scheme A program providing second-timer families with children living in public rental flats the opportunity to receive grants for a new standard 2-room Flexi or standard 3-room flat on a shorter lease. Budget 2025 increased the grant amount from S$50,000 to S$75,000. GLS (Government Land Sales) GLS Programme is where the Government sells usable state land to developers through a bidding process. This is the main way in which the government releases land for residential use and is always 99-years lease[1]. HDB Conversion Scheme A program allowing owners of adjoining HDB flats to legally combine them into a single, larger unit subject to specific conditions[5]. HDB Fire Insurance Scheme A mandatory insurance scheme for all HDB flat owners to protect against fire damage to the internal structures, fixtures, and areas built by HDB[5]. HDB Flat Eligibility (HFE) Letter A document issued by HDB confirming an applicant's eligibility to purchase a new or resale HDB flat[5]. HDB Intent to Buy (ITB) A declaration by prospective buyers of their intention to purchase an HDB flat, usually submitted through HDB's online portal[5]. Home Improvement Program (HIP) A government initiative to upgrade older HDB flats, addressing common maintenance issues and improving living conditions[5]. Joint Singles Scheme (JSS) A scheme allowing two or more single Singapore citizens to jointly purchase an HDB resale flat[5]. Joint Singles Scheme Operator-Run (JSS-OR) An extension of the Joint Singles Scheme with specific operational guidelines for singles co-purchasing HDB flats[5]. Sale of Balance Flats (SBF) Unsold flats from previous HDB launches offered to eligible buyers, providing additional opportunities to secure public housing[5]. Staggered Downpayment Scheme A payment option allowing eligible HDB flat buyers to make their downpayment in two installments instead of one lump sum[5]. Financial and Tax Terms ABSD (Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty) A tax imposed on property owners in Singapore when acquiring additional properties, paid on top of the Buyer's Stamp Duty. Foreigners pay different rates from Permanent Residents who pay different rates from Singaporeans. Addendum A supplementary agreement to an original sales contract covering points agreed to thereafter. It is a separate agreement in its own right and, if it contradicts the original in any way, it is presumed to overrule it[8]. Amortization and Amortization Schedule Repayment of the loan principal from scheduled mortgage payments above the interest paid. An amortization schedule is a table showing all monthly mortgage payments broken down by interest and amortization, with the remaining loan balance[2]. Annual Percentage Rate (APR) The yearly rate charged for borrowing, expressed as a percentage that represents the actual yearly cost of funds over the term of a loan[5]. Annual Value The estimated annual rental income a property would generate if rented out, used to calculate property tax. Tax rates are progressive, with higher-valued properties subject to higher tax rates. Appraisal (or Valuation) The process of determining the market value of a property, typically required by banks when issuing mortgage loans[2]. Approval-in-principle / In-principle approval (IPA) Granted by banks for a home loan, subject to additional conditions. This preliminary approval indicates how much you can borrow[1][5]. Bridge Loan A short-term loan used to bridge the gap between the sale of one property and the purchase of another[2]. Buyer's Stamp Duty (BSD) Rates

term: What happens if a fiduciary fails to fulfil their duty
definition: When a fiduciary duty is breached, the beneficiary can take legal action against them. To succeed in a lawsuit, the beneficiary must provide evidence that a fiduciary duty existed, was violated, and resulted in harm. The beneficiary may seek monetary compensation for lost profits, income, or property losses. In addition to damages, the Singapore Courts offer other remedies for breaching a fiduciary duty, including: • Cancelling a contract that involved the breach of fiduciary duty. • Requiring the fiduciary to provide fair compensation to the beneficiary. • Requiring the fiduciary to account for any profits gained from the breach. • Transferring ownership of property from the fiduciary to the beneficiary. • Obtaining court orders to prevent the fiduciary from further breaches. term: a mortgage
definition: Simply put, a mortgage is a loan you take to purchase land or property. These loans typically span a period of 25 years, though the term can be shorter or longer depending on your preferences and circumstances. The catch is that the loan is ‘secured’ by the value of your home until it’s fully paid off. In other words, if you’re unable to keep up with the repayments, the lender has the legal right to reclaim your home and sell it to recoup their money. In the context of Singapore, mortgages are primarily provided by banks, and for HDB flats, the Housing and Development Board (HDB). The nuances such as terms and conditions, interest rates, and repayment schedules can be quite diverse among different mortgage providers.  Source: Mortgage in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-mortgage-in-singapore/  (index: Mortgage in Singapore)

term: Factors influencing mortgage and the application process
definition: A myriad of factors come into play in the mortgage process and in shaping the terms of the mortgage. These include your income and credit history, the value of the property in question, the size of the down payment, and the prevailing market conditions. Applying for a mortgage isn’t a spontaneous act—it involves several steps. First off, you’ll need to evaluate your financial standing to determine what you can afford. Then, it’s time to shop around and compare different mortgage options to find the one that resonates with your needs. Once you’ve settled on a mortgage, you’ll need to apply for it. This typically involves providing your financial information and undergoing a credit check.  Source: Mortgage in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-mortgage-in-singapore/  (index: Mortgage in Singapore)

term: Comparing mortgage with other real estate terms
definition: Mortgages are often juxtaposed with other real estate terms such as loans and deeds. While a loan is a generic term for borrowed money, a mortgage refers to a loan specifically earmarked for real estate. Conversely, a deed is a legal document denoting property.  Source: Mortgage in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-mortgage-in-singapore/  (index: Mortgage in Singapore)

term: Advantages and disadvantages of mortgage
definition: The primary advantage of a mortgage is that it empowers individuals to become homeowners without the need to pay the full price upfront. This opens up homeownership to a wider audience who might otherwise be unable to afford it. However, mortgages come with their fair share of pitfalls. They represent long-term financial obligations that can become challenging to manage if your financial situation takes a turn for the worse. Moreover, they entail interest payments, which can accumulate into a significant sum over the loan’s lifespan.  Source: Mortgage in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-mortgage-in-singapore/  (index: Mortgage in Singapore)

term: Types of mortgages
definition: Singapore offers a variety of mortgage options. These include fixed-rate mortgages, where the interest rate remains constant for a specified period, and variable-rate mortgages, where the interest rate is subject to change. HDB loans also feature in the mix, but these are exclusive to HDB flats and have terms and conditions that differ from bank loans. [HEADING-H3] Conclusion To wrap it up, securing a mortgage is a profound financial decision that demands careful thought. It’s crucial to fully comprehend the terms of your mortgage and ensure it aligns with your financial roadmap.  Source: Mortgage in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-mortgage-in-singapore/  (index: Mortgage in Singapore)

term: Step 1: Access My HDBPage

term: income tax in Singapore
definition: Income tax is a tax imposed by governments on the income earned by businesses and individuals within their jurisdiction. Taxpayers must file an annual income tax return to determine the amount of tax they owe. Governments collect income taxes as a source of revenue. The funds generated from these taxes are utilised to support public services, fulfil government obligations, and provide goods for the benefit of citizens.  Source: Income tax Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/income-tax-singapore/  (index: Income tax Singapore)
aliases: What is income tax in Singapore?

term: Who pays income tax in Singapore
definition: Income tax rates are determined based on an individual’s tax residency status. To be considered a tax resident for a specific Year of Assessment (YA) in Singapore, you must meet one of the following criteria: • If you are a Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident, you will be treated as a tax resident if you reside in Singapore, with the exception of temporary absences. • If you are a foreigner, you will be considered a tax resident if: a. You have stayed or worked in Singapore for at least 183 days in the previous calendar year. b. You have worked in Singapore continuously for 3 consecutive years, regardless of whether your stay in Singapore was less than 183 days in the first and/or third years. • For foreign employees, if you have worked in Singapore for a continuous period that spans 2 calendar years, and your stay is at least 183 days, you will be treated as a tax resident. This condition applies to employees who have entered Singapore but excludes directors of a company, public entertainers, or professionals. This 183-day time frame includes the period immediately before and after your employment, taking into account your physical presence. If you do not meet any of the above mentioned conditions, you will be considered a non-resident of Singapore for tax purposes. • Taxes imposed on employment income for non-residents are charged at a fixed rate of 15% or the higher tax amount determined by the progressive resident tax rates. • For income derived from director’s fees, consultation fees, and other sources, non-resident individuals are subject to a tax rate of 22%. This tax rate applies to all types of income, including rental income from properties, pension income, and director’s fees, except for employment income and specific types of income subject to reduced withholding rates.  Source: Income tax Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/income-tax-singapore/  (index: Income tax Singapore)

term: When to pay income tax in Singapore

For instance, if you are filing in 2023, you will report the income you received or derived in 2022. If you prefer to file using a paper form, submit the completed tax form to the IRAS headquarters by 15 April. term: What is joint tenancy?
definition: Joint tenancy refers to a type of property ownership where all co-owners share equal ownership rights to the property, regardless of their individual financial contributions towards purchasing it. In the event of one owner’s death, their share in the property automatically transfers to the surviving co-owner(s), regardless of whether they had made a will.  Source: Joint tenancy  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/joint-tenancy/  (index: Joint tenancy)

term: Joint tenancy vs Tenancy-in-common – What’s the difference
definition: Tenancy-in-common enables you and your co-owners to have individual ownership stakes in the property in different proportions. Essentially, your home’s ownership is divided into distinct shares by mutual agreement on the percentage of ownership each person has. Unlike joint tenancy, there is no automatic transfer of ownership to the surviving co-owner(s) if one co-owner dies. If a co-owner passes away, the remaining co-owners’ individual shares in the property stay the same.  Source: Joint tenancy  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/joint-tenancy/  (index: Joint tenancy)

term: Can joint tenancy be changed to tenancy-in-common
definition: It is possible to switch to the other form of ownership. HDB property owners need to inform and receive assistance from HDB, while private property owners will require the assistance of a law firm. If you and your co-owner opt to switch ownership from joint tenancy to tenancy-in-common, it can only be done if the property is split exactly down the middle, with each owner holding a 50% share. However, if achieving the equal split involves giving up a portion of your share, you may be required to pay stamp duty fees. Similarly, it is also possible to convert tenancy-in-common to joint tenancy, but only if the shares have already been divided equally.  Source: Joint tenancy  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/joint-tenancy/  (index: Joint tenancy)

term: What is Buyer’s Stamp Duty (BSD)?
definition: The Buyer’s Stamp Duty (BSD), a tax on legal documents related to acquiring or leasing real estate, applies to all real estate purchases in Singapore, including those of HDB flats. The tax only applies to the buyer. The amount of BSD payable is determined by whichever is higher: the property’s purchase price as stated in the signed sale and purchase agreement or the property’s market value as determined by appraisal reports. Even if the buyer can negotiate a lower purchase price, the BSD rate will still be based on the higher of the two amounts. For instance, if you negotiate a S$1.7 million apartment down to S$1.5 million, the larger of the two amounts will still be used to determine your BSD rate. It is illegal to utilise a document that hasn’t had its stamp duties paid. Only documents with paid stamp duties will be considered valid evidence in a property dispute that goes to court. As a result, all potential buyers should budget for the buyer’s stamp duty and, if applicable, Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty (ABSD).  Source: Buyer’s Stamp Duty (BSD)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/buyers-stamp-duty-bsd/  (index: Buyer’s Stamp Duty (BSD))

The rates at which residential and non-residential properties are taxed under BSD differ slightly. Residential property purchases are subject to a maximum BSD rate of 6%, while non-residential property purchases are subject to a maximum BSD rate of 5%. This change was made in Budget 2023 and will be effective immediately for any properties purchased on or after February 15th, 2023. term: Waiving contingencies: The risky real estate gambit that could make or break your deal
definition: In today’s competitive real estate market, many home buyers are resorting to risky manoeuvres to get their offers accepted. One increasingly common tactic is waiving contingencies – but this gambit could make or break your deal. [HEADING-H3] What are contingencies? Contingencies are conditions written into an offer that must be met for the purchase to move forward. Common contingencies include: • Home inspection contingency – Gives the buyer time to have the property thoroughly inspected and the right to cancel if major issues are found. • Appraisal contingency – Allows the buyer to back out if the home appraises for less than the offer price. • Loan contingency – Let the buyer walk away if they are unable to secure financing by a set date. • Sale contingency – Dependent on the buyer first selling their current home. [HEADING-H3] Why are buyers waiving contingencies? With housing inventory at record lows, buyers are getting desperate. By waiving contingencies, they hope to make their offer more appealing to sellers. This signals that the buyer is serious, financially secure, and willing to take on risk. Sellers often favour offers without contingencies because they seem less likely to fall through.  Source: Waiving  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/waiving-singapore/  (index: Waiving)

term: The Dangers of Waiving Contingencies
definition: While waiving contingencies can help your offer stand out, it also exposes you to significant financial risk: • Waiving the inspection contingency means you could be stuck with expensive hidden repairs or flaws. • Without an appraisal contingency, you risk overpaying if the home appraises for less than your offer. • Waiving loan and sale contingencies leaves you vulnerable if you ultimately can’t secure financing or sell your current home in time. • In a worst-case scenario, you could forfeit your earnest money deposit and have no home to move into. [HEADING-H3] How to Protect Yourself If you decide to waive contingencies, take steps to mitigate the risk: • Have the home thoroughly inspected before making an offer, so you are aware of any issues. • Build a cushion between your offer price and expected appraisal value. • Get pre-approved for a mortgage and have a backup plan if your current home doesn’t sell in time. • Negotiate an option period to address any deal-breaking problems that arise. Waiving contingencies is risky, but can help your offer stand out. Proceed with extreme caution, get professional guidance, and take steps to limit your exposure. With the right preparation, this gambit could pay off with your dream home.  Source: Waiving  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/waiving-singapore/  (index: Waiving)

term: zoning in Singapore
definition: Zoning is a concept in urban planning that refers to the division of a city into different areas, or “zones,” within which certain land uses are permitted or prohibited. In Singapore, the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) is the national urban planning authority responsible for zoning. The URA’s Master Plan guides the country’s development over the next 10 to 15 years, and this plan is reviewed every five years to ensure it stays responsive to changing needs.  Source: Zoning in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-zoning-in-singapore/  (index: Zoning in Singapore)

term: Factors affecting zoning and the application process in Singapore
definition: The zoning process in Singapore is affected by several factors, such as the current and future needs of the population, economic growth requirements, the availability of infrastructure, and environmental considerations. To apply for a zoning change, a proposal must be submitted via URA, detailing the proposed development and demonstrating its alignment with the Master Plan’s objectives.  Source: Zoning in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-zoning-in-singapore/  (index: Zoning in Singapore)

term: main difference between zoning and other planning terms
definition: Zoning is often compared with other planning terms. While zoning refers to the division of land into zones with specific uses, land use refers to the purpose for which land is used, such as residential, commercial, or industrial. Density refers to the number of units or people that can be accommodated within a certain area.  Source: Zoning in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-zoning-in-singapore/  (index: Zoning in Singapore)
aliases: What is the main difference between zoning and other planning terms

term: Advantages and disadvantages of zoning in Singapore
definition: Zoning has advantages and disadvantages. On the one hand, it helps to prevent conflicts by keeping incompatible land uses apart, allows for orderly urban development, and ensures the availability of necessary amenities and services. On the other side, zoning can limit land use flexibility, may not always be able to adapt to changing needs or trends, and may lead to the underutilization of land.  Source: Zoning in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-zoning-in-singapore/  (index: Zoning in Singapore)

term: Types of zoning in Singapore
definition: In Singapore, several types of zoning are outlined in the URA Master Plan, including Residential, Commercial, Business, Industry, and Special Use zones: • Residential with Commercial at 1st Storey: These zones are primarily used for residential development with commercial use at the 1st storey only. • Commercial & Residential: These zones are used mainly for mixed residential and commercial purposes. • Commercial: These areas are primarily used for commercial development. • White: These zones are used for a variety of uses including commercial, hotel, residential, sports & recreational, and other compatible uses, or a combination of these as a mixed-use development. • Business Park: These zones are primarily used for business park operations. • Business Park – White: These zones are used mainly for business park operations and uses permissible under the White zone as a mixed-use development. • Business 1 (B1): These zones are primarily used for clean industry, light industry, warehouse, public utilities, and telecommunication uses. • Business 2 (B2): These zones are intended for clean industry, light industry, general industry, warehouse, public utilities, and telecommunication uses. • Business 1 – White: These zones are used mainly for uses permissible under the B1 zone and the White zone as a mixed-use development. [HEADING-H3] Conclusion Understanding zoning is crucial for anyone involved in property development or investment in Singapore. It not only determines what can be built, but also influences property values and the potential for future development. term: Is there an income ceiling to purchase an Executive Condominium (EC)
definition: While private condominiums are generally available for individuals with the necessary financial means, ECs have additional requirements. Similar to the eligibility criteria for obtaining an HDB flat, you must meet one of the following schemes to qualify: At least one applicant must be a Singapore citizen, and one of the applicants must be at least 21 years old. term: What does HDB MOP eligibility mean
definition: HDB MOP is an abbreviation for HDB’s Minimum Occupation Period, which is a restriction that prohibits you from selling or renting out the entire apartment for the first few years after you move in (usually five years). You are also not permitted to purchase another private property during the MOP. The HDB MOP helps to deter homeowners from immediately “flipping” their freshly bought units for a profit. This policy is set in place to prevent the artificial inflation of public housing prices. It should be noted that the HDB MOP begins on the day you receive your keys and only covers the time you are staying in the unit.  Source: HDB MOP Eligibility  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/hdb-mop-eligibility/  (index: HDB MOP Eligibility)

term: process of HDB MOP eligibility
definition: You will be notified of the current Ethnic Integration Policy (EIP)/ Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) quota for your apartment after registering an Intent to Sell on the HDB Resale Portal. Through your Intent to Sell on the HDB Resale Portal or the EIP/ SPR quota e-Service, you can keep track of the monthly changes. Updated on the 1st of every month, the EIP/SPR quota will apply to finished resale applications* that are sent in within the same month. *A resale application is only complete when HDB gets the required supporting papers and both the buyers’ and sellers’ portions of the resale application. How does the EIP and SPR quota apply here? When selling an HDB apartment, the Ethnic Integration Policy (EIP) quota must be met. Non-Malaysian SPR families must also fulfil the SPR quota. You will be qualified to sell the HDB apartment considering the following; • The number of households belonging to your ethnicity continues to exist within the boundaries of your block and neighbourhood after the sale of your apartment. • The number of SPR households for non-Malaysian residents stays within the SPR quota. • You and the buyer share the same ethnicity and family citizenship.  Source: HDB MOP Eligibility  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/hdb-mop-eligibility/  (index: HDB MOP Eligibility)

term: Can I sell my flat despite the HDB MOP
definition: The following are some exemptions in situations involving bankruptcy, divorce, and other special cases: If selling your apartment and moving into a less expensive one will help you escape bankruptcy, HDB may allow you to do so. However, its process may vary for a Singaporean and a non-Singaporean; • Under the Housing and Development Act, if a Singapore Citizen is one of the owners of an HDB apartment, the sale of the flat does not require approval from the Official Assignee. • If none of the flat owners is a Singaporean citizen, they must first obtain approval from the Official Assignee before selling the apartment. Divorce is a major reason most individuals sell their HDB apartments before the MOP expires. In this instance, the parties can sell the property and split the revenues. For HDB to examine your application, you must submit the following documents: • A writ of judicial separation • Certificate of interim judgment as well as Certificate of Making Interim Judgment Final • If you are a Muslim, you will need a divorce certificate and a court of law’s decision. Aside from divorce and bankruptcy, the HDB also considers the following features when permitting you to sell your house early: • When a family’s sole breadwinner is unable to work due to disability or death, they may be permitted by HDB to sell their flats before the MOP expires. • In cases of a terminal illness. However, HDB will first assess your case. • When there is a loss or renouncement of citizenship. You may, for example, decide to relocate permanently to another country. In such cases, HDB may allow you to sell your home before the scheduled time and also retrieve your CPF funds. term: How many types of Notice of Assessment (NOA)

It is also used for advance tax assessments. • NOA Type 3 After successfully filing your company’s Form C and Form C-S, the IRAS prepares this type of notice. • NOA Type 4 This is the final notice after the IRAS conclusively assesses your company’s chargeable income and the corresponding tax amount. term: Avoid buyer’s remorse: A guide to navigating real estate due diligence
definition: Buying a home is one of the biggest financial decisions most people will ever make. While the process can be exciting, it can also lead to buyer’s remorse if you don’t take the proper precautions. Conducting thorough due diligence can help avoid regrets after closing on a property. This guide will walk you through the key steps of real estate due diligence so you can make an informed decision and avoid buyer’s remorse. [HEADING-H3] Research the property and neighbourhood Before making an offer, learn everything you can about the property, neighbourhood, and local market conditions. Drive by the home at different times of the day and walk around the area to get a feel for things like noise levels and pedestrian traffic. Check crime statistics for the neighbourhood. Research prices of recently sold comparable homes nearby to determine if the asking price is in line with the market. Look into future local developments that could impact property values. [HEADING-H3] Inspect the property thoroughly Schedule an in-depth home inspection by a licensed professional. Attend the inspection and ask questions. Ensure all major systems like the roof, foundation, electrical, plumbing, and HVAC are in good working order. Look for signs of water damage, pest infestation, poor renovations, structural issues, and other red flags. Get quotes to repair any problems discovered. [HEADING-H3] Review the seller disclosures Carefully examine the seller’s property condition disclosure statement detailing any known defects. Follow up on any issues mentioned that weren’t uncovered during the home inspection. Ensure potential problems are priced into your offer or will be addressed by the seller. [HEADING-H3] Assess your finances Get pre-approved for a mortgage so you know your budget before house hunting. Verify you can afford the monthly mortgage payments, property taxes, insurance, HOA fees, and maintenance costs. If purchasing in a new area, research the tax rates. Include moving expenses and expected near-term home repairs and upgrades in your budget. [HEADING-H3] Hire an attorney Retain an experienced real estate attorney to review the purchase contract before signing. They can help negotiate terms, navigate complex transactions, and ensure proper due diligence is conducted. Your attorney can also review title documents, CC&Rs, and other items that may impact the property. Conducting thorough due diligence takes time but is essential for making a confident home-buying decision. Following these steps will help avoid unwanted surprises and costly buyer’s remorse down the road. Do your homework so you can enjoy your new investment with peace of mind. term: A smart investor’s guide to navigating the ups and downs of real estate
definition: Real estate investing can offer substantial rewards, but it also involves significant risks. Successfully navigating the fluctuations of the real estate market requires a combination of knowledge, experience, and discipline. As the saying goes, “the greater the risk, the greater the reward.” However, savvy investors understand the importance of effectively managing risk to increase their chances of success. Thorough research is key: Before investing in any property or market, thorough research and understanding of associated risks are essential. Analyse historical trends in home prices and rental rates, employment trends, demographic data, zoning regulations, and other relevant factors. Identify markets with strong economic fundamentals and growth potential, paying attention to supply and demand dynamics. Informed decisions are crucial for success. Have an exit strategy: Having a clear plan to exit an investment if necessary is crucial. Set realistic goals for the duration of property ownership and expected returns. Understand your options for exiting, such as selling or refinancing. Regularly monitor your portfolio’s performance and be prepared to divest from underperforming assets without emotional attachment. Diversify your portfolio: Avoid putting all your resources into one type of property or market. Diversify across different property types (single-family, multifamily, commercial, etc.) and various geographic locations. This helps mitigate risks associated with downturns in any particular sector. Further diversification within markets, such as investing in neighbourhoods with different price points and demographics, is also beneficial. Maintain sufficient capital reserves: Avoid overextending financially across multiple properties. It’s crucial to have adequate cash reserves to cover unexpected expenses like repairs, vacancies, and property taxes. Lack of liquidity poses a significant risk to real estate investors. Aim to maintain at least six months’ worth of reserves for all properties to weather unforeseen circumstances. Invest in the right insurance policies: Insurance plays a vital role in protecting investments against potential losses. Landlord insurance is essential for rental properties, and other policies like title insurance and loss of income coverage for commercial assets provide additional protection. Regularly review and update your insurance policies to ensure adequate coverage. The real estate market is cyclical and inherently risky, but investors who manage risk wisely, maintain sufficient reserves, and diversify their portfolios can thrive across market cycles. Careful navigation of market fluctuations can lead to long-term profitability and success.  Source: Risk management  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/risk-management/  (index: Risk management)

term: Understanding CPI
definition: The CPI is derived by tracking price fluctuations for each item in a predetermined basket of goods and services, and then averaging them. These items are weighted based on their significance. Variations in the CPI are employed to evaluate price changes linked to the cost of living. The CPI plays several roles in Singapore’s economy. They include: Adjusting eligibility levels for certain types of government assistances and to automatically prove cost-of-living wage adjustments to numerous workers in Singapore.  Source: Consumer Price Index (CPI)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/decoding-the-consumer-price-index-cpi-in-real-estate/  (index: Consumer Price Index (CPI))

term: Importance of CPI in real estate
definition: The CPI includes a housing component, which tracks changes in rental and owner-occupied housing prices. Shifts in the housing segment of the CPI can offer insights into trends in Singapore’s property market, proving beneficial for property investors and homebuyers. The CPI impacts nearly all Singaporeans due to its extensive applications. Comprehending how the CPI is formulated and what it measures can aid in understanding the health of Singapore’s economy. Here’s a quick rundown of how CPI is formulated: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) in Singapore measures the average price changes of a fixed basket of goods and service commonly purchased by households. It’s rebased every year, with the latest base year being 2019, to reflect current consumption patterns. And here’s a quick rundown of how CPI’s measurements aid understanding of Singapore’s economy: Inflation measurement: The CPI is primarily used to measure inflation, which is the rate at which the general level of prices of goods and services is rising. A moderate level of inflation is a sign of healthy economy, including that the economy is growing. However, high inflation can erode purchasing power and may signal an overheating economy, while deflation (negative inflation) can be a sign of economic stagnation. Policy decisions: The government and the central bank use the CPI to formulate economic and monetary policies. For instance, if the CPI indicates high inflation, the central bank might raise interest rates to cool the economy. Conversely, if the CPI shows low inflation or deflation, the central bank might lower interest rates to stimulate economic activity. Cost of living adjustments: The CPI can be used to adjust salaries, pensions, and social security benefits to keep pace with the cost of living. This ensures that people’s income keeps up with inflation and maintains their purchasing power. Economic analysis: The CPI can help analyse the relative cost of living over time or compare the cost of living between different regions. It can also provide insights into consumer behaviour and changes in consumption patterns. Real value calculation: The CPI is used to calculate the real value of money, wages, and contracts. By adjusting for inflation, economists can compare the value of money in different time periods. [HEADING-H3] Conclusion The CPI is an invaluable instrument for discerning trends in Singapore’s property market. By monitoring changes in the housing component of the CPI, investors and homebuyers can gain insights into market conditions and make informed decisions. The CPI serves multiple roles in Singapore’s economy. It’s used as a macroeconomic indicator of inflation, as a tool by the government and the Monetary Authority of Singapore for inflation targeting, and as a deflator of the economy’s production value over time. It’s also used to adjust people’s eligibility levels for certain types of government assistance and to automatically provide cost-of-living wage adjustments to numerous workers in Singapore.  Source: Consumer Price Index (CPI)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/decoding-the-consumer-price-index-cpi-in-real-estate/  (index: Consumer Price Index (CPI))

term: Streamline real estate disputes with arbitration
definition: Buying or selling a home is often the largest financial transaction a person will make in their lifetime. While most real estate deals go smoothly, disputes can occasionally arise between buyers, sellers, agents, and other parties. When disagreements occur, arbitration can provide an efficient alternative to resolving real estate conflicts compared to lengthy court battles. This article explores using arbitration to streamline real estate disputes. [HEADING-H3] The benefits of arbitration Arbitration offers several advantages over traditional litigation when real estate deals go sour. First, arbitration is usually much faster than court cases, which routinely drag on for months or years. Arbitration hearings are typically scheduled within a few weeks or months of filing the claim. This allows all parties to resolve issues quickly and move forward. Arbitration is also less expensive than litigation. Attorney fees, expert witnesses, depositions, paperwork and other court costs can be staggering. Arbitration eliminates much of this financial burden through simpler procedures and rules of evidence. Further, arbitration provides a private, confidential process away from the public nature of courts. Real estate disputes often involve sensitive issues like finances, property conditions, contracts and more. The privacy of arbitration shields parties from airing dirty laundry in a public forum. [HEADING-H3] How arbitration works Arbitration involves hiring a neutral third-party arbitrator to resolve the real estate disagreement. All parties present evidence and make arguments at a hearing. The arbitrator then issues a binding decision to settle the matter. Parties in arbitration have flexibility in choosing the arbitrator and setting parameters like location, rules of evidence, and arbitration style. Arbitrators are often real estate attorneys familiar with typical property issues and disputes. Their expertise leads to fair, informed decisions the parties are obligated to follow. Arbitration is voluntary unless a prior agreement compels it. Many real estate contracts mandate arbitration for future conflicts. These provisions are generally enforceable. If arbitration is optional, parties must mutually agree to the process. Even without a contractual clause, arbitration still provides an efficient alternative to court when both sides are willing to participate. [HEADING-H3] Is arbitration right for you? Arbitration is not ideal for every scenario. Claims seeking to set broader legal precedents or enact social change may be better suited for court. The confidential nature of arbitration also precludes notifying other impacted parties like in a class action lawsuit. However, for most real estate disputes between the principal parties, arbitration offers a quicker, cheaper and more private route to resolve issues. If faced with a real estate disagreement, consider proposing arbitration as an effective way to streamline the process and get back to business. The simplicity, speed and cost savings of arbitration can be a “win-win” over the alternative of a draining court battle. Thoroughly weigh all options and consult qualified local counsel for guidance when evaluating the best path forward to resolve real estate conflicts.  Source: Arbitration  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/arbitration/  (index: Arbitration)

term: CPF
definition: The Central Provident Fund (CPF) is a comprehensive social security savings plan that plays a crucial role in Singapore’s real estate market. It provides working Singaporeans and permanent residents with the means to finance their home purchases.  Source: Central Provident Fund (CPF)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/central-provident-fund-cpf/  (index: Central Provident Fund (CPF))

term: Understanding CPF
definition: CPF is a mandatory savings scheme funded by contributions from employers and employees. The CPF Board, a statutory board under the Ministry of Manpower, administers the fund. The contributions go into three accounts: Ordinary Account (OA), Special Account (SA), and Medisave Account (MA), each serving different needs. The Ordinary Account is primarily used for housing, payment of home loans, investment, and education. This makes CPF a critical player in the real estate market, as it provides a source of financing for home purchases.  Source: Central Provident Fund (CPF)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/central-provident-fund-cpf/  (index: Central Provident Fund (CPF))

term: Importance of CPF in Real Estate
definition: CPF plays a critical role in the real estate market as it provides a source of financing for home purchases. It allows Singaporeans to leverage their savings for property investment, which can be a significant step towards financial security. Furthermore, the use of CPF for housing purposes is encouraged by the government, with various schemes and grants available to assist homeowners. The CPF system is designed to help Singaporeans save for their retirement in a disciplined and structured manner. It also provides a safety net for Singaporeans, ensuring that they have the necessary funds for healthcare and housing, which are two of the most significant expenses for most households. [HEADING-H3] Conclusion Understanding the role of CPF in Singapore’s real estate market is essential for both homebuyers and investors. It not only provides a source of financing for property purchases but also offers a pathway towards financial security and wealth accumulation. The CPF system has been praised for its role in providing financial security for Singaporeans. However, it has also been criticised for its complexity and for the restrictions it places on how individuals can use their savings. Despite these criticisms, the CPF remains a crucial part of Singapore’s social security system. term: Notarisation
definition: The notary then stamps the documents with their official seal and signature, essentially verifying the authenticity of the signing. This prevents fraud such as forgery or impersonation and provides legal proof that the documents were properly executed should any disputes arise later.  Source: Notarisation  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/notarisation/  (index: Notarisation)

term: Key documents to notarise
definition: During a real estate transaction, there are a few key documents that should always be notarised: • Deeds: This transfers legal ownership of the property from the seller to the buyer and must be signed by both parties and notarised. • Mortgages: The mortgage contract pledging the home as collateral for the loan needs to be notarised, as required by lenders to verify identities. • Affidavits: These legally binding statements declaring facts are often required. For example, an affidavit stating the seller has not conducted commercial activity on the property. • Powers of Attorney: If someone is signing on behalf of another person, the POA form giving them legal authority must be notarised. Notaries are also available to notarise other supporting documents like real estate closing statements.  Source: Notarisation  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/notarisation/  (index: Notarisation)

term: The consequences of skipping notarisation
definition: Attempting to cut corners by skipping notarisation can cause major headaches down the road. Here are some potential consequences: • Documents can be rendered invalid without a notary seal, which may not meet legal standards, potentially delaying or derailing the entire transaction. • Issues proving identity or authenticity may arise, as disputing parties can more easily claim forms were forged or signed under false pretences, leading to lengthy legal battles. • Difficulty verifying documents may occur as lenders may refuse to accept non-notarised mortgage contracts, and title companies may also reject deeds and affidavits. • No backup if fraud occurs, as the third-party verification offered by notarisation provides additional fraud protection. Skipping it removes a key safeguard. Clearly, notarisation plays a pivotal role in real estate deals. Taking the time to have documents notarised properly can prevent legal headaches and liability down the road. Protect your interests and investment by ensuring notarisation is never overlooked.  Source: Notarisation  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/notarisation/  (index: Notarisation)

term: HDB resale levy
definition: The HDB resale levy is a fixed sum that HDB requires flat owners to pay upon selling their first HDB flat or receiving the keys to their second HDB unit, whichever comes later. The amount payable may differ depending on the flat type they previously owned. The levy is interest-free.  Source: HDB resale levy  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/hdb-resale-levy/  (index: HDB resale levy)

term: purpose of the HDB resale levy
definition: The purpose of the resale levy is to ensure equal distribution of public subsidies between first-time buyers and existing homeowners who have already bought subsidised flats. The levy also helps prioritise the allocation of grants to groups that need them the most, such as first-timer families looking to purchase an HDB flat to start and nurture their growing household.  Source: HDB resale levy  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/hdb-resale-levy/  (index: HDB resale levy)

term: Do I need to pay for an HDB resale levy
definition: If you purchase a subsidised housing unit and later decide to purchase a second subsidised flat, you will need to pay a resale levy. A subsidised housing unit is defined as; • A flat obtained from HDB • A resale flat obtained with the CPF housing grant • A Design Build and Sell Scheme (DBSS) flat purchased from a property developer • An Executive Condominium (EC) unit bought from a property developer • Or other types of housing subsidies, such as benefits obtained through the Selective En bloc Redevelopment Scheme (SERS) or privatisation of HUDC estate However, if you do not have the intention to purchase a second subsidised flat from HDB, such as a resale flat or private residential property, you don’t need to pay the resale levy.  Source: HDB resale levy  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/hdb-resale-levy/  (index: HDB resale levy)

term: How much money do I need to spend on the HDB resale levy
definition: The resale levy amount depends on the type of subsidised flat you previously had and whether you used the singles grant. Note that the resale levy is always halved for those who bought their previous flat using the singles grant: • 2-room flat: S$15,000 (S$7,500 if you used singles grant) • 3-room flat: S$30,000 (S$15,000 if you used singles grant) • 4-room flat: S$40,000 (S$20,000 if you used singles grant) • 5-room flat: S$45,000 (S$22,500 if you used singles grant) • Executive flat: S$50,000 (S$25,000 if you used singles grant) • EC: S$55,000 (singles grant is not applicable for this type of property) Note that the above rates have applied since 3rd March 2006. Before this date, the resale levy was quite different – it was previously based on a percentage of the resale price, or 90% of the valuation, whichever was lower. HDB removed the old system because it caused uncertainty in the resale levy amount. For a closer look at the figures and how much you need to spend if you sell your HDB before the stipulated date, head over to the Housing and Development Board website here.  Source: HDB resale levy  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/hdb-resale-levy/  (index: HDB resale levy)

term: Does the HDB resale levy apply to senior citizens
definition: Starting in 2015, elderly second-time buyers who are interested in moving to a 2-room Flexi flat have been exempted by HDB from paying the interest accumulated on the resale levy.  Source: HDB resale levy  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/hdb-resale-levy/  (index: HDB resale levy)

term: How do I pay for the HDB resale levy
definition: The resale levy amount is determined only when you secure your second subsidised unit Payment for the levy can only be made in cash or through the sale proceeds of your first flat, as it cannot be paid using your home loan or CPF funds. If you sell your first flat after receiving the keys to your second one, the resale levy will be deducted from the sale proceeds, and any outstanding balance must be settled in cash. However, if you sell your first flat before receiving the keys to the second subsidised unit, the resale levy needs to be paid in cash upon key collection. term: How does condemnation in Singapore real estate work

The Land Acquisitions Act in Singapore enables the government to implement selective en bloc redevelopment schemes for urban renewal, which may entail acquiring private property for public infrastructure, transportation, or other public projects. The process of condemnation or eminent domain is governed by specific laws and regulations to ensure equitable compensation for property owners facing the loss of their property. term: Navigating the condemnation process – What homeowners need to know
definition: Discovering that your home has been condemned or labelled as “unfit for habitation” can be an overwhelming and perplexing situation. This scenario unfolds when a city inspector deems a property hazardous and uninhabitable due to violations of building codes or safety concerns. If you receive a condemnation notice, it is crucial to grasp the legal process and take prompt action to address the situation. The initial step involves examining the inspector’s report to understand the reasons behind the condemnation of your home. Common issues include faulty wiring, leaky roofs, deteriorating foundations, pest infestations, and more. The report should outline specific violations that render the home unsafe, and depending on the severity of the problems, you might be required to vacate the premises immediately. Following this, seeking guidance from professionals becomes essential to assess if the issues can be rectified. Hiring a licensed contractor to provide a detailed estimate for all necessary repairs is advisable. Additionally, consulting with an attorney can help you understand the legal process and your rights as a homeowner. In some cases, you may need to request an extension or a stay of condemnation from the city to allow sufficient time for repairs. To lift the condemnation order, it is imperative to address all violations mentioned in the inspector’s report. Your contractor will need to obtain necessary permits, complete repairs up to code, and arrange for a re-inspection of the property. Maintaining open communication with the city inspector throughout this process is important, as they will conduct a final walkthrough to ensure that all unsafe conditions have been properly rectified before deeming the home habitable again. If repairing the issues proves unfeasible due to high costs or other factors, you may have to explore options such as selling the condemned home “as is” or considering demolition. Consulting with your real estate agent and attorney is crucial to understanding available options. Additionally, you can request a hearing to appeal the condemnation order, but you will need evidence demonstrating that your home is safe and compliant with building codes. While having your home condemned can be highly stressful, taking swift action, understanding your rights, enlisting professional help, and making necessary repairs can lead to the lifting of the order, making your home safe and habitable once again. With concerted effort, you can successfully address the issues and move forward.  Source: Condemnation  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/condemnation/  (index: Condemnation)

REIB offers intellectually stimulating work and typically commands higher compensation compared to many other roles within the real estate sector. term: liquidity
definition: Liquidity refers to how easily and smoothly an asset or financial instrument can be turned into readily available funds without causing any impact on its market value. The most straightforward example of this is cash itself. The extent of an asset’s liquidity plays a key role in defining how easily and effectively it can be changed into cash. Assets with lower liquidity require more time and could potentially come with higher associated costs.  Source: Liquidity  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/liquidity/  (index: Liquidity)

term: liquidity risk in real estate
definition: Liquidity risk’s emergence signals the potential necessity for individuals to sell assets at discounted rates to raise essential funds. Within the expansive realm of real estate, whether one is leasing an apartment or owning a house, many financial obligations weigh on both tenants and property owners. These financial commitments encompass a spectrum of expenses, ranging from rentals and mortgages to insurance premiums and warranty agreements, among others. Liquidity risk becomes a prominent concern when homeowners struggle to manage their mortgage payments. Such a scenario often unfolds when individuals no longer possess the financial capacity to cover rent or service debt due to adverse circumstances like job loss. Consequently, they find themselves in a position where relinquishing their property at a reduced value becomes necessary.  Source: Liquidity  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/liquidity/  (index: Liquidity)
aliases: What is liquidity risk in real estate?

term: What factors influence liquidity in real estate
definition: In the context of real estate, liquidity takes on a unique perspective. Unlike stocks or bonds, properties are tangible assets, often with a slower turnover rate. Various factors influence the liquidity of real estate, including: • Market conditions: The state of the real estate market, whether it’s a buyer’s or a seller’s market, impacts the liquidity of properties. In a hot seller’s market, properties sell quickly due to high demand, enhancing liquidity. Conversely, in a buyer’s market, properties may stay on the market longer, reducing liquidity. • Location: The location of a property significantly affects its liquidity. Properties in prime, desirable locations with good infrastructure and amenities tend to have higher liquidity. These properties attract a larger pool of potential buyers, facilitating quicker sales. • Property type: The type of property also plays a role in liquidity. Residential properties are generally more liquid than commercial properties due to the broader base of potential buyers, including homeowners and investors. • Property condition: Well-maintained properties are more likely to attract buyers quickly, enhancing their liquidity. Properties in disrepair might have a limited pool of interested buyers, leading to lower liquidity. • Economic factors: Economic conditions, such as interest rates and job market stability, influence buyer sentiment and, consequently, the liquidity of real estate. Favourable economic conditions can spur demand and improve liquidity.  Source: Liquidity  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/liquidity/  (index: Liquidity)

term: How to quickly liquidate your real estate assets
definition: Real estate can serve as a lucrative investment opportunity; however, certain situations may necessitate the quick liquidation of these assets. Whether you require capital for a new venture or are encountering financial constraints, there exist strategies to expedite the sale of properties without significant loss in value. This guide outlines six proven methods for converting real estate into cash promptly. • Lowering the price: One direct approach to achieving a swift sale involves reducing the asking price well below the market value. This action generates interest and motivates potential buyers to act swiftly. Establish a minimum acceptable sale price and decrease the original asking price by 15-20%. Be prepared to engage in negotiations, as accepting a lower offer is preferable to enduring a prolonged listing period. • Lease with Option to Buy: Also referred to as a rent-to-own agreement, this arrangement allows a tenant to lease the property with the option to purchase it within a specified timeframe. While earning rental income, you can market the property for sale to the tenant. Set a purchase price, with a portion of the rent credited towards the eventual down payment. In the event the tenant is unable to buy, you regain control to pursue a traditional house sale. • Home Equity Line of Credit (HELOC): A HELOC enables you to access funds by leveraging the equity in your property as collateral. Unlike selling the home, HELOCs involve repaying the funds over time. Keep in mind that HELOCs feature variable interest rates, making them a short-term solution. Utilise HELOC funds to address immediate financial needs while allowing time to sell the property. • Hard money loans: Hard money lenders offer short-term loans secured by the property, with less stringent qualifications compared to traditional banks. Although hard money loans come with high interest rates and fees, they provide swift access to capital. This option can bridge urgent financial needs while allowing you to manage the sale according to your timeline. Repay the loan upon selling the home. Disclaimer: Before implementing any of the strategies outlined above, it’s essential to consult with financial and real estate professionals to assess your unique situation and determine the most suitable course of action.  Source: Liquidity  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/liquidity/  (index: Liquidity)

term: a reverse mortgage
definition: In a reverse mortgage, elderly individuals who have fully paid off their mortgages can approach a bank to borrow money against the value of their homes. However, the amount they can borrow is limited by a lower Loan-to-Value ratio (LTV) compared to a traditional mortgage. This type of financing allows borrowers to access some immediate cash based on their property’s value, but it comes with the requirement to pay interest, typically through the eventual sale of the house.  Source: Reverse mortgage  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/reverse-mortgage/  (index: Reverse mortgage)

term: What type of reverse mortgage is available in Singapore
definition: DBS has partnered with Singapore’s Central Provident Fund (CPF) to assist elderly individuals in accessing equity in their private homes while continuing to reside in them. Singaporeans and permanent residents between the ages of 65 and 79, who own and live in fully paid private properties, can apply for the Home Equity Income Loan (EIL) to add funds to their CPF retirement savings. The borrowed amount is then utilised to increase the monthly payouts received for life through CPF Life. This is achieved by making a lump sum contribution to the individual’s CPF retirement account. These customers can then request an adjustment to their monthly CPF Life payouts through the CPF Board. The loan duration can be up to 30 years, provided the property has a remaining lease of at least 30 years when the loan reaches maturity. The lump sum repayment is made only at the end of the loan term. Customers also have the option to sell their property at any time and repay the loan without incurring any penalty fees.  Source: Reverse mortgage  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/reverse-mortgage/  (index: Reverse mortgage)

term: What measures are in place to ensure the protection of borrowers’ interests
definition: If the value of the property decreases during the loan period, borrowers are not obliged to make any payments to reduce the remaining loan amount as long as there are no triggering events that lead to early termination of the loan. In the event of early loan termination, such as the borrower’s passing away or outliving the loan, DBS assures that they will not repossess the property immediately. Instead, they will explore all other mutually acceptable options with the borrower or their estate. Seniors who exceed the loan tenure or individuals who inherit property under a reverse mortgage have the opportunity to consider alternative methods of repaying the loan before the bank takes back the property. To be eligible for the loan, borrowers must possess or establish a Lasting Power of Attorney. This legally binding document allows the borrower to designate one or more individuals who can make decisions and act on their behalf if they lose mental capacity. This provision safeguards their interests and ensures appropriate decision-making in case they become incapable of doing so independently.  Source: Reverse mortgage  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/reverse-mortgage/  (index: Reverse mortgage)

term: Pro rata
definition: You’ve probably come across the term “pro rata” in business, finance, or even daily life. It comes from Latin and means “in proportion.” Essentially, pro rata is a way of fairly distributing something based on each party’s share of the total. It ensures that everyone gets their fair portion depending on their contribution, ownership, or time. This method is widely used in various industries to allocate costs, benefits, or payments in a proportionate manner.  Source: Pro rata  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/pro-rata/  (index: Pro rata)

term: How does Pro rata work
definition: Pro rata works by assigning amounts based on ownership, usage, or time worked. This approach ensures fairness, especially when dividing costs or payments. Here are some common ways pro rata is used: • Finance: Shareholders receive dividends based on how many shares they own. • Insurance: Premiums are prorated when coverage lasts for only part of a term. • Retirement accounts: Withdrawals are divided into taxable and non-taxable portions based on the ratio of contributions. • Employment: When an employee leaves before the year ends, their bonus is adjusted based on the time they worked.  Source: Pro rata  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/pro-rata/  (index: Pro rata)

term: How to calculate pro rata
definition: To calculate pro rata, you use a simple formula: • Pro rata share = (Number of true items / Maximum quantity possible) • Pro rata distribution = Pro rata share × Quantity of related item For example, imagine you’re eligible for an annual bonus of S$12,000 but leave your job on April 15. You worked 105 days out of 365. • Pro rata share = 105 / 365 = 28.77% • Bonus earned = 28.77% × $12,000 = S$3,452.88 This method ensures that you receive only the portion you’ve earned based on the time you worked.  Source: Pro rata  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/pro-rata/  (index: Pro rata)

term: Does pro rata work
definition: Yes! Pro rata applies proportional logic to various calculations. It relies on the principle that two fractions must be equal. For instance, if two people split a pizza with four slices, each gets 2 out of 4 slices – maintaining the 50% proportion. The same logic applies when prorating payments, premiums, or bonuses.  Source: Pro rata  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/pro-rata/  (index: Pro rata)

term: Practical applications – Examples of pro rata in various fields
definition: Shareholders receive dividends based on the number of shares they own. Example: • A company distributes S$500 in total dividends with 200 shares outstanding. • Shareholders with 80, 60, 40, and 20 shares receive S$200, S$150, S$100, and S$50, respectively. If you need insurance for less than a full term, your premium is adjusted accordingly. Example: • A S$1,200 annual insurance policy is needed for 240 days. • Pro rata premium = (S$1,200 / 365) × 240 = S$787.67. Interest for partial periods is calculated using a pro rata basis. Example: • A 12% annual interest rate applied over three months: • (12% / 12) × 3 = 3% interest. When selling a bond before the next coupon payment, the interest owed is prorated. Formula: Accrued Interest = Face Value × Coupon Rate × (Days Since Last Payment / Days in Payment Period). Example: • A S$2,000 bond with a 6% coupon rate is sold on July 1. • Buyer pays seller S$19.78 in accrued interest. term: a Mill levy
definition: A mill levy is a property tax assessed on real estate. It’s calculated by taking the total property tax revenue needed and dividing it by the taxable value of all properties. This determines the tax rate per $1,000 of a property’s assessed value, also known as the mill rate. For example, say a county needs $10 million in property taxes. The total assessed value of all properties is $1 billion. Dividing $10 million by $1 billion equals 0.01. This means the mill levy would be 10 mills, or $10 per $1,000 of assessed value. A high mill levy means you’ll pay more in property taxes, while a lower mill levy results in lower taxes.  Source: Mill levy  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/mill-levy/  (index: Mill levy)

term: Are mill levies used in Singapore property tax
definition: In Singapore’s property tax framework, mill levies are not explicitly utilised. Instead, property tax rates are computed based on the Annual Value (AV) of the property and the prevailing property tax rate. The AV is established through rental transactions of similar properties, ensuring consistent property tax assessment for owners. Subsequently, the property tax due is determined by multiplying the AV by the specific property tax rate relevant to the property’s classification, whether residential or non-residential. Hence, although mill levies are not directly incorporated into Singapore’s property tax structure, the calculation methodology revolves around the property’s AV and the corresponding tax rates based on its classification.  Source: Mill levy  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/mill-levy/  (index: Mill levy)

term: How do Mill levies impact homebuyers
definition: For prospective homebuyers, the mill levy directly affects affordability. Property taxes are bundled into your monthly mortgage payment along with principal, interest, and insurance. The higher the mill levy, the larger your total monthly payment. Here’s an example: House A is in a district with a mill levy of 40 mills. The home’s assessed value is $300,000, so the annual property tax would be: 40 mills x ($300,000 / $1,000) = $12,000 House B has the same assessed value, but the mill levy is just 20 mills. The annual property tax would be: 20 mills x ($300,000 / $1,000) = $6,000 With House A, your monthly mortgage payment would need to cover an extra $500 per month in taxes compared to House B. That adds up quickly over the life of a 30-year loan.  Source: Mill levy  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/mill-levy/  (index: Mill levy)

term: How to calculate Mill levies
definition: When viewing listings and attending open houses, ask the real estate agent for the property’s mill levy rate. If it’s not readily available, you can look it up on your county assessor’s website by searching the property address. It’s also smart to calculate the actual dollar amount by multiplying the mill levy and assessed value. This gives you the real financial impact rather than just looking at the rate alone. In addition, compare mill levies across neighbourhoods you’re considering. There can be significant variance even within a few miles. This will help you determine the most affordable areas. term: a Joint Singles Scheme (JSS)
definition: The Joint Singles Scheme (JSS) was introduced in 1990 by Singapore’s Housing and Development Board (HDB) as a unique housing solution for single Singaporean individuals. This scheme allows single men and women aged 35 to jointly purchase or rent an HDB flat, regardless of their relationship or gender. The primary objective of the JSS is to cater to the housing needs of low-income Singaporeans, especially those who require public rental flats. By allowing singles to share a flat, HDB can optimise utilising its limited resources and accommodate more individuals within the public housing system. Apart from the practical advantage of housing affordability, the JSS also addresses the social aspect of living arrangements, promoting companionship and mutual support, particularly for older tenants who may benefit from living with like-minded individuals.  Source: Joint Singles Scheme (JSS)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/joint-singles-scheme-jss/  (index: Joint Singles Scheme (JSS))
