term: eligibility requirements of a Joint Singles Scheme (JSS)
definition: To be eligible for the JSS, certain requirements must be met: • Both you and your proposed applicant(s) must be Singapore citizens (SCs). • You and your proposed applicant(s) must fall into one of the following categories: Single and at least 35 years old. Divorced or legally separated, and at least 35 years old. Widowed or orphaned, and at least 21 years old. • Single and at least 35 years old. • Divorced or legally separated, and at least 35 years old. • Widowed or orphaned, and at least 21 years old. The additional criteria considered for this scheme are as follows: • Income Your income plays a role in determining your housing budget and options. Applications are reviewed comprehensively, taking into consideration factors such as household size and individual circumstances. While most applicants have a household income below S$1,500, you can still apply if your income exceeds this amount. • Property ownership None of the individuals included in your application should have any ownership, interest, or estate in any type of property, whether local or overseas, residential or non-residential. If you previously owned property, the proceeds from its sale will be considered when assessing your housing budget. • Existing HDB residents None of the individuals in your application should be owners or essential occupants of an HDB flat. Individuals currently participating in HDB’s rental schemes are not eligible as well. • Family support If any of your children are capable of accommodating you in their home or are financially able to provide housing for you (e.g., through renting in the open market), you will not be eligible. Note that family support will be assessed for all individuals included in your application. term: Singapore MRT Ticketing and Payment System
definition: Singapore’s MRT system provides multiple ticketing options to fulfill the needs of different types of commuters, whether you’re a frequent traveler or a tourist exploring the city.  The ticket options include: 1. Standard Ticket: Designed for single or return trips, the Standard Ticket is best for occasional riders or tourists who may not require a reusable card. Where to buy: These tickets can be purchased from ticketing machines at any MRT station. Simply select your destination, pay the fare, and the machine will dispense your ticket. Usage: The ticket is valid for one journey (or two if it’s a return ticket) and must be tapped on the card reader at the entry and exit gates. 2. EZ-Link Card: A reusable smart card ideal for regular commuters. It offers lower fares compared to Standard Tickets and allows for seamless transfers between buses and trains. Where to buy: EZ-Link cards can be purchased and topped up at: a) MRT station ticket offices b) Passenger Service Centres c) Convenience stores like 7-Eleven or Cheers for a small convenience fee d) EZ-Link kiosks located at various public locations Usage: Tap the card on the reader at the entry and exit gates. The fare is automatically deducted based on the distance traveled. 3. Singapore Tourist Pass: A special pass for tourists that offers unlimited rides on MRT and buses for a fixed period (1, 2, or 3 days). Where to get: Available at TransitLink Ticket Offices located at major MRT stations, including Changi Airport, Orchard stations, and City Hall. Benefits: Ideal option for visitors looking to explore the city without worrying about topping up fares. 4. Contactless payment options: Commuters can use credit or debit cards with contactless payment features (e.g., Visa PayWave, Mastercard PayPass) or mobile payment platforms like Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Samsung Pay for quick and easy access. How to use: Tap your card or device on the card reader at the gates. Fares are charged directly to your bank account. [HEADING-H3] Essential Tips for Using MRT: – Always check the balance on your EZ-Link card or ensure sufficient funds on your contactless payment card before boarding. – For Standard Tickets, keep the ticket intact until the end of your journey, as you’ll need it to exit the system. – Consider the Singapore Tourist Pass if you plan to use public transport extensively during your visit. term: custodians in Singapore real estate
definition: Property custodians within the Singapore real estate sector are individuals or organisations tasked with overseeing and managing properties for owners or stakeholders. Their primary responsibility lies in upholding the maintenance, security, and adherence to regulations concerning real estate assets. Property custodians typically provide a variety of services, such as property upkeep, repairs, cleaning, and ensuring regulatory compliance. These custodial duties are invaluable for property owners who lack the necessary time, knowledge, or resources to efficiently manage their properties. Moreover, property custodians play a pivotal role in preserving the value of real estate assets by ensuring they remain well-maintained and secure. term: Why are property custodians critical to real estate success
definition: When it comes to managing and maintaining real estate properties, property custodians play a vital yet often overlooked role. Though their duties may seem simple on the surface – cleaning, landscaping, maintenance – custodians are absolutely essential to the day-to-day functioning and long-term success of any property. While brokers, property managers, and investors may get most of the glory, custodians are the unsung heroes that keep things running smoothly behind the scenes. Here’s a closer look at why they’re so critical to real estate success: One of the custodian’s most important jobs is maintaining the exterior appearance of a property. This curb appeal is enormously important for attracting prospective tenants or buyers. A clean, neatly landscaped, and well-maintained exterior conveys that the interior space will be equally well cared for. Custodians ensure the grounds are regularly mowed, trimmed, and weeded. They also properly maintain building exteriors by pressure washing, painting, and conducting routine inspections for needed repairs. Inside a property, custodians handle all the fundamental cleaning duties – sweeping, mopping, dusting, window washing, and sanitising. They thoroughly clean vacant units to prepare them for new occupants. For occupied spaces, custodians provide routine cleanings of common areas. Their diligent work maintains cleanliness and prevents buildup of grime or damage that could lower a property’s value. Ensuring a high standard of cleanliness also reduces tenant complaints and turnover. In addition to cleaning tasks, property custodians conduct preventative maintenance by routinely inspecting properties. Checking for potential issues like leaks, faulty equipment, weathering, or damage allows problems to be addressed promptly before they worsen. Whether it’s replacing air filters, greasing door hinges, checking smoke detectors, or servicing appliances, custodians handle a wide range of basic maintenance duties that keep properties in reliable working order. Custodians ensure properties remain safe and accessible. They also maintain security by locking gates, repairing fences, and reporting any suspicious activity. Having a regular custodial presence deters crime and gives occupants peace of mind. The preventative maintenance and diligent care provided by custodians preserves the structural and aesthetic integrity of properties. By promptly fixing minor issues before they escalate and keeping everything clean and orderly, custodians help extend the usable lifespan of buildings and equipment. This maximises owners’ return on investment. Though their individual contributions may seem minor, custodians collectively play an enormous role in upholding real estate investments. Their unrelenting hard work improves safety, satisfaction, and ultimately, the bottom line. While investors and managers may handle the big strategic picture, custodians provide the hands-on diligence needed to turn their vision into reality. term: Are there any penalties on late payment of property tax

term: Application for subletting of HDB leased land
definition: Subletting HDB leased land in Singapore means renting out HDB properties, or parts of them, to other people. Strict rules govern this practice to ensure public housing goals are achieved and a peaceful living environment is maintained.  Source: HDB lease land subletting  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/hdb-lease-land-subletting/  (index: HDB lease land subletting)

term: Understanding HDB leased land
definition: HDB flats in Singapore are constructed on land leased from the government for a 99-year period. Though HDB flat owners may live in and use their flats, the government still owns the land they’re built on. This leasehold agreement sets specific limitations and responsibilities for owners, particularly with subletting.  Source: HDB lease land subletting  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/hdb-lease-land-subletting/  (index: HDB lease land subletting)

term: Eligibility criteria for subletting
definition: Before considering subletting, flat owners must meet specific eligibility conditions: • Citizenship: Only Singapore Citizens may sublet their entire HDB flat. Singapore Permanent Residents may not do so. • Minimum Occupation Period (MOP): Owners must have occupied their flat for at least five years before applying to sublet the whole unit. • Flat type: Owners of 3-room or larger flats can rent out spare bedrooms, provided they continue to live in the flat during the rental period.  Source: HDB lease land subletting  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/hdb-lease-land-subletting/  (index: HDB lease land subletting)

term: Regulations and conditions
definition: Several regulations govern the subletting of HDB flats: • Rental period: The minimum rental period is six months per application. The maximum is three years if all tenants are Singaporeans or Malaysians, and two years if any tenant is a non-Malaysian non-citizen. • Occupancy cap: To prevent overcrowding, there are limits on the number of occupants: 1-room and 2-room flats: Maximum of four occupants. 3-room flats: Maximum of six occupants. 4-room and larger flats: Maximum of eight occupants. • 1-room and 2-room flats: Maximum of four occupants. • 3-room flats: Maximum of six occupants. • 4-room and larger flats: Maximum of eight occupants. • Non-Citizen Quota: To maintain a balanced ethnic mix, there is a Non-Citizen Quota for renting out flats. If the quota is reached in a neighbourhood or block, only Singaporeans and Malaysians can rent flats there. This quota does not apply to the renting out of bedrooms.  Source: HDB lease land subletting  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/hdb-lease-land-subletting/  (index: HDB lease land subletting)

term: Responsibilities of flat owners
definition: Owners who sublet their flats have specific responsibilities: • Ensure tenant eligibility: Verify that tenants are legally living in Singapore and possess valid passes. • Compliance with regulations: Ensure that tenants adhere to all HDB regulations and do not engage in unauthorised activities. • Inform HDB of changes: Notify HDB of any changes in tenancy, including renewals or terminations, within seven days. • Maintain the flat: Ensure that the flat is well-maintained and that tenants do not cause disturbances to the neighbourhood.  Source: HDB lease land subletting  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/hdb-lease-land-subletting/  (index: HDB lease land subletting)

term: Consequences of non-compliance
definition: Failure to adhere to HDB’s subletting regulations can cause serious consequences: • Financial penalties: Owners may be fined for unauthorised subletting or breaches of regulations. • Repossession of flat: In severe cases, HDB may compulsorily gain the flat. • Legal action: Owners may face legal proceedings under the Housing & Development Act. Renting out a portion of your HDB leased land allows flat owners to generate income and have more flexibility. It is crucial to follow HDB regulations closely to ensure compliance and protect the quality of public housing in Singapore. term: forfeiture
definition: In cases where a tenant violates the terms of the tenancy agreement, such as by failing to pay rent, the landlord has the option to forfeit the tenancy and regain possession of the property to evict the tenants.  Source: Forfeiture  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/forfeiture/  (index: Forfeiture)

term: How does forfeiture work
definition: Forfeiture entails the landlord either peacefully entering the premises or seeking legal recourse through court proceedings to regain possession. Generally, forfeiture is only considered if the tenant consistently fails to pay rent despite being given opportunities to do so. To re-enter the premises, the landlord must formally demand that the tenant vacates. If the tenant refuses, the landlord typically engages a solicitor to initiate legal proceedings for possession by issuing an originating claim. For the landlord to proceed with forfeiture, the tenancy agreement must explicitly stipulate a right of re-entry. Additionally, the landlord must serve a notice under section 18 of the Conveyancing and Law of Property Act, specifying the breach, the compensation sought, and the remedy expected from the tenant. However, tenants can seek relief against forfeiture by applying to the court. Considering forfeiture as a severe remedy, the court usually grants the tenant an additional reasonable time of 4 weeks to pay the rent before any action is taken. The information provided was accurate at the time of publication. For the latest changes and updates, head over to the official websites. term: Home Improvement Program (HIP)
definition: The Home Improvement Programme (HIP) aims at renovating flats constructed prior to 1997. This includes addressing common issues like broken pipes and cracked walls. HDB HIP makes the process of fixing these problems easier for residents by carrying out the renovations in a systematic way. This means residents will experience less inconvenience during the upgrading process. In addition to improving the safety and livability of your HDB flat, HIP can also improve its value over time.  Source: Home Improvement Program (HIP)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/home-improvement-program-hip/  (index: Home Improvement Program (HIP))
aliases: What is Home Improvement Program (HIP)?|Home Improvement Program|HIP

term: What types of work are included in the Home Improvement Programme (HIP)
definition: The following are three types of upgrades under the HIP, including; This category covers compulsory upgrades and repairs implemented to ensure public health, safety, and technical purposes. • Fixing structural cracks and spalling concrete • Substituting waste or soil discharge stacks (The pipes will be replaced if they are made of cast iron, a mix of cast iron and UPVC, or if they are UPVC and there are leaks and cracks) • Replacing pipe sockets with new clothes drying racks • Upgrading electrical load (this improvement will be done if required, after the completion of HIP works) These upgrades are available to all HDB flat owners. If you are a Singapore Citizen, the government will pay for all of the upgrades under this category. However, if you are a Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR), you will need to pay for the full cost of these upgrades. You can choose to have additional improvements done to your flat under the Optional Improvements category. As such, you will only need to pay for your share of the cost of the improvements you choose. These additional improvements include: • Upgrading your existing toilet or bathroom • Installing a new entrance door or grille gate • Getting a new refuse chute hopper, if necessary If you choose to opt out of upgrading your toilet or bathroom, it must first pass a water test for leaks to prevent ceiling leaks in the flat below. You can also choose between a fire-rated or non-fire-rated main door, depending on whether your flat requires one based on SCDF’s Fire Code. If your flat does not require a fire-rated door, you can opt for the non-fire-rated door provided under HIP. HDB has recently updated its HIP package to include more contemporary and better-quality items such as an external retractable clothes drying rack. These new items apply to HIP projects polled after March 2020. EASE was introduced as an optional improvement to make HDB flats safer and more comfortable for senior citizens. You can choose from the following options based on your needs: • Slip-resistant treatment for floor tiles in two toilets/bathrooms • Grab bars in two toilets/bathrooms (available in white or reddish brown) • Ramps to address level differences within the flat and at the main entrance (where technically feasible and compliant with authorities’ requirements) If your flat has a single-step entrance, up to four single-step ramps will be offered within the flat, and a single-step ramp will be provided as a default option at the main entrance. If your flat has a multi-step entrance, you can choose from a portable ramp, a customised ramp for 2 to 3 steps, customised ramp for more than 3 steps, or a wheelchair lifter.  Source: Home Improvement Program (HIP)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/home-improvement-program-hip/  (index: Home Improvement Program (HIP))

term: Do I need to pay for the Home Improvement Program (HIP)
definition: Payment for the HIP may be different for Singapore Citizens, SPR, and senior citizens. Here is the detailed information about HIP payment in Singapore for different kinds of citizens: As mentioned previously, if you’re a Singapore Citizen, the government will fully cover the cost of Essential Improvements in your household. For the Optional Improvements, the cost-sharing ratio ranges from 5% to 12.5%, depending on the type of flat. The amount payable for the full optional improvement package with a fire-rated main door and home fire alarm device ranges from S$550 to S$1,375, while the amount payable for the package with a non-fire-rated main door ranges from S$545 to S$1,362.50. SPRs will not be eligible for any subsidies. They will be required to bear the entire cost of essential improvements, as well as any optional or EASE improvements they opt for. Nonetheless, in case the flat owner acquires Singapore citizenship within a year from the billing date, the upgrading subsidy may be reimbursed to them. If a resident decides to opt for all EASE items, the cost would be significantly reduced, with the charges amounting to approximately S$2,500 (with a single-step ramp at the main entrance), S$2,940 (with a portable ramp at the main entrance), or S$3,840 (with a customised ramp at the main entrance). The government will fully finance the improvement items for elderly residents who reside in HDB rental flats. Moreover, SC households can seek financial assistance to defray the upgrading cost. Homeowners with a monthly household income of less than S$2,000 may extend their payment period to up to 25 years. term: Boost your real estate investment income with dividend yield
definition: Real estate investing can provide a steady stream of income through rental payments and property appreciation over time. However, some investors are looking to boost their income even further through dividend-paying real estate investment trusts, or REITs. Adding REITs to an investment portfolio is an effective way to increase dividend income.  Source: Dividend yield  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/dividend-yield/  (index: Dividend yield)

term: dividend yield
definition: Dividend yield refers to the annual dividend payments from a stock or REIT expressed as a percentage of the current share price. For example, if a REIT pays $1 per share in dividends over the year and its share price is $25, the dividend yield is 4% ($1 dividend ÷ $25 share price). The higher the dividend yield, the more income you’ll receive relative to the share price.  Source: Dividend yield  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/dividend-yield/  (index: Dividend yield)

term: Advantages of REIT dividends
definition: REITs are required to pay out at least 90% of taxable income to shareholders in dividends. This results in yields that are typically much higher than dividends from stocks. Here are some key benefits of REIT dividend income: • High yields – Average REIT yields range from 2-12%, which can significantly boost portfolio income. • Reliable payouts – REITs consistently pay dividends and often increase payouts over time. • Diversification – Adding REITs can balance a portfolio heavily weighted in stocks and bonds. • Low volatility – REIT share prices are generally less volatile than stocks. • Inflation hedge – REIT dividends tend to rise during inflationary periods as rents and property values increase.  Source: Dividend yield  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/dividend-yield/  (index: Dividend yield)

term: How to pick high-dividend yield REITs
definition: Not all REITs are created equal when it comes to dividends. Look for REITs that exhibit the following characteristics: • Track record of consistent dividend payments • Focused on stable property sectors like apartments, offices, warehouses • Debt levels appropriate for its portfolio and growth prospects • Growth in funds from operations (FFO) to support increasing dividends • High occupancy and tenant retention rates • Reasonable payout ratio (percentage of FFO paid as dividends)  Source: Dividend yield  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/dividend-yield/  (index: Dividend yield)

term: Diversify your REIT investments
definition: Since different property types have unique market cycles, it’s important to diversify your REIT portfolio holdings. definition: The GST Voucher programme encompasses four key areas, each catering to different household needs: This component offers financial assistance to lower-income Singaporeans to address their immediate needs. The cash grant is disbursed annually in August. During Budget 2023, the Government unveiled its plan to raise the quantum of GSTV – Cash, potentially by an additional S$350. This increment will be gradually implemented throughout the years 2023 and 2024. term: a Letter of Credit
definition: A letter of credit (LC) is a widely used financial instrument in international trade, ensuring secure payment between the buyer and seller. The International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) establishes the rules for LCs through its Uniform Documentary Letter of Credit Practice, which is adopted globally by producers and traders. When parties engage in transactions, they use an intermediary, such as a bank or financial institution, to issue the LC and guarantee that payment will be made for the goods or services received.  Source: Letter Of Credit  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/letter-of-credit/  (index: Letter Of Credit)

term: Why is a Letter of Credit important
definition: Trust plays a significant role in the relationship between buyer and seller. Whether you are the buyer, seller, or end user, it’s crucial to understand each party’s intentions in overseas transactions and ensure they fulfil their obligations. While domestic trading often benefits from established relationships with suppliers, dealing with lesser-known overseas suppliers can pose challenges. As a result, many suppliers now request full payment in advance, despite around 80% of global trade being conducted on an open account basis (buy now, pay later). For businesses, a letter of credit not only provides reassurance about the protection of goods but also offers flexible payment terms, addressing these concerns effectively. The main advantages of having a LC, include: • Preventing possible conflicts in foreign transactions. • Offering a payment guarantee to sellers and suppliers. • Allowing for versatility and different types of LCs. • Providing secure payment methods accepted in major markets. • Shifting the risk of non-payment from the buyer to the bank. • Often required by national border/exchange management agencies.  Source: Letter Of Credit  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/letter-of-credit/  (index: Letter Of Credit)

term: How does a Letter of Credit work
definition: The process of using letters of credit follows the guidelines of the International Chamber of Commerce’s Uniform Customs and Practise for Documentary Credits (UCP600). It is a straightforward process for businesses involved in buying and selling goods and services. Typically, one party, often the importer, will engage a bank as an intermediary to assure the seller that the payment for the goods will be made as per the agreed terms. All parties must agree to these terms and sign the contract, which significantly mitigates business risks. Although the guidelines and format for letters of credit are generally consistent, the actual content may vary. Therefore, both the buyer and seller must carefully examine the documents to identify any errors that could lead to delays, additional costs, or deferred payments. Even a minor oversight can prove costly, so having multiple individuals review the documents thoroughly is recommended.  Source: Letter Of Credit  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/letter-of-credit/  (index: Letter Of Credit)

Step 2 • Seek assistance from any Ministry of Manpower’s Assurance, Care and Engagement (ACE) officers present at the dormitory. • Consult the MOM through a Zoom session by visiting www.mom.gov.sg/make-appt-zoom. • Contact the MOM at (+65) 6438 5122. • Visit the MOM Services Centre in person at 1500 Bendemeer Road, Singapore 339946. term: Why home buyers need escape clauses
definition: Buying a home is one of the biggest financial decisions most people will ever make. Your nest egg – the money you’ve worked so hard to save up – is on the line. That’s why home buyers must protect themselves by making sure their purchase agreements contain escape clauses. What exactly are escape clauses? They are provisions written into contracts that allow either the buyer or seller to walk away from the deal relatively easily and without major penalties if certain conditions aren’t met. For home buyers, common escape clauses include inspection contingencies, appraisal contingencies, and financing contingencies. Let’s look at each of these in more detail: [HEADING-H3] Inspection contingencies An inspection contingency gives you the right as the buyer to have the home thoroughly inspected and to cancel the contract if issues are found that you aren’t willing to take on. Without this clause, you could be stuck buying a money pit riddled with defects, repairs, and safety hazards. That’s a huge risk to take with your hard-earned nest egg. A good inspection contingency will give you ample time to get an inspection done and review the results. [HEADING-H3] Appraisal contingencies You must add an appraisal contingency too. This allows you to back out and get your earnest money deposit returned if the home appraises for less than the agreed-upon purchase price. Without this, you could end up overpaying by tens of thousands of dollars or more. An appraisal contingency protects you from grossly overpaying. [HEADING-H3] Financing contingencies Lastly, don’t forget the financing contingency. This gives you the ability to cancel if you’re unable to secure a loan under the agreed-upon terms. Rates and regulations change frequently these days, so locking in financing can’t be guaranteed. Without this clause, you could lose your deposit and have no home if your financing falls through. The bottom line is that home buying is a risky business, especially in today’s fast-moving market. Don’t gamble your nest egg on a purchase without escape clauses built into the contract. Lean on your experienced real estate agent to make sure these contingencies are added and worded correctly to fully protect your interests as the buyer. An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.  Source: Contingencies  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/contingencies/  (index: Contingencies)

term: What should SOR borrowers expect
definition: There are two options for borrowers: • SORA Conversion Package Borrowers who have not yet switched from their SOR residential loan package will be automatically converted to the SORA Conversion Package in October 2022 by their bank to avoid any disruption to their loan when SOR is discontinued. In this option, the bank will take the following steps: The borrower’s SOR loan will be converted to a SORA loan by adding a standardised Adjustment Spread (Retail) to the original loan margin. An adjustment spread is necessary to account for term and credit risks, which SOR factors in but SORA does not. Therefore, SORA is generally lower than SOR. The Adjustment Spread (Retail) will be calculated based on the average difference between SOR, and 3-month SORA compounded in advance over the previous three months, with a minimum of zero. There will be no additional fees or lock-in period if the borrower switches to the SORA Conversion Package their existing bank provides. • Switch to any other loan package that your bank is currently offering Your bank may have other loan packages you can choose from instead of the SORA Conversion Package. These include fixed-rate or floating-rate property loans based on the bank’s board rate or fixed deposit rates. Even if your SOR loan has already been converted to the SORA Conversion Package, you can still switch to another loan package offered by your bank. If you choose to do so before June 30 2023, you will not incur any fees. It is advisable to contact your bank at the earliest opportunity to discuss your options and prevent any interruptions to your loan when SOR ends. term: en bloc potential
definition: A developer’s interest in acquiring numerous adjacent properties to redevelop them is called En Bloc Potential. term: Factors affecting en bloc potential and the process in Singapore
definition: En Bloc Potential of a property can be affected by many different aspects, including the worth of a property which is determined by different aspects like its age and land area as well as its location or potential for development. In addition to the government’s master plan, there are noteworthy restrictions by way of zone legislation. Selling through En Bloc is a multi-step process that requires a lot more effort. The first step in selling properties held jointly between multiple investors or groups typically involves securing agreement from eighty percent (by share value and total area) or more. A group for selling is then established who will deal with all the necessary legal proceedings in order to negotiate with clients. Finding a buyer and agreeing on a price necessitates getting clearance from either the Strata Titles Board or the High Court to sanction the deal. term: Key Difference between en bloc sales and other property sales
definition: It is common practice to compare En Bloc with individual property sale processes. During En Bloc sales all units within the designated development get sold as opposed to individual selling where only one unit is involved. A rise in the total sale price is possible only when most owners give their consent.  Source: En bloc potential in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-en-bloc-potential-in-singapore/  (index: En bloc potential in Singapore)

term: Advantages and disadvantages of en bloc sales
definition: The potential for a more profitable sale is what makes En Bloc sales advantageous, and it is a common occurrence in real estate when someone who owns property receives compensation beyond what they would get at a fair price. This extra amount is frequently referred to as ‘a premium’ and can be highly beneficial. However, En Bloc sales also have disadvantages. They can be a lengthy and uncertain process, and there’s no guarantee of success. Owners also need to find a new home after the sale, which can be a challenge, especially in a competitive property market.  Source: En bloc potential in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-en-bloc-potential-in-singapore/  (index: En bloc potential in Singapore)

term: Types of en bloc sales
definition: There are two types of En Bloc sales in Singapore, voluntary and compulsory. Here is the quick explanation of it: • Voluntary En Bloc sales occur when the owners initiate the process and agree to the sale. • Compulsory En Bloc sales occur when the government acquires the land for public purposes, such as urban renewal or infrastructure development. [HEADING-H3] Conclusion In conclusion, while En Bloc sales can offer a significant financial benefit, they also contain risks and challenges. Property owners should carefully consider these factors and seek professional advice before deciding to pursue an En Bloc sale. definition: An underwriter is a person or company that evaluates and assumes another party’s risk for a fee, such as a commission, premium, spread, or interest. term: Understanding underwriters
definition: Underwriters assess the risk and exposures of potential clients. term: Importance of underwriters in real estate
definition: In the context of real estate, underwriters play a crucial role in the mortgage lending process. They review the borrower’s credit history, assess the property’s value, and determine whether the lender should grant the mortgage loan. The underwriter’s decision can influence the interest rate, loan amount, and other terms of the mortgage. term: Key criteria in underwriting

Self-employed individuals may need additional documentation. • Assets: Lenders want to ensure you possess enough assets and reserves to cover the down payment and closing costs, necessitating bank and investment statements. • Credit: Your credit reports and scores are scrutinised for late payments, defaults, and overall borrowing history, with a minimum credit score often being a requirement. • Debt-to-income ratio: This metric measures the portion of your gross income allocated to debt payments, with approval often contingent on it not exceeding a specific percentage. • Property appraisal: A professional appraisal is conducted to determine the fair market value of the property, ensuring it serves as adequate collateral. term: Key features of community care apartments
definition: [HEADING-H3] 1. Senior-friendly design and minimal renovation Every CCA unit, measuring 32 square meters, is carefully planned to meet the requirements of elderly inhabitants. The open floor plan features sliding partitions that can divide the living and bedroom spaces, offering versatility and seclusion. The units are equipped with necessary features already, reducing the need for extra renovations. • Wide, wheelchair-accessible main doors with built-in benches. • Spacious, wheelchair-friendly bathrooms equipped with grab bars and slip-resistant flooring. • Built-in wardrobes and kitchen cabinets. • A furnished kitchen area (excluding appliances like refrigerators and washing machines). • A service yard accessible from the bathroom, complete with a clothes-drying rack. Every floor has a common area designed to promote socialising among residents and build a strong community. [HEADING-H3] 2. Integrated care services To support independent living, residents must subscribe to a Basic Service Package. • 24-hour emergency monitoring and response. • Basic health checks. • An on-site community manager who organizes regular activities and programs. • Help with simple home repairs. • Key card access to individual flats. [HEADING-H3] 3. Eligibility criteria To be eligible for a CCA, both the applicants and their spouses (if they have one) need to be at least 65 years of age. Applicants have the option to select a lease lasting from 15 to 35 years, in increments of five years, ensuring coverage until they reach at least 95 years old. Candidates who received housing aid twice before and bought a Studio Apartment or a short-term 2-room Flexi flat are disqualified. [HEADING-H3] 4. Upfront payment and lease conditions Those who are approved need to make complete payment for the flat upfront, using cash and/or CPF funds. The Basic Service Package offers the option of paying in full upfront or making partial payments with monthly fees over the lease period. Unlike regular HDB flats, CCAs cannot be sold or leased. Residents who no longer need the apartment can return it to HDB and get a refund depending on the remaining lease value. [HEADING-H3] Developments and future plans [HEADING-H3] Conclusion Community Care Apartments in Singapore mark a major step forward in public housing, providing seniors with a special mix of independent living and comprehensive care services. CCAs offer a supportive environment for seniors to gracefully age in the community by integrating well-designed living spaces with necessary services. With Singapore’s ongoing development of more apartments in different areas, they will play a crucial role in the country’s senior living strategy. term: a capitalisation rate
definition: Also known as the cap rate, the capitalisation rate tells you how risky an investment is and how much money you can expect to make in return. While investors seek to maximise their returns, it is not as simple as choosing the investment with the highest returns. The risk-return trade-off involves balancing expected returns with the associated risks. Everyone has their way of balancing risks and returns, so it’s important to figure out what works for you before investing your money.  Source: Capitalisation rate  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/capitalisation-rate/  (index: Capitalisation rate)

term: How to calculate the capitalisation rate
definition: To calculate the cap rate, divide the Net Operating Income (NOI) by the Property’s Purchase Price. The NOI is the property’s income minus expenses like vacancy voids, bad debt allowance, working expenses, and debt service. The Purchase Price is the amount paid to acquire the property. This calculation only includes the property’s generated income and does not factor in the mortgage debt.  Source: Capitalisation rate  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/capitalisation-rate/  (index: Capitalisation rate)

term: What influences the capitalisation rate
definition: Various market factors can influence the capitalisation rate of a property. The location is a significant factor determining the commercial property’s returns, with high-traffic areas typically having a higher capitalisation rate. Besides, other factors like competing properties in the local market also need consideration. Due to competitive pressure, properties tend to have lower cap rates in larger, well-established markets. Changes in the local market, such as growth or decline, can also impact the long-term capitalisation rate for a property. Finally, the amount of capital invested in a property, such as a renovation that enhances its appeal, can raise rental prices and boost the owner’s operating income.  Source: Capitalisation rate  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/capitalisation-rate/  (index: Capitalisation rate)

term: restrictions of the capitalisation rate
definition: The usefulness of the capitalisation rate depends on a property’s income stability. It may not be as dependable for properties with erratic cash flows. A discounted cash flow model could be a more suitable way to assess investment property returns. The capitalisation rate also does not consider potential future risks, such as depreciation or rental market changes that could result in income fluctuations. Investors should consider these risks when relying on cap rate calculations.  Source: Capitalisation rate  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/capitalisation-rate/  (index: Capitalisation rate)

term: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on the Resale Flat Listing (RFL)
definition: [HEADING-H3] For sellers: How do I list my flat on the HDB Flat Portal? You must register an intent to sell with HDB. You can then create a listing by uploading photos and descriptions of your flat. Essential details like address, flat type, and floor area will be automatically filled from HDB’s data. Can I manage my listing myself or do I need an agent? You can manage your listing yourself or appoint a property agent to handle it on your behalf. What information is required for my listing? Besides the automatically filled details (address, flat type, floor area), you need to upload photos and provide a description of your flat. What if I want to sell my flat at a higher price than recent transactions? If your listing price is 10% above the highest recent transaction price of similar units nearby, you will receive a prompt. You can then adjust your price if necessary. How many listings can I create for my flat? Each seller can post only one listing to avoid duplicates. How are viewing appointments managed? Once your flat is listed, you can create viewing appointments that interested buyers with a valid HFE letter can book. When is my listing removed? The listing is automatically taken down once a buyer submits a request for value after being granted an option to purchase. [HEADING-H3] For buyers: Who can access the listings on the HDB Flat Portal? Any prospective buyer can browse the listings, but only those with a valid HFE letter can obtain sellers’ contact details and schedule viewings. What is an HFE letter and how do I get one? An HFE letter indicates your eligibility to buy a flat, receive grants, and take up a housing loan. You can apply for it through HDB’s services. What information is available in the listings? Listings include recent transaction prices of similar flats, amenities in the area, ethnicity and citizenship quotas, and other relevant details. Can I compare different flats on the portal? After exercising your option to purchase, you can submit your resale application through the HDB Flat Portal. [HEADING-H3] For property agents: How can property agents use the HDB Flat Portal? Is there a cost for using the RFL service? The service will be free of charge for the time being, unlike other property portals that charge subscription fees. Can agents create multiple listings for the same flat? No, only one listing per flat is allowed to prevent duplicates. [HEADING-H3] General: When will the new RFL service be officially launched? The official launch will be later in May, following a soft launch on May 13. How does the RFL service enhance transparency? The service includes features like automatic prompts for high listing prices, verified listings to prevent duplicates, and detailed information about recent transactions and amenities. What measures are in place to ensure the reliability of listings? Listings are verified by HDB, and duplicate listings are prevented. Sellers receive prompts for unrealistic pricing, and listings are automatically deactivated when transactions progress. term: How does bankruptcy work in Singapore
definition: The General Division of the High Court is the only court that hears bankruptcy applications. Once an individual or firm is declared bankrupt, their property will be vested in a court-appointed trustee, who will manage the bankrupt’s financial affairs. All bankruptcy cases are to be handled by private trustees in bankruptcy, with the exception of cases where the Official Assignee considers that there is public interest. A person applying to the court for bankruptcy, whether by a creditor against a debtor or by a debtor for themselves, is required to nominate a licensed insolvency practitioner to administer the bankruptcy case.  Source: Bankruptcy  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/bankruptcy/  (index: Bankruptcy)

term: How to get out of bankruptcy in Singapore
definition: There are two ways in which an individual can get out of bankruptcy in Singapore: annulment or discharge by the High Court or by Certificate of the Official Assignee. Bankruptcy is usually considered a last resort option, and debtors are encouraged to look for alternative solutions to settle their debts before considering applying for bankruptcy.  Source: Bankruptcy  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/bankruptcy/  (index: Bankruptcy)

term: How to avoid bankruptcy as a real estate investor
definition: Investing in real estate carries inherent risks that, if not approached carefully, can result in financial setbacks and even bankruptcy. It’s crucial to recognise that real estate itself isn’t the direct cause of bankruptcy; rather, it stems from imprudent financial decisions. To flourish as a real estate investor without facing bankruptcy, it is essential to exercise prudence. Here are some recommendations to steer clear of financial pitfalls: • Thorough due diligence: Before purchasing any property, conduct comprehensive due diligence. Gain a complete understanding of costs, risks, and profit potential to assess its viability as a sound investment. Avoid relying solely on intuition. • Conservative financing: Exercise caution with financing, avoiding over-leverage with high-risk loans. Aim to provide a substantial down payment, preferably 20% or more, and opt for fixed-rate loans. Ensure access to a reserve capital equivalent to 6-12 months. • Know your limits: Be mindful of your management capabilities and avoid taking on more than you can handle. Consider hiring property managers if necessary, especially if you’re a new investor. Start small before venturing into larger commercial properties. • Thorough tenant screening: Screen tenants meticulously to prevent potential issues. Check credit history, references, employment records, and criminal background to avoid problematic renters who might lead to financial troubles. • Contingency fund: Maintain a sizable contingency fund to address unexpected expenses, such as property repairs or tenant defaults. Automate contributions to this fund to ensure it stays robust. • Market monitoring: Keep a close eye on the market. If your local real estate market is declining, consider selling properties with slower appreciation before prices drop further. Be prepared to exit underperforming investments. • Adequate insurance: Invest in comprehensive insurance coverage, including property insurance, liability insurance, and umbrella policies. This safeguards your personal assets from potential risks, and cutting corners here is not advisable. • Professional collaboration: Work with experienced professionals such as real estate attorneys, brokers, accountants, and property managers. Relying on their expertise can help you avoid costly mistakes, especially if you’re a novice investor. By arming yourself with the right knowledge, maintaining discipline, and exercising caution, real estate investment can yield significant returns without leading to financial ruin. Steer clear of greed, shortcuts, and inadequate planning, and the likelihood of facing bankruptcy diminishes considerably.  Source: Bankruptcy  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/bankruptcy/  (index: Bankruptcy)

term: a tax assessment
definition: Distinctions in tax rates exist for owner-occupied and non-owner-occupied properties. Notably, owner-occupied residential properties enjoy significantly lower property tax rates. Conversely, non-owner-occupied properties are subject to a progressive tax rate, with rates generally higher than those applied to owner-occupied properties.  Source: Assessment  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/assessment/  (index: Assessment)

term: How are property tax assessments calculated
definition: The calculation of tax for owner-occupied properties involves multiplying the monthly market rent by 12 to determine the yearly value, and then applying the property tax rate using the formula: Yearly Value x Property Tax Rate = Property Tax Payable The market rent considered here is the rental amount after deducting fees for furniture and maintenance. Property owners can calculate their tax liability by utilising the tax rates provided by the IRAS and the annual value assigned to their property.  Source: Assessment  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/assessment/  (index: Assessment)

term: Are there any exemptions or deductions for property tax in singapore
definition: In Singapore, there are certain exemptions and deductions for property tax, which can help reduce the taxable value of a property and lower the property tax payment. These include: • Owner-occupied property tax exemption: If you live in the property you own, you benefit from significantly lower property tax rates, making the tax system fairer. • Tax exemptions for registered charities: Properties owned and used by registered charities, like places of public religious worship or public schools receiving government grants, can enjoy tax exemptions. This also applies to properties used for charitable or social development purposes in Singapore. • Partial exemption for land occupied by the building: Section 6(7) of the Property Tax Act allows exemption from property tax payment if the land is occupied by a building under development or intended for use primarily for purposes specified in Section 6(6).  Source: Assessment  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/assessment/  (index: Assessment)

term: Can I appeal my tax assessment
definition: If you believe your property has been overassessed, you can challenge the valuation with the following guideline: • Assess the justification for an appeal: Gather factual evidence to support your claim and determine if appealing is justified. Your personal opinion on the fairness of your property assessment is not sufficient. • Adhere to all rules: Appeals have specific deadlines and procedures. Familiarise yourself with these procedures and meet the deadlines to ensure your appeal is considered. • Submit the Notice of Appeal: If you decide to appeal, submit the completed notice of appeal in the prescribed form along with the necessary payment and the notice of the decision by the Chief Assessor and/or Comptroller of Property Tax. • Clearly state the grounds for your appeal: In your Notice of Appeal, specify the grounds for your appeal and whether you have any representation. • Pay the Appeal Fees: There are fees associated with filing an appeal. For residential properties taxed at owner-occupier rates, a S$50 fee is applicable, while other property types incur a S$200 fee. • Consider seeking third-party expertise: A comparative appraisal conducted by a reputable third-party expert can significantly strengthen your case in the appeal process.  Source: Assessment  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/assessment/  (index: Assessment)

term: Per Square Foot (PSF) in Singapore
definition: PSF stands for Per Square Foot, a term that refers to the standard unit for quantifying the size of a property’s area. As such, a higher PSF would indicate a greater property size, whereas a lower PSF value would suggest a smaller area. PSF is a more widely used metric in Singapore than square metres, although the two terms are sometimes used interchangeably. When putting your home on the market, accurately calculating the size of the property is important in establishing the appropriate asking price.  Source: PSF – Per Square Foot  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/psf-per-square-foot/  (index: PSF – Per Square Foot)

term: price Per Square Foot (PSF) in Singapore
definition: Price PSF represents the estimation of the money you pay for each square foot of usable living area. PSF is a benchmark to evaluate the cost of a property. The lower the PSF value, the more economical the property.  Source: PSF – Per Square Foot  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/psf-per-square-foot/  (index: PSF – Per Square Foot)
aliases: What is the price Per Square Foot (PSF) in Singapore?|PSF|PSFS

term: How to calculate the price Per Square Foot (PSF) in Singapore
definition: Here is the formula to calculate the price per square foot: Price per square foot = Total price of the property ÷ total square footage of the property  Source: PSF – Per Square Foot  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/psf-per-square-foot/  (index: PSF – Per Square Foot)

term: Is per Square Foot (PSF) the only main indicator when comparing property prices
definition: When comparing property prices, it is not enough to just look at the PSF figure. Other factors that should be taken into account include: • Smaller units tend to have a higher price PSF, while larger units have a lower price PSF. • Smaller units have a lower overall cost, while larger units have a higher overall cost. • Newer units have higher monthly maintenance costs, while older units have higher upkeep costs. • Smaller units may have a more efficient layout, while larger units may not maximise the unit space. • New launch units may not be available for immediate move-in, while resale units are ready for immediate move-in. • Smaller developments may have more units squeezed into the plot, while larger developments may have more space for additional features. • Newer units may be less furnished than resale, resulting in higher renovation costs. term: an en bloc sale agreement
definition: An en bloc sale, or as it’s often known, a collective sale, is when a cluster of property owners band together to sell their properties to a singular buyer—usually a property developer. The term ‘en bloc’ originates from French and translates to ‘in its entirety’, encapsulating the essence of this type of sale. In Singapore, the Land Titles (Strata) Act governs en bloc sales, with the Strata Titles Board overseeing the process.  Source: En bloc sale agreement in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-en-bloc-sale-agreement-in-singapore/  (index: En bloc sale agreement in Singapore)
aliases: What is an en bloc sale agreement?

term: Factors influencing en bloc sale and the application process
definition: Various factors impact the feasibility and success of an en bloc sale. These encompass the age and condition of the property, the potential for redevelopment, the prevailing real estate market conditions, and the interest level among property developers. Initiating an en bloc sale requires a few steps. To start, a minimum percentage of owners (determined by the age of the development) must consent to the sale. Once this threshold is achieved, a Collective Sale Committee comes into the picture to negotiate with potential buyers and manage the sale process. If a sale is agreed upon, it must secure approval from the Strata Titles Board or the High Court before it can take place.  Source: En bloc sale agreement in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-en-bloc-sale-agreement-in-singapore/  (index: En bloc sale agreement in Singapore)

term: Comparing en bloc sales with other real estate transactions
definition: En bloc sales often draw comparisons with individual property sales. While individual sales involve a single property and its owner, en bloc sales include multiple property owners and can be more intricate due to the need for collective agreement and legal scrutiny.  Source: En bloc sale agreement in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-en-bloc-sale-agreement-in-singapore/  (index: En bloc sale agreement in Singapore)

term: Understanding the ins-and-outs of lease agreements: An essential guide for tenants and landlords
definition: A lease agreement is a legally binding contract between a landlord and a tenant that outlines the terms and conditions of a rental property. For both parties, it’s crucial to fully understand lease agreements before signing on the dotted line. This guide will provide tenants and landlords with a comprehensive overview of common lease provisions, negotiable terms, and best practices for lease agreements. [HEADING-H3] The key sections of a lease While specific lease terms can vary, most standard agreements contain several key sections: • Parties – Names and addresses of landlord and tenant(s) • Premises – Details about the rental unit and common areas • Term – Move-in date, length of lease, and expiration date • Rent – Amount due, payment frequency, late fees, and increased schedule • Security deposit – Deposit amount and conditions for a full or partial refund • Use – Permitted use of premises and occupancy limits • Maintenance – Division of repair responsibilities between landlord and tenant • House rules – Pet policies, noise restrictions, guest policies, etc. • Termination – Conditions for ending the lease early • Signatures – Date and signatures of landlord and tenant(s) [HEADING-H3] Negotiable lease terms While some provisions like rent amount are non-negotiable, other common lease terms have room for discussion: • Length of lease – Consider a shorter or longer initial term. • Security deposit – Request a lower deposit or instalment plan. • Maintenance – Divide responsibilities in a way that suits both parties. • House rules – Negotiate pet policies, parking, subletting, etc. • Termination – Add conditions like a military clause for early termination. Being flexible and open to negotiation allows both parties to craft a personalized lease. However, any agreed-upon terms should always be included in the written agreement. [HEADING-H3] Best practices for tenants and landlords By following lease best practices, tenants and landlords can promote a positive rental experience. Tenants should: • Read the entire lease before signing • Clarify any unclear or unspecified terms • Acquire renters insurance for liability and personal property coverage • Document the condition of the unit at move-in and move-out • Pay rent and maintain premises as outlined in the lease landlords should:- Use a current lease template that complies with state laws • Add specific terms like maintenance duties and house rules • Outline all costs like rent, deposits, fees, utilities, etc. • Disclose any defects like mould, leaks, damage, etc. • Maintain premises in habitable condition throughout the tenancy Following lease best practices demonstrates good faith for both parties and helps prevent future disputes. Understanding key lease provisions is the first step to establishing a healthy landlord-tenant relationship built on clear communication and accountability. With a comprehensive lease agreement, tenants and landlords can enjoy a mutually beneficial rental experience.  Source: Lease  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/lease/  (index: Lease)

term: force majeure
definition: Force majeure is a legal term that refers to unforeseeable circumstances that prevent someone from fulfilling a contract. In Singapore’s real estate market, force majeure clauses are often included in property contracts.  Source: Force majeure  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/force-majeure-defintion-understanding-importance/  (index: Force majeure)

term: Understanding force majeure
definition: A force majeure clause is a contract provision that allows a party to suspend or terminate the performance of its obligations when certain circumstances beyond their control arise, making performance inadvisable, commercially impracticable, illegal, or impossible. The types of events covered by a force majeure clause can vary, but they often include natural disasters, wars, strikes, riots, or government actions.  Source: Force majeure  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/force-majeure-defintion-understanding-importance/  (index: Force majeure)

term: Importance of Force Majeure in Real Estate
definition: In the context of real estate contracts, a force majeure clause can protect the parties involved in the event of unforeseen circumstances such as natural disasters, war, or pandemics. For instance, if a construction company is unable to complete a project on time due to a natural disaster, a force majeure clause could allow the company to delay completion without facing penalties. [HEADING-H3] Conclusion Force majeure clauses play a crucial role in real estate contracts, providing protection for the parties involved in the event of unforeseen circumstances. Understanding these clauses can help property buyers and sellers navigate their contractual obligations. However, the application of force majeure clauses can be complex, and it’s often advisable to seek legal advice when dealing with these issues.  Source: Force majeure  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/force-majeure-defintion-understanding-importance/  (index: Force majeure)

term: debt-to-income ratio
definition: Before approving new credit, lenders typically examine your credit report, credit score, and debt-to-income ratio (DTI). While these factors demonstrate your capacity to repay borrowed money, your DTI ratio reveals whether you possess the resources to manage repayment. Simply put, it represents the ratio of your debt to your income. When analysing your DTI ratio, lenders consider the proportion of your monthly earnings devoted to servicing your existing debt. A low DTI ratio suggests that your income surpasses your debt, while a high DTI ratio implies that a larger portion of your salary is spent on debt payments. Lenders generally prefer borrowers with low DTI ratios since they handle their monthly debt payments well. Therefore, banks and other financial institutions usually require a low DTI ratio before granting a loan to a prospective borrower.  Source: Debt-to-income ratio  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/debt-to-income-ratio/  (index: Debt-to-income ratio)

term: an ideal debt-to-income ratio
definition: To qualify for a mortgage, a borrower should generally have a debt-to-income ratio below 43%, with no more than 28% of the debt being used to cover the cost of a mortgage or rent payment. Ideally, lenders prefer a lower DTI ratio of less than 36%. In Singapore, DTI is measured based on Total Debt Servicing Ratio (TDSR) or Mortgage Servicing Ratio (MSR), depending on the purchased property type.  Source: Debt-to-income ratio  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/debt-to-income-ratio/  (index: Debt-to-income ratio)

term: How to calculate the debt-to-income ratio
definition: You can determine your DTI ratio by dividing your gross monthly income, which is your income before taxes and other deductions, by your total monthly payments. This includes credit card bills, rent or mortgage, car loans, and student loan payments.  Source: Debt-to-income ratio  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/debt-to-income-ratio/  (index: Debt-to-income ratio)

term: The unsung heroes: How facility managers are the secret weapon for corporate real estate success
definition: Facility managers are the unsung heroes of corporate real estate. While executives and brokers get the limelight for major deals, facility managers work tirelessly behind the scenes to ensure that buildings run smoothly on a day-to-day basis. Though their contributions often go unnoticed, facility managers play a crucial role in maximizing real estate assets and creating productive work environments. This makes them a secret weapon for success in corporate real estate. [HEADING-H3] Optimizing building operations Facility managers oversee all building operations, from maintenance and repairs to security and janitorial services. By coordinating these activities, they optimize costs and productivity. For example, preventative maintenance avoids major repairs down the road, while efficient cleaning schedules keep tenants happy without overspending on labour. Facility managers find the perfect balance to run buildings smoothly for the long term. [HEADING-H3] Managing vendors and contractors To deliver the best building operations, facility managers cultivate relationships with vendors and contractors. They identify trustworthy partners for outsourced work and negotiate contracts that meet budget requirements. With their extensive networks and purchasing expertise, facility managers secure quality services at the right price. They serve as the central coordinator between ownership, tenants, and service providers to align interests. [HEADING-H3] Improving sustainability Facility managers also spearhead sustainability initiatives that reduce environmental impact and costs. They research and implement technologies like LED lighting, high-efficiency HVAC systems, and automated building controls. With their deep knowledge of buildings, facility managers identify opportunities for savings through conservation. This focus on sustainability lowers operating expenses while demonstrating commitment to corporate social responsibility. [HEADING-H3] Creating ideal work environments At the core, facility managers create comfortable, productive work environments. They handle daily tenant requests and issues quickly and effectively. Facility managers understand how factors like indoor air quality, ergonomics, and aesthetics influence tenant satisfaction and retention. Their hands-on approach to enhancing workspaces makes buildings more desirable places to do business. The job of a facility manager is tough and thankless, but their impact is undeniable. Facility managers are the secret weapon for optimizing building operations, managing costs, improving sustainability, and creating ideal work environments. Though they work behind the scenes, savvy corporate real estate leaders recognize facility managers as true unsung heroes.  Source: Facility management  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/facility-management/  (index: Facility management)

term: a housing estate
definition: The Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) has categorised Singapore’s housing estate into three primary regions, referred to as “market segments”. These three regions, namely the Core Central Region (CCR), the Rest of Central Region (RCR), and the Outside Central Region (OCR) encompass a total of 28 districts in Singapore. term: What is the Core Central Region (CCR)?
definition: The CCR comprises three districts, namely 9, 10, 11, along with the Downtown Core Planning Area and Sentosa, and is considered the heart of Singapore. It encompasses the city’s prime metropolitan area, primarily the CBD district, where major commercial buildings are located. This region offers easy access to many amenities, including high-end restaurants, shopping malls, and hotels. One of the main reasons why residential or commercial properties in this area are among the most expensive in Singapore is the limited land availability and proximity to the city’s financial district. term: a leasehold
definition: Land tenure is a set of rules that decide who owns a piece of land. This can be a person, a company, or the government. Simply put, it pertains to the duration of property ownership. Singapore has two types of land ownership: freehold and leasehold. Freehold ownership means the land is owned entirely by the owner, with no restrictions on passing it on to future generations. To be classified as freehold, a property must possess two characteristics: Firstly, it must be immobile or attached to land in some way. Secondly, it must have an uncertain duration or lack a specified endpoint. Leasehold ownership refers to when the duration of ownership is specified. Generally, residential leasehold titles are valid for 99 or 999 years, while industrial leases are valid for 60 or 30 years, with a few exceptions. Once the lease term expires, the ownership of the land is returned to the State.  Source: Leasehold  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/leasehold/  (index: Leasehold)

However, homeowners requesting a lease extension must be willing to pay a significant premium for the extension. If their appeal is unsuccessful, homeowners must be prepared to relocate without compensation.  Source: Leasehold  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/leasehold/  (index: Leasehold)

term: Unlocking the potential of debentures in commercial real estate finance
definition: Commercial real estate financing is critical for developers, investors, and property owners. With rising interest rates and tightening lending standards, alternative financing options like debentures are garnering more interest. Debentures provide flexible, low-cost capital that can unlock the potential of commercial real estate projects. [HEADING-H3] What are debentures? A debenture is a type of debt instrument that is not secured by any collateral. The debenture holder is lending money based solely on the creditworthiness of the borrower. Debentures are attractive to borrowers because they do not require pledged assets. For lenders, the lack of collateral means debentures carry a higher risk and interest rate compared to secured loans. Debentures are commonly used to raise capital for large projects and acquisitions. They can be issued by governments, corporations, and real estate investment trusts (REITs). In commercial real estate, developers utilize debentures as an alternative to traditional bank financing. The flexibility and cost savings can improve returns on projects. [HEADING-H3] Benefits of debentures for commercial real estate There are several advantages to using debentures for commercial real estate finance: • Lower interest rates: Debentures typically carry lower interest rates than other debt products, improving project feasibility. • No collateral required: The unsecured structure avoids tying up assets as collateral. • Customizable terms: Debentures can be structured with flexible repayment schedules tailored to the project. • Preserves bank lines: Using debentures preserves bank credit lines for future projects. • Quick access to capital: Debenture issuance can provide fast access to growth capital. [HEADING-H3] Risks to consider While debentures offer many benefits, they also come with risks: • Higher interest rates than secured debt: The lack of collateral results in higher rates than secured loans. • Risk of default: No pledged assets mean a higher risk of default for debenture holders. • Subordinate to other debt: Debentures sit below secured debt in priority during bankruptcy. • Lack of oversight: Debenture financing does not involve the same oversight as bank loans. Debentures can provide an efficient, low-cost way to access capital for commercial real estate. Weighing the risks and rewards allows developers to make informed financing decisions. With proper structuring, debentures offer untapped potential to fund growth in commercial real estate markets.  Source: Debenture  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/debenture/  (index: Debenture)

term: a real estate mandate
definition: A real estate mandate is a written agreement between a home seller and a real estate agent giving that agent the exclusive right to represent and sell the seller’s property within a defined period. Unlike a traditional listing agreement which allows the seller’s home to be shown by any agent, a mandate restricts showings to only the exclusive agent. [HEADING-H3] Why do savvy sellers use mandates? There are several key benefits to listing a property through an exclusive seller mandate rather than an open listing: • Increased exposure – With an exclusive mandate, you can rest assured knowing your agent will dedicate 100% of their time and resources to marketing and selling your home above all others. • Better service – Exclusive agents are incentivized to go above and beyond since they don’t have to compete for the listing. You’ll get personalized attention and service. • Higher sales price – Studies show homes listed on a mandate sell for more on average than comparable open listings. Scarcity and exclusivity drive demand. • Privacy – Mandates allow the agent to qualify all potential buyers before showings, keeping looky-loos away. • No conflicts of interest – Open listings create the potential for unethical bait-and-switch tactics. Mandates avoid any split loyalties. For homeowners who are serious about getting top dollar in the shortest time with the least hassle, an exclusive real estate mandate is the way to go. The exclusivity creates scarcity and demand, leading to better exposure, service and ultimately sales price. In a crowded market, savvy sellers use mandates to unlock the full power of their listing.  Source: Mandate  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/mandate/  (index: Mandate)

term: The benefits of real estate counselling: How professional advice can help you make informed decisions
definition: [HEADING-H3] The role of real estate counselling Buying or selling a home is one of the biggest financial decisions most people will ever make. Navigating the complexities of the real estate market, with its myriad of factors such as pricing, negotiations, contracts, and regulations, can be daunting. This is where the expertise of a real estate counsellor becomes indispensable. Real estate counselling offers clients expert, unbiased advice, assisting them in making informed decisions about real estate transactions. A proficient counsellor is well-versed in all aspects of the local market and stays current with the latest trends, laws, and conditions affecting deals. Their guidance is crucial in determining reasonable asking prices, devising effective marketing strategies to attract qualified buyers, and identifying potential red flags that could impact a property’s value. [HEADING-H3] Navigating negotiations During the negotiation phase, a real estate counsellor acts as an impartial third party, facilitating communication and compromise between buyers and sellers. They aid clients in formulating suitable counteroffers, mediating disputes, and ensuring that the interests of all parties are equitably represented. This role is vital in preventing negotiation stalemates and promoting smoother transaction processes. [HEADING-H3] Fiduciary duty and ethical standards A key aspect of real estate counselling is the fiduciary duty owed to clients. Counselors are ethically and legally obligated to offer advice that serves the client’s best interest, not their own. They steer clear of conflicts of interest and refrain from receiving commissions or referral fees for endorsing specific properties, brokers, lenders, or home inspectors. Their fee structure is based solely on the time and expertise they offer, ensuring that clients receive impartial, value-maximizing guidance. [HEADING-H3] The benefits of having a counsellor In the fast-paced and often intricate world of real estate, having a knowledgeable counsellor on your side can be the defining factor in achieving a satisfying deal. Their insights help clients set realistic expectations, sidestep expensive errors, and navigate complex transactions with increased assurance. Investing in real estate counselling is a wise decision that yields invaluable dividends for both home buyers and sellers, providing them with a significant advantage in one of life’s most substantial financial undertakings. term: Who gets paid? Understanding payees and how they work in financial transactions
definition: [HEADING-H3] Understanding payees in financial transactions Payees play a critical role in financial transactions by receiving payments in exchange for goods or services. As a key participant, it’s important to understand what a payee is and their function when money changes hands. A payee refers to the party on the receiving end of a payment within a financial transaction. Also known as the recipient, the payee is the individual or business to whom payment is made. For instance, when you purchase groceries at the supermarket, the grocery store is the payee. Or if you take your car to the auto shop for repairs, the auto repair shop is the payee. In both cases, you are the payer providing money and the grocery store and auto shop are the payees receiving the funds. [HEADING-H3] Types of payees Payees can be people or organizations of all types and sizes. Some common examples of payees include: • Retail stores and service providers – Any business you patronize as a customer is a payee when you exchange money for products or services. This includes grocery stores, restaurants, gas stations, department stores, auto mechanics, doctors offices, etc. • Landlords – If you rent a home or apartment, your landlord is the payee who receives rental payments from you every month. • Lenders – Banks, credit card companies, mortgage companies, and other lending institutions are payees when you send them loan payments. • Contractors and freelancers – When you hire contractors like electricians, plumbers, lawyers, and consultants they are payees who receive payment from you upon completion of work. • Friends and family – If you owe money to friends or family members, they become the payee when you pay them back. • Government entities – The IRS and other government bodies are payees when you submit tax payments or pay fees. • Charities – Nonprofit organizations and charities are payees when they receive donations from donors and supporters. No matter the type of transaction, the payee’s role remains the same – to receive the payment amount in exchange for an item purchased or service rendered. As the recipient of funds, payees must provide invoices, account numbers, or payment information to clearly identify wheremoney should be sent. Proper payee identification ensures payments go to the correct party and are accounted for properly. [HEADING-H3] The bottom line Understanding the meaning and function of a payee is useful when examining any type of financial transaction. Payees represent a core component of money changing hands in an economy. Whether you’re the one making a payment or receiving it as the designated payee, being familiar with this key term is essential.  Source: Payee  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/payee/  (index: Payee)

term: a CPF Ordinary Account (OA)
definition: The CPF Ordinary Account (OA) is a component of Singapore’s Central Provident Fund (CPF) scheme. It is a savings account designed to meet individuals’ housing, insurance, investment, and education needs. When individuals and their employers make monthly CPF contributions, a portion of the funds is allocated to their CPF OA. The specific contribution and allocation rate are dependent on their age. The funds in the CPF OA serve as a savings mechanism and earn interest. The first S$20,000 in the account earns a higher interest rate, typically around 3.5%, while any amount above S$20,000 earns a lower interest rate, usually around 2.5%. However, upon reaching age 55, there are revisions to the interest rates, and the interest rates may vary depending on the individual’s CPF Retirement Account (RA) balance. term: Full Retirement Sum (FRS)
definition: By the age of 55, there are three savings targets linked to your CPF Retirement Sum that you can aim to achieve. Depending on which target you reach, your retirement payouts will be categorised as follows: The CPF Retirement Sum refers to the complete sum of your CPF savings that should be allocated to ensure a comfortable retirement lifestyle. Upon reaching age 65, monthly payouts will be provided and will persist throughout your lifetime. These sums represent the amount you should set aside in your Retirement Account (RA) by age 55 to ensure a certain level of monthly payouts during your retirement years. The Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) serves as the minimum threshold, while the Full Retirement Sum (FRS) and Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS) provide higher payout levels.
