term: How to negotiate for the best real estate deals
definition: Whether you’re a first-time homebuyer or an experienced real estate investor, honing your negotiation skills can potentially save you thousands of dollars. Here are seven savvy tips to help you navigate and master the art of negotiating in the property market. Get pre-approved for a mortgage: Demonstrating financial readiness is crucial. Obtain pre-approval for a mortgage to show sellers that you are a serious and capable buyer. Armed with a pre-approval letter, you not only exhibit commitment but also highlight the maximum loan amount you can secure, aiding in negotiations. Know the seller’s situation: Investigate the seller’s motivations for listing the property. Understanding their circumstances, such as job changes, family growth, or retirement, can provide insight into their flexibility regarding offers. Tailor your negotiation strategy based on their urgency and needs. Make a strong first offer: Your initial offer sets the tone for negotiations. Offer a competitive price, aiming for 5-10% below the listing price if justified by your research. Provide evidence supporting the offer’s reasonableness, signalling your genuine interest in making a fair deal. Be ready to negotiate and compromise: Anticipate counteroffers and be prepared for a back-and-forth exchange. Identify areas where you can compromise, such as agreeing to the seller’s closing date or leaseback options. Define your non-negotiables and be willing to make concessions within your limits to facilitate a successful deal. Bring in an experienced real estate agent: Enlist the expertise of a skilled real estate agent to represent your interests. A knowledgeable agent can offer insights into the local market, craft effective proposals, and navigate negotiations. Rely on their experience to guide you through the process and secure favourable terms. Trust your instincts: Listen to your intuition during negotiations. Trust your gut feelings about whether an offer is fair or unrealistic. Avoid being swayed by emotions and be prepared to walk away from a deal that doesn’t align with your standards. Additionally, scrutinise seemingly advantageous deals by inspecting the property for potential issues. By following these tips, you can prepare yourself for successful real estate negotiations, making informed decisions and ultimately securing the keys to your dream property. term: How to create a Doing Business As (DBA) in real estate that is memorable
definition: In the competitive real estate industry, having a strong brand identity is crucial for success. Your DBA name, or “Doing Business As” name, is a key component of your brand and should be carefully crafted to help you stand out. With some strategic thinking, you can develop a DBA name that maximises your visibility and memorability in the real estate market. Your DBA name should reflect what makes your real estate business different and valuable compared to others. This could relate to your area of expertise, your approach to client relationships, or your niche market. For example, “The First-Time Home Buyer Specialists” immediately conveys an area of specialisation. “Your Neighborhood Realtors” communicates a local, relationship-driven approach. Take time to identify your competitive advantage and work it into your DBA name. In an industry saturated with real estate agents, a forgettable or generic DBA name simply will not cut it. You need a name that is sticky in the minds of potential clients and stands out from the competition. Using alliteration, rhymes, puns, or unique word combinations can help with memorability. “Property Pros” has a catchy alliteration. “Home Sweet Home Realty” uses a rhyme and familiar phrase. Get creative brainstorming possibilities! While you want your name to be memorable, don’t make it overly clever or complex. Real estate is based on relationships, so you want people to easily recall and pronounce your business name when recommending you to friends and family. Stay away from convoluted plays on words or obscure references. The clearer and simpler your DBA is, the better. Once you have a few strong name candidates, check that the domain and social media handles are actually available before selecting your final DBA name. There is nothing more frustrating than falling in love with a name, only to find the .com has been taken since 1996. Do your research to ensure the name you want aligns with available web properties you can use to build your brand’s digital presence. If you work under a larger real estate brokerage, check whether they have guidelines about agents using DBA names, and whether your proposed name needs approval. Some brokerages expressly prohibit DBA names to maintain consistent branding. Others allow it but have parameters around not including the brokerage name. Know the rules of your specific company. Once you settle on your perfect DBA name, look into your state and local requirements for registering it as a legal business name. The filing process is typically very straightforward. Congratulations, you now have an exceptional DBA name to start building your standout real estate brand! term: Design, Build and Sell Scheme (DBSS)

The primary objective of the DBSS was to provide Singaporeans with a broader range of high-quality flats that were slightly more expensive than regular HDB flats but more affordable than executive condominiums or private condos. Unlike typical HDB flats with standardised layouts, DBSS flats offer unique features and resemble private condominium units. Residents enjoy condo-like designs, including balconies, study areas, and floor-to-ceiling windows that enhance natural light. Once the construction was completed, the responsibility for maintaining common areas and ensuring compliance with renovation guidelines and lease conditions was transferred to the HDB, similar to other HDB flats. However, the developers had the authority to set the launch prices for the flats, which, coupled with complaints about poor workmanship and finishing, led to the discontinuation of the scheme in 2012 after just eight years. Despite its relatively short lifespan, DBSS flats gained popularity in the resale market due to their unique features, desirable locations, and limited availability. term: caveat emptor
definition: The legal principle of “caveat emptor,” or “buyer beware,” means that if you were responsible for examining the property for defects before purchasing it, the Court would not intervene to save you from a bad deal. It is crucial to remember that once you sign a contract in Singapore, you are legally bound by all of its terms. If the contract includes an “as is, where is” clause, the Court will interpret this as your agreement to buy the property in its current state, regardless of whether or not you have examined it. Since the contract states that you have accepted the property’s condition, it will be challenging to seek compensation from the seller if you discover any issues or flaws with the property.  Source: Caveat emptor  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/caveat-emptor/  (index: Caveat emptor)

term: Must the seller inform me of any property defects
definition: In most situations, the seller is not obligated by law to inform the buyer about any property quality flaws that may impact its value. This regulation applies to both patent and latent defects. • Patent defects can be detected if the buyer is reasonably attentive during the property inspection. An example of such a defect is a large hole in the wall or visible water leaks. The law assumes that the buyer can identify such an obvious defect and raise concerns with the buyer. • Latent defects are problems with a property that cannot be expected to be discovered through a reasonable inspection. Under the principle of caveat emptor, a seller is not obligated to disclose latent defects in the quality of the property, even if they are aware of them. However, if the seller fails to disclose existing defects when asked, they may be held responsible for misrepresentation, which would allow the buyer to cancel the contract and seek compensation for any damages incurred. You assume responsibility for all defects in the property, regardless of whether they are easily noticeable or not. If you encounter defects after the purchase is finalised, you might have to consult a lawyer to determine if you have any legal options against the seller. If you do not have any legal options, you might have to accept the property’s condition as is.  Source: Caveat emptor  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/caveat-emptor/  (index: Caveat emptor)

term: What measures can you take as a buyer to protect your legal rights
definition: If you’re purchasing property under “as is where is” conditions, there are certain measures you can take to safeguard your legal rights as a buyer. Here are some tips: During negotiations for your Option To Purchase (OTP), request the opportunity to conduct a second inspection of the property before finalising the purchase. If the seller agrees, hire reputable contractors or property inspectors to examine the entire property thoroughly. Including this clause in the OTP makes the seller less likely to allow the property to deteriorate from its initial condition. You should also reserve the right to postpone the sale until the property is acceptable. Take photos and videos during your initial inspection of the property to have evidence of its condition. This can be beneficial if legal action is needed to enforce your rights as a buyer. However, remember that such evidence may not be useful if you discover underlying structural issues or damage that was not visible during the inspection. Most caveat emptor states mandate sellers to provide a property condition disclosure statement outlining known defects. Review this statement carefully and investigate any red flags. Verify permits for renovations to ensure compliance with building codes. Additionally, inspect the property at night to check for noise issues the seller may have omitted. Title insurance safeguards against claims that could challenge your ownership of the property, such as legal claims by previous owners’ relatives. It covers legal expenses to defend your rights as the property owner and protects against errors in the title search process. Although it involves a one-time cost, title insurance provides invaluable peace of mind. Make your offer contingent upon inspections and other due diligence processes to have an exit strategy if issues arise. Contingencies allow you to withdraw your offer and retrieve your earnest money deposit if the property fails to meet specific criteria. Common contingencies include financing, appraisal value, and inspection outcomes. Collaborate with a knowledgeable real estate attorney and agent familiar with caveat emptor laws in your state. They can offer guidance on contingency language, required seller disclosures, and other protective measures. A competent agent will also possess extensive knowledge of the local market and potential red flags. If something doesn’t feel right about the property or the seller’s disclosures, listen to your intuition. Request repairs or credits, or be prepared to walk away from the deal. Avoid succumbing to pressure to waive contingencies or inspections. Purchasing a “money pit” filled with hidden issues is never worthwhile. Stay objective – if significant problems arise, the home probably isn’t the right fit for you.  Source: Caveat emptor  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/caveat-emptor/  (index: Caveat emptor)

term: Common Area Maintenance (CAM)
definition: Common Area Maintenance (CAM) is a crucial term in the world of real estate. It refers to the costs associated with maintaining common areas in a commercial property, such as lobbies, hallways, parking lots, and shared restrooms. These costs are typically borne by tenants in addition to their base rent, under the terms of their lease agreement. If we consider a commercial building, the owner is responsible for its upkeep. However, the expenses incurred for maintaining the shared spaces are usually passed to the tenants. This is where CAM comes into play. It ensures that the shared spaces in a commercial building are well-maintained and functional, providing a clean and safe environment for everyone in the building.  Source: Common Area Maintenance (CAM)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-common-area-maintenance-cam/  (index: Common Area Maintenance (CAM))

term: Calculating CAM and influencing factors
definition: CAM charges are usually calculated on a pro-rata basis., meaning each tenant pays a portion of the total CAM costs proportional to the amount of space they lease in the building. For example, if a tenant leases 20% of the total leasable space in a building, they would be responsible for 20% of the total CAM costs. Several factors influence CAM charges. These include the size of the leased space, the type of property, the location, and the specific terms of the lease agreement. Additionally, the actual costs of maintenance, repairs, and improvements to the common areas also play a significant role in the determining CAM charges. term: Ingress and Egress
definition: Ingress denotes the entitlement to enter a property, whereas egress signifies the right to exit. Collectively, ingress and egress encompass the legal privileges to access and depart from private property. These entitlements are linked to the ownership and utilisation of the property. For instance, tenants inhabiting an apartment possess the right to ingress and egress from the premises. The landlord cannot prevent the renters from entering or exiting as this forms part of their utilisation rights. Similarly, the landlord maintains ingress and egress privileges to reach the property for maintenance and repairs.  Source: Ingress and Egress  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/ingress-and-egress/  (index: Ingress and Egress)

term: Ingress and Egress easements
definition: A prevalent method of establishing ingress and egress rights is through an easement. An easement entails the right to utilise or access another individual’s property for a specified purpose. For instance, if you own a landlocked piece of land lacking road access, you may acquire an ingress/egress easement from a neighbour. This would enable you to traverse a portion of their land to access your property. Easements can be granted in writing or may be established through historical usage and precedent.  Source: Ingress and Egress  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/ingress-and-egress/  (index: Ingress and Egress)

term: Emergency access rights
definition: Crucially, government authorities possess the authority to enter private property without consent during emergency scenarios. This encompasses police officers, firefighters, and medical personnel responding to an emergency call. The right to breach property restrictions for emergency response aims to safeguard public health and safety. Furthermore, utility workers often possess easement rights to access and repair electric, gas, water, and other utility lines, even on private property. This exception allows them to restore disrupted services that impact the community.  Source: Ingress and Egress  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/ingress-and-egress/  (index: Ingress and Egress)

term: Limits on Ingress and Egress rights
definition: While ingress and egress rights are extensive, they are not without bounds. Reasonable restrictions may be imposed, provided they do not entirely impede access or exit from a property. For instance, gated communities may mandate guests to check-in before entry. Rental properties can establish basic regulations and hours for tenants accessing common areas. Additionally, private landowners may take suitable measures to prevent trespassers from unlawfully entering their property. Nevertheless, restrictions designed to unlawfully target specific groups or individuals may contravene federal and state laws against discrimination. term: Ways to avoid ABSD (and why you should think twice before doing it)
definition: The Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty (ABSD) in Singapore targets buyers who purchase multiple residential properties to manage speculation and stabilise the market. Purchase under one spouse’s name A couple can purchase their initial property under only one spouse’s name, allowing the other spouse to buy a second property without facing ABSD. This method causes that the only owner has enough financial resources to sustain the mortgage on their own. [HEADING-H3] 2. Decoupling ownership [HEADING-H3] 3. Setting up a trust for this method can be complicated, therefore it is advisable to consult a legal expert. [HEADING-H3] 4. Sell existing property before purchasing another Selling your current property before buying a new one can help you qualify as a first-time buyer and bypass ABSD. Invest in commercial properties Buying commercial properties is an alternative investment strategy to avoid paying ABSD, which is applicable only to residential properties. term: The legal and ethical implications of group boycotting in real estate
definition: Group boycotting in the real estate industry has become an increasingly controversial topic. While some argue it helps level the playing field, others see it as unethical and potentially illegal. This article examines the complex issues surrounding group boycotting and why it often crosses legal and ethical lines.  Source: Boycotting  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/boycotting-singapore/  (index: Boycotting)

term: group boycotting
definition: Group boycotting refers to when multiple real estate brokers or agents collectively agree to not work with or share commissions with certain other brokers or agents. For example, a group of agents may decide to never show houses listed by a particular brokerage or never refer clients to a specific agent. The goal is to freeze out and weaken the business of targeted individuals or companies. On the surface, group boycotting may seem like fair competition. If agents don’t want to work with someone, that should be their choice, right? But in reality, group boycotting often violates antitrust laws and ethical business practices for several key reasons. [HEADING-H3] Restraint of trade Group boycotting essentially amounts to collusion among competitors. When agents collectively agree not to work with a broker or agent, they are restraining trade and reducing competition in the marketplace. This violates antitrust laws, such as the Sherman Antitrust Act, which prohibits anticompetitive agreements. [HEADING-H3] Access denied Group boycotting often cuts off access to an essential service that certain brokers or agents need to properly conduct business. Limiting access to the MLS database or refusing to show certain listed properties makes it very difficult for targeted individuals to fully participate in the market. [HEADING-H3] Client steering Boycotting groups will frequently steer clients away from doing business with the agent or brokerage they are targeting. This interferes with the client’s ability to freely choose who they want to work with. Client steering based on a group boycott rather than the client’s best interests is unethical. [HEADING-H3] Divisiveness Group boycotting breeds divisiveness and toxicity within the real estate community. It creates an “us vs. them” mentality that damages professional cooperation and problem-solving. This toxic environment ultimately hurts consumers. While competition breeds excellence, group boycotting tends to breed dysfunction. There are more ethical ways for real estate professionals to further their interests without resorting to potentially illegal and unprofessional tactics. Change is better accomplished through constructive action, not punitive boycotting.  Source: Boycotting  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/boycotting-singapore/  (index: Boycotting)

term: a Progressive Payment Scheme (PPS)
definition: The Progressive Payment Scheme (PPS) is applicable to properties in the construction process, commonly referred to as Buildings Under Construction (BUC). This typically ranges from 5 to 10% of the property purchase price at specific milestones during construction. In the case of resale condos, a 25% down payment is required, and monthly repayments begin immediately. For instance, you would make an instalment to the developer upon completion of the foundation, another payment when the walls are erected, and a further one when the roofs are prepared. The benefit of this scheme is that it offers lower initial monthly repayments, and even if delays in the developer’s timeline or milestones are not met, the loan repayments remain unchanged. The payment must be made to the developer within 14 days of receiving the notice, as failure to do so will result in the application of late payment charges. term: a break-even price
definition: The break-even price refers to the point at which a transaction or investment yields neither profit nor loss. It represents the price at which the revenue generated from selling a product or asset covers all the costs associated with its acquisition, ownership, or production. Break-even prices are applicable across various scenarios and transactions. For instance, in the context of property ownership, the break-even price would be the selling price that allows the owner to recover all expenses related to the property. This includes the purchase price, mortgage interest, insurance, property taxes, maintenance costs, improvements, closing costs, and real estate sales commissions. The homeowner would not generate a profit or incur losses at this price. For instance, consider an individual who invests S$750,000 in purchasing and maintaining a house. They would reach the break-even point by selling the property for the same amount. Alternatively, if they rent the house for S$2,500 per month, it would take approximately 300 months to reach the break-even point. Break-even prices also apply if the individual decides to develop the land and construct the house independently. In such cases, the break-even price would represent the amount that covers the costs of land acquisition, construction materials, labour, permits, and other associated expenses.  Source: Break-even Price  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/break-even-price/  (index: Break-even Price)

term: Land theft through fear: The devastating reality of intimidation tactics in land grabbing
definition: Land grabbing refers to illegally or fraudulently acquiring land that a person or party is not legally entitled to. This often involves intimidation tactics such as threats or the use of force to compel the legal owner to give up their land. Though land disputes are not uncommon, especially in developing countries, the practice of land grabbing through intimidation is illegal, unethical, and causes great distress. One common tactic is when an individual or business coerces farmers into handing over the land title through deception, manipulation, or outright threats. They may take advantage of poor, uneducated farmers who lack the resources to defend their rights. Violence is also used in some cases, where armed gangs force people off their ancestrally owned land. Some common methods of illegal land grabbing through intimidation include: • Making false claims to the land with forged title deeds or other fraudulent documents. This is common when land records are poorly maintained. • Threatening violence or retaliation against the landowner and their family if they do not comply with demands to give up the land. This can involve verbal threats or physical assault. • Destroying or damaging property, livestock, crops, or homes is an act of intimidation. The aim is to make continued ownership practically impossible. • Bribing local officials to turn a blind eye or actively assist with the illegal land seizure. • Taking advantage of political instability, weak governance, and lack of legal protections in certain regions. Land grabbing affects vulnerable groups worldwide, especially rural farmers in developing nations. However, it violates basic human rights and causes emotional trauma in addition to financial loss. Intimidation is an unscrupulous method to acquire land illegally at the expense of others. Governments must strengthen property laws, improve land record-keeping, and prosecute land grabbers to protect owner rights. Victims should also unite with local and international advocacy groups working against land grabbing. With vigilance and a stand for human rights, communities can counter intimidation and uphold justice.  Source: Intimidation  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/intimidation/  (index: Intimidation)

term: The art of the deal: How mediation helps opposing parties find common ground
definition: In any negotiation or dispute, parties often become entrenched in their positions and fail to see potential areas for compromise. The mediator creates a safe space for open dialogue, ensuring all voices are heard. They identify key issues, interests, and needs on each side. By translating anger into understanding, a skilled mediator transforms conflict into cooperation. The mediator asks probing questions to uncover why the dispute arose and what is truly at stake. Oftentimes, beneath the surface arguments lie deeper motivations – the real roots of discord. For example, noise complaints between neighbours may stem from a need for security, not just annoyance. The mediator helps reframe positions into interests to find win-win solutions. Parties shift focus from hardened positions to the underlying interests, needs, and concerns that drive them. New options emerge as shared goals are uncovered. A business dispute over contract terms may reveal mutual interests in profitability and continued partnership. Suddenly, collaborative problem-solving becomes possible. Parties also begin to understand the legitimacy of the other side’s perspective. Empathy develops, tensions ease, and creative problem-solving expands. Vision broadens from narrow self-interest to the bigger picture and collective good. [HEADING-H3] The win-win mindset Ultimately, mediation is about finding win-win solutions that work for all involved. When parties reach a mutual understanding and satisfy core interests, durable agreements result. Mediation transforms the mindset from adversarial to cooperative, from zero-sum to positive sum. With an expert mediator’s guidance, skilful negotiation turns conflict into an opportunity for gain rather than loss. Even bitter foes can find common ground with the art of the deal that mediation facilitates. Mediation provides a path beyond impasse for opposing parties. Through facilitated dialogue, shared interests are uncovered, innovative solutions emerge, and mutually beneficial settlements are reached. With patience and an open mind, the art of negotiation can lead to breakthroughs where all sides feel heard, respected, and satisfied. term: Home Protection Scheme (HPS)
definition: The Home Protection Scheme (HPS) is an insurance that reduces mortgages. The scheme aims to safeguard HDB owners from unforeseen circumstances that could hinder them from repaying their housing loans. Administered by the Central Provident Fund Board (CPFB), HPS provides claim eligibility to your family if you pass away, get diagnosed with a terminal illness, or become permanently disabled. The claim amount from HPS is the remaining balance of your HDB home loan. In other words, if you pass away with S$50,000 still owed in your housing loan, HPS will cover the entire amount, relieving your family of the repayment burden. HPS is comparable to mortgage insurance policies offered by some insurance companies. If you purchase an HDB flat with HPS coverage, there is no need to buy a separate insurance policy. It’s also worth noting that HPS is significantly less expensive than other private mortgage insurance.  Source: Home Protection Scheme (HPS)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/home-protection-scheme-hps/  (index: Home Protection Scheme (HPS))

HPS exclusively applies to HDB or DBSS flats, but not to private residences such as condominiums, executive condominiums (ECs), HUDC flats, and landed properties. term: vesting
definition: Vesting refers to how ownership of real estate is held. When you purchase a home, the deed and title to the property must be vested, or granted, to the owner or owners. There are several common ways homes can be vested: • Sole ownership: The home is titled and deeded only to one individual. This is the simplest form of vesting. • Joint tenancy: Joint tenancy establishes equal ownership interest between two or more people. If one owner dies, their share automatically goes to the surviving owner(s). This avoids probate. • Tenancy in common: Like joint tenancy, tenancy in common involves shared ownership between two or more people. However, each owner holds a separate share that can be willed to another person upon death. • Community property: In some states, property acquired during a marriage is considered jointly owned by both spouses. Each spouse has an undivided equal interest. • Trusts: Property can be titled and ownership vested into a living trust. This allows a designated person to manage the property on behalf of the beneficiaries. [HEADING-H3] Choosing the right vesting When purchasing a home, it’s important to consider how you want the property vested. This decision should be made carefully with your plans for the home in mind. If you purchase with a spouse or partner, joint tenancy with the right of survivorship ensures your partner will inherit your share. For unrelated co-buyers, tenancy in common allows more flexibility. Trusts can be useful for estate planning purposes. Consult with a real estate attorney to decide the optimal vesting method for your situation. Vesting protects your rights and outlines exactly who owns the property. Be sure to understand this legal component before buying or selling real estate. With the right vesting approach, you can avoid complications down the road.  Source: Vesting  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/what-is-vesting-in-real-estate/  (index: Vesting)

term: The power of bonds: How they secure real estate deals and protect your investment
definition: Real estate deals can be risky business. The process of buying, selling, or developing property often requires large investments upfront, with the hope of profits down the road. However, unforeseen circumstances can derail a real estate project, leaving investors exposed. This is where the power of bonds comes in. [HEADING-H3] What is a bond? A bond is a financial instrument that provides a form of insurance on a real estate project. The three main types of bonds used in real estate are: • Bid bonds – A guarantee a contractor will follow through on their bid for a project. • Performance bonds – A guarantee a contractor will complete the project as specified in the contract. • Payment Bonds – Guarantee subcontractors and suppliers will be paid for their work. • The party purchasing the bond pays a premium to the surety company issuing the bond. If the bonded party fails to uphold their end of the deal, the surety company pays the damages up to the bond amount to make the injured party whole. [HEADING-H3] Securing the deal For real estate investors, requiring bonding from contractors is a prudent way to secure deals and mitigate risks. Bid bonds weed out contractors who cannot complete a project. Performance and payment bonds provide assurance contractors will perform the work properly and pay their subcontractors. This transfers risk away from the investor. Without these bonds, investors take on substantial risks in hiring contractors. Shoddy workmanship, cost overruns, and abandoned projects can quickly turn profits into losses. Requiring bonding aligns incentives and ensures contractors have skin in the game. [HEADING-H3] Protecting your investment Bonding also plays a vital role in protecting investments if problems do arise. For example, if a contractor fails to complete a project, the surety company behind the performance bond will step in to find a new contractor or provide financial compensation. This protects the investor’s capital outlay. Likewise, payment bonds give subcontractors and suppliers recourse if the general contractor fails to pay. The surety company satisfies these obligations, preventing liens on the property that could inhibit sale or occupancy. This preserves the asset’s value. Bonds provide a crucial backstop for real estate investors, limiting financial risk and preventing deals from going sideways. Given the large sums often involved, paying bond premiums is inexpensive and worthwhile insurance. While bonding does not eliminate all real estate risks, its ability to transfer and mitigate key perils makes it an indispensable tool for securing transactions and protecting investments. The power of bonds brings peace of mind to even the most complex deal.  Source: Bonds  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/what-is-a-bond/  (index: Bonds)

term: equalisation
definition: Equalisation rates play a pivotal role in real estate by ensuring fairness and consistency in property valuation. These rates, also known as assessment ratios or assessment levels, are integral to the property tax system and are used to align property values with market realities. Simply put, equalisation rates are calculated to balance assessed property values with their fair market values.  Source: Equalisation  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/equalisation/  (index: Equalisation)

term: How do equalisation rates work
definition: They are expressed as a ratio or percentage and reflect the relationship between the assessed value of a property and its actual market value. In a perfect scenario, the equalisation rate would be 100%, indicating that the assessed and market values are identical. However, due to the dynamic nature of real estate markets, assessed values may lag behind or exceed market values. This is where equalisation rates come into play. If an area’s real estate market is experiencing rapid appreciation, property assessments might not keep up with the escalating values. Conversely, assessments could remain higher than the current market conditions warrant in a declining market. Assessors and tax authorities adjust property values using equalisation rates to rectify these discrepancies. For instance, if the equalisation rate is below 100%, it implies that the assessed values need to be increased to align with the market. Conversely, an equalisation rate above 100% signals that assessed values should be reduced to match the market. This process helps ensure that property owners are taxed fairly based on their property’s true value.  Source: Equalisation  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/equalisation/  (index: Equalisation)

term: How to calculate equalisation rates
definition: If we have an equalisation rate of 0.80, it means that the value assigned to a property for tax purposes is 80% of its total worth. Let’s imagine there’s a property that’s evaluated to be worth S$100,000, and the equalisation rate is 0.80. To figure out the whole value, the formula employed is: Full Value = Assessed Value divided by Equalisation Rate. This calculation yields a Full Value of S$125,000.  Source: Equalisation  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/equalisation/  (index: Equalisation)

term: What factors influence equalisation rates
definition: Several factors influence the determination of equalisation rates, including: • Real estate market trends: The primary driver is the state of the local real estate market. If property values are rapidly increasing or declining, it affects the relationship between assessed values and market values. • Data collection and analysis: Accurate assessment requires reliable data on property sales, local economic conditions, and market trends. Effective data collection and analysis methodologies contribute to more precise equalisation rates. • Property types: Different property types, such as residential, commercial, and industrial, might experience varying market trends, affecting the overall equalisation rate.  Source: Equalisation  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/equalisation/  (index: Equalisation)

term: Enhanced CPF Housing Grant (EHG)
definition: The Enhanced CPF Housing Grant (EHG) is a housing grant provided through CPF, specifically designed for first-time flat buyers who are either applying for a new Build-To-Order (BTO) flat or purchasing a resale flat in the open market. Its main purpose is to improve housing affordability and make housing more accessible to Singaporeans.  Source: Enhanced CPF Housing Grant (EHG)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/enhanced-cpf-housing-grant-ehg/  (index: Enhanced CPF Housing Grant (EHG))

term: Am I eligible for the Enhanced Housing Grant
definition: To qualify for the EHG, you must meet the following requirements: • You must be a first-time applicant for a flat. • Your average gross monthly household income for the previous 12 months must be below S$9,000. • You must have been continuously employed for the past 12 months before applying for the flat. • The flat must have a lease duration that covers the youngest buyer until they reach the age of 95. If the remaining lease is insufficient, the provided EHG will be prorated accordingly. Exceptions are made for buyers of 2-room Flexi flats on short leases. • You cannot own any private properties or land, whether locally or overseas. Additionally, you should not have disposed of any of these properties within the last 30 months. Note that first-time single citizens purchasing a flat under the Single Singapore Citizen Scheme or Joint Singles Scheme are limited to only buying 2-room Flexi flats. Nonetheless, they can still take advantage of the EHG.  Source: Enhanced CPF Housing Grant (EHG)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/enhanced-cpf-housing-grant-ehg/  (index: Enhanced CPF Housing Grant (EHG))

term: How much Enhanced CPF Housing Grant (EHG) can I get
definition: According to the new property cooling measures 2024, eligible first-time families seeking new flats can now receive an EHG of up to S$120,000, while eligible first-time singles can benefit from an EHG (Singles) of up to S$60,000. For eligible first-timer singles who buy a resale flat, they can receive up to $115,000 in housing grants comprising the revised EHG of up to $60,000, a CPF Housing Grant of up to $40,000, and a PHG of up to $15,000. term: a Power of Attorney (POA)
definition: A Power of Attorney (POA) is a legal instrument in which one person delegates authority to another. It is often used for legal transactions like purchasing, selling, or renting real estate. The donor is the individual who created the document, while the person authorised to act on behalf of the person granting the POA is called the donee. term: types of Power of Attorney (POA) available in Singapore
definition: The following are 5 types of POAs, each serving different purposes; If the POA agreement does not clearly outline the donee’s authority in particular situations, then the general POA allows the donee to represent the donor in all cases. With a general POA, the donee has the power to perform various tasks, such as engaging in legal and financial transactions, handling property, signing contracts for the donor, submitting tax returns, and other related duties. A general POA remains effective unless it is cancelled in the following instances; • Revocation by the donor • Death of the donor • Incapacity of the donor • Or when a particular event is specified in the POA. Under this type of POA, the donee is authorised to act on behalf of the donor but only in the designated areas. A special POA can be revoked in similar ways to a general POA. An individual can use the LPA to give legal authority to a donee to manage their affairs in the case of a loss of mental capacity. In Singapore, the LPA is regulated by the Mental Capacity Act. The LPA permits the donee to make decisions on behalf of the donor regarding their personal, financial, and property matters when the donor cannot do so. By having an LPA, the donor and their family can avoid potential uncertainty and issues arising from mental incapacity. To ensure that the donor understands the purpose and consequences of the LPA, the certificate issuer must confirm that the LPA is valid and was created without any fraud, coercion, or undue pressure. Follow these general steps to create an LPA: • Complete the LPA application by selecting a trusted donee who is at least 21 years old and specifying the powers to be granted. • Obtain certification from an LPA certificate issuer (E.g., a practising lawyer, a psychiatrist, or an accredited medical practitioner) • Submit the completed LPA application to the Office of the Public Guardian. The Housing and Development Board (HDB) POA is the most common type of POA in Singapore. It is required when a homebuyer is unable to attend the appointment to collect their keys or appear in person for the signing of various documents, including; • Sales Contract • Lease Contract • Option to Purchase Agreement • Deed of Assignment • Lease in Escrow • and Mortgage in Escrow Individuals located overseas who cannot sign legal documents in Singapore will also use HDB POAs, typically by hiring a lawyer to act on their behalf. The POA will outline the specific rights granted to the attorney, such as the authority to complete transactions, sign documents, and return funds to the CPF Board. The Springing POA, also called the Conditional POA, is a type of POA that is activated only when a specific event occurs. During the creation of the POA, it is important to define the specific event that will trigger the activation of the POA. For example, the POA may grant authority to the donee only when the donor is located overseas. term: Who is a Notary Public
definition: A Notary Public in Singapore is a qualified lawyer appointed by the Board of Commissioners for Oaths and Notaries Public to perform notarization of documents. These lawyers must meet certain criteria, such as being at least 40 years old and having a minimum of 15 years of legal experience. The Notaries Public Act governs the activities of Notaries Public in Singapore. To qualify as a Notary Public, individuals must be deemed “fit and proper persons” and currently practising advocates and solicitors in Singapore. Those who have declared bankruptcy, been struck off the advocates and solicitors’ roll, or found guilty of misconduct rendering them unsuitable for the role will have their appointments revoked.  Source: Notary Public  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/notary-public/  (index: Notary Public)

term: What does a Notary Public do
definition: The main role of a Notary Public is to witness, authenticate, and certify the execution of documents. When you sign a document before a Notary Public, you are affirming the truthfulness of its information. Their primary responsibility is to prevent fraud and ensure that individuals sign documents willingly and without coercion.  Source: Notary Public  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/notary-public/  (index: Notary Public)

term: Do I need a Notary Public
definition: Engaging a Notary Public becomes necessary when there is a legal requirement for notarization, and it is often a prerequisite when sending documents from Singapore to overseas entities. Here are some instances where you might need to involve a Notary Public: • Verifying the signature and execution of documents like deeds, contracts, powers of attorney, incorporation papers, property transfers, Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) assignments, and other instruments to be used abroad. In business transactions, relevant parties may need to be present at the signing, and the Notary Public acts as a witness to ensure compliance with such requirements. • Administering oaths or affirmations for affidavits or statutory declarations, and attesting such documents. • Certifying true copies of documents such as passports and bank statements. The Notary Public verifies that the copies are genuine representations of the originals through a visual comparison. • Handling protests for bills of exchange, which are signed orders for payment. If the bill is dishonoured, the Notary Public can be involved in protesting the bill. • Recording a ship’s protest, a statement that protects shipowners and crew members from liability by attributing damages to maritime perils rather than negligence. Even when notarization is not explicitly required, going through the notarization process can help reduce the risk of document forgery and assure business parties that the documents are authentic.  Source: Notary Public  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/notary-public/  (index: Notary Public)

term: redlining
definition: Redlining is a discriminatory practice in real estate, typically involving lenders that refuse to lend money or extend credit to borrowers in certain areas of a city. While redlining is illegal and not practiced in Singapore, understanding its implications is important for a global perspective on real estate. term: Understanding redlining
definition: Redlining originated in the United States in the 1930s, when government-sponsored corporations created maps of urban areas, marking “risky” neighbourhoods in red. These areas, often home to racial or ethnic minorities, were then used by banks and insurance companies to deny or price services. This discriminatory practice led to a lack of investment in these neighbourhoods, contributing to their decline and perpetuating socio-economic disparities.  Source: Redlining  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/redlining-definition-understanding-importance-in-real-estate/  (index: Redlining)

term: Importance of redlining in real estate
definition: While redlining is not practiced in Singapore, understanding this discriminatory practice can provide insights into the importance of fair lending practices and regulations in maintaining a healthy and inclusive real estate market. It underscores the need for regulations to prevent discrimination in lending and to ensure equal access to housing. [HEADING-H3] Conclusion Redlining is a discriminatory practice that has shaped urban landscapes and perpetuated socio-economic disparities. While not practiced in Singapore, its history serves as a reminder of the importance of fair lending practices in real estate. It underscores the need for vigilance and regulation to ensure that everyone has equal access to housing opportunities. term: loan-to-value (LTV) ratio
definition: The LTV decides the highest amount of money you can borrow to fund your house. This affects how much cash or CPF Ordinary Account savings you must pay as a down payment. It’s applicable whenever you take a home loan to finance your property purchase, regardless of whether it’s your first, second, or subsequent mortgage. For example, if your LTV ratio is 70%, you can borrow as much as 70% of the value of your property, or the price you pay to purchase it, whichever is lower. Remember that for newly launched properties such as new HDB flats, new executive condos (ECs), and new launch condominiums, the LTV ratio will always be based on the purchase price. LTV ratios are implemented as a precaution to prevent borrowers from borrowing too much money and becoming over-leveraged. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) establishes the LTV limits, which differ based on whether you obtain a bank or HDB loan.  Source: Loan-to-value (LTV) ratio  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/loan-to-value-ltv-ratio/  (index: Loan-to-value (LTV) ratio)

term: What types of loan-to-value (LTV) ratios are there
definition: There are two primary types of LTV to consider when buying a property locally. If you’re buying an HDB property, including BTO flats, sales of balance flats, re-offer of balance flats, or resale flats, you can get a maximum LTV ratio of 75% from HDB. This means you can borrow up to 75% of the property’s value from HDB. You can use cash or a mix of cash and savings from your CPF OA to pay the down payment. If you want a bank loan instead of an HDB loan, the maximum LTV ratio is also 75% for the first loan. When paying the remaining 25% of the property price, you must pay 5% of it in cash. The remaining 20% can be paid using cash and savings from your CPF OA. Note that the HDB or banks are not obligated to approve the full LTV amount. They may approve a lower LTV limit or even reject your application completely. The information provided was accurate at the time of publication. For the latest changes and updates, head over to the official websites. term: amortisation
definition: Amortisation divides a loan into fixed payments over time, allowing the borrower to pay off the principal and loan interest without making a large lump sum payment. As a result, each monthly payment includes both interest and principal payments, with the proportion varying throughout the repayment period. The process involves calculating the precise amount of each payment so that the loan can be paid off within a predetermined period, usually 15 to 30 years. This predetermined time frame is commonly referred to as the loan term by bankers and brokers. Opting for amortisation can make a home loan more affordable by providing a fixed-rate payment method that can be budgeted for each month. In Singapore, mortgages generally follow a fully amortising system. This implies that if a loan has a 25-year term, the borrower will have fully repaid the principal amount by the end of the term as long as they have made regular monthly payments.  Source: Amortisation  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/amortisation/  (index: Amortisation)

term: What does an amortisation loan schedule look like
definition: The amortisation schedule provides a detailed monthly breakdown of the principal and interest payments for an amortised loan. While the monthly payments are constant, the amount of interest and principal paid will vary each month due to the changing loan balance. Initially, the payment’s interest portion typically makes up a larger portion of the total payment and gradually decreases over time. Conversely, the principal portion of the payment is initially smaller and increases towards the end of the repayment period. Understanding how to read and use an amortisation schedule is essential for managing your mortgage payments. The borrower and lender can track future payments and remaining loan balances using the schedule.  Source: Amortisation  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/amortisation/  (index: Amortisation)

term: How would an unamortised loan work
definition: If a lender has an unamortised loan, they will only pay the interest during the loan period, with the principal balance paid in a lump sum at the end of the loan term. Although monthly payments are lower in unamortised loans, the borrower needs to plan and save for the balloon payment due at the end of the term. However, the lender can make extra monthly payments to the principal loan during the loan term, easing the burden of paying the balloon payment all at once. term: mortgage subordination
definition: Mortgage subordination changes the priority status of different loans secured against your home. It ensures that your original mortgage keeps the first lien position, while the HELOC or second mortgage gets a lower priority status. term: Why is subordination necessary

To avoid early repayment, you need to get the lender’s permission to take out a second loan. This is done through subordination. Though, when it comes to home loans, while subordination is a common practice in Western markets, it’s not frequently seen in Singapore due to the difficulty in finding a bank willing to agree to subordinate its lien.  Source: Subordination  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/subordination/  (index: Subordination)

term: How does subordination work
definition: You start by requesting subordination from your original mortgage lender. This gives them priority over the new lender in case of default. If approved, you’ll sign a subordination agreement stating that the second lender cannot foreclose or otherwise jeopardise the first mortgage. This satisfies the original lender while allowing you to access your equity.  Source: Subordination  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/subordination/  (index: Subordination)

term: benefits of subordination

It also lets you consolidate high-interest debt at a lower rate through a second mortgage or HELOC. Overall, subordination provides flexibility in using your equity. term: Money market funds 101: Your complete guide to understanding these low-risk investments
definition: Money market funds are a popular low-risk investment option for those looking to earn a modest return while keeping their principal safe. If you’re new to investing or want a conservative place to park your cash, money market funds deserve a close look. This guide will explain what money market funds are, who they are suitable for, their risks and returns, and how to invest in them. [HEADING-H3] What are money market funds? A money market fund is a type of mutual fund that invests in highly liquid, short-term debt instruments such as Treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit (CDs), and repurchase agreements. The fund’s investments have maturities of one year or less. Money market funds aim to keep their net asset value (NAV) at a stable $1 per share. Money market funds allow you to earn interest on your cash while enjoying easy liquidity. You can typically invest or withdraw at any time without fees or redemption gates. This makes them a safe place to put your cash as you wait to deploy it elsewhere. [HEADING-H3] Who are money market funds for? Money market funds are appropriate for conservative investors who want to earn modest yields without much risk. They can be a good fit if you: • Have excess cash from an inheritance, home sale, or other windfall • Keep an emergency fund or cash for short-term goals • Park funds for a large upcoming purchase like a down payment • Prefer low-risk investments over stock market volatility Businesses also use money market funds as a safe place to hold operating cash. [HEADING-H3] Risks and returns of money market funds Money market funds have ultralow risk profiles. They are not guaranteed by the FDIC, but they are seen as very safe. The biggest risk is the remote possibility that the fund’s share price could dip below $1 if investments default. This last occurred during the 2008 financial crisis when the Reserve Primary Fund “broke the buck.” Money market funds pay modest yields. Over the past decade, their average annual returns have hovered between 0% and 2%. That’s much lower than stock returns but higher than a regular savings account. When short-term rates rise, money market yields also increase. [HEADING-H3] How to invest in money market funds You have a few options for investing in money market funds: • Workplace retirement plans often have a money market investment option. You can direct some of your contributions here if you want a cash allocation. • Brokerage firms like Fidelity and Vanguard offer money market mutual funds that you can purchase through a standard or IRA account. • Banks sell money market deposit accounts, which are FDIC-insured savings products with check-writing privileges. However, MMA yields are lower than true money market funds. Look at factors like minimum investments, fees, and historical returns when choosing a specific money market fund. Leading providers like Fidelity and Vanguard offer very competitive options. Money market funds offer a blend of high liquidity, ultralow risk, and modest yields. Keep them in mind if you have excess cash and want a safe place to invest it for the short term. They can play an important role in a conservative portfolio.  Source: Money market funds  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/money-market-funds/  (index: Money market funds)

term: Using Net Asset Value to Analyze REITs
definition: Real estate investment trusts (REITs) are a popular way for investors to gain exposure to real estate assets without having to directly own or manage properties. When analyzing REITs to determine their value and potential as an investment, one of the most useful metrics is net asset value (NAV). Here’s an overview of how NAV works and why it’s so insightful for REIT analysis. [HEADING-H3] What is net asset value? Net asset value, commonly referred to as NAV, represents the net value of a REIT’s assets minus its liabilities. In other words, it’s what shareholders would receive if the REIT sold off all its assets and paid back debts. NAV is calculated per share, so it shows the intrinsic value of each share if liquidated. NAV differs from a REIT’s market price per share, which fluctuates daily based on market factors. NAV aims to show the REIT’s stable value based solely on its portfolio and finances. [HEADING-H3] Why NAV for REITs? For most stocks and securities, metrics like the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio and price-to-book (P/B) ratio are used to evaluate valuation. However, these don’t work as well for REITs because accounting rules cause their earnings and book values to be less meaningful. REITs must depreciate their real estate assets over time, even as the properties maintain or gain value. This depresses earnings and book value on paper. NAV avoids this issue by appraising the real estate at current market prices. NAV also accounts for the value of all assets and liabilities. With P/E and P/B, intangibles like management skills, brand value, and off-balance sheet debts aren’t considered. NAV provides a more comprehensive look at what shareholders would receive from a REIT if dissolved. Comparing a REIT’s NAV per share to its actual market price is one of the most useful applications of NAV. The relationship indicates whether the REIT may be overvalued or undervalued. If the market price is lower than NAV, the REIT could be undervalued. Investors can buy shares for less than their actual worth. If the market price is higher than NAV, the REIT may be overvalued. Investors are paying a premium above the value of the REIT’s assets. Of course, NAV isn’t a perfect measure. Appraisals can be imprecise, and NAV doesn’t account for factors like management skills that affect value. But it provides an insightful reference point for comparison to market pricing. Looking at how a REIT’s NAV changes over time is also illuminating. Growth in NAV indicates the portfolio is becoming more valuable – a positive sign for shareholders. Declining NAV may be a red flag, signalling property values are decreasing. Comparing NAV trends for different REITs helps identify those with the most appreciation and strongest portfolios. REITs with rising NAV per share are typically sound long-term investments. [HEADING-H3] The bottom line Net asset value shines light on a REIT’s intrinsic value from its real estate holdings. Analyzing NAV versus market price over time provides useful valuation metrics for REITs that other ratios can’t offer. While not perfect, NAV gives investors a vital data point for evaluating REIT performance, growth potential, and downside risk.  Source: Net asset value  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/net-asset-value/  (index: Net asset value)

term: a CMBS
definition: A CMBS is a financial product comprising bundled commercial real estate loans. These loans are packaged together by issuers and sold to investors. term: Tranches in CMBS
definition: Central to understanding CMBS is the notion of tranches. When commercial mortgages are bundled into a CMBS, the cash flows from these loans are organised into different tranches or classes. Each tranche possesses distinct risk levels, interest payments, and maturity periods. Typically, a CMBS structure includes: • Senior tranche: The highest-rated tranche with the lowest risk, prioritised for interest payments and principal repayment. • Mezzanine tranche: Exhibits higher risk compared to the senior tranche, with lower credit ratings and payments received after the senior tranche. • Junior tranche: Also known as the equity or first-loss tranche, it carries the highest risk and lowest rating, absorbing losses first in case of loan defaults. • IO Strip: Some CMBS include an interest-only strip, receiving only interest payments with no claim to principal repayment. This tiered structure enables fixed income investors to assume exposure to commercial real estate debt across various risk and reward levels.  Source: CMBS  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/cmbs/  (index: CMBS)

term: Benefits of CMBS Tranches
definition: The segmentation of CMBS deals into different risk levels offers advantages for both investors and lenders: • Investors can select their desired risk-return profile, with conservative investors favouring senior tranches and risk-tolerant investors opting for junior tranches. • Risk is distributed across multiple investors rather than concentrated with a single lender, enhancing market stability. • Issuers can tailor tranches to meet investor demand, facilitating easier CMBS sales. • Lenders can originate larger loans since they can sell them off via securitisation, thereby providing more capital to the commercial real estate market.
