term: Am I Eligible for the Family Grant Proximity Housing Grant (PHG) in Singapore
definition: To be eligible for the PHG, the individual must meet the following requirements: • They should hold Singapore Citizenship (SC). • Their family nucleus must comprise at least one individual who is either an SC or a Singapore Permanent Resident. • If applying as a family, they must be at least 21 years old or older. • If applying as a single, they must be 35 years old or older. • They should not have previously received the PHG subsidy. • The resale flat intended for purchase must have a lease of 20 years or more. • The HDB resale flat must fulfill one of the following criteria: It should be located within 4 km of their parents’ HDB flat. It should be situated within 4 km of the private residential property where their parents reside. • It should be located within 4 km of their parents’ HDB flat. • It should be situated within 4 km of the private residential property where their parents reside.  Source: Family Grant Proximity Housing Grant (PHG)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/family-grant-proximity-housing-grant-phg/  (index: Family Grant Proximity Housing Grant (PHG))

term: How much can I get from the Family Grant Proximity Housing Grant (PHG)
definition: Individuals planning to purchase a resale flat to reside with their parents will be entitled to a grant of S$30,000. However, if they buy a resale flat near their parents, they will receive a grant of S$20,000. Eligible single individuals, on the other hand, will receive S$15,000 and S$10,000, respectively, for living with or near their parents. The information provided was accurate at the time of publication. For the latest changes and updates, you can check the Singapore official website.  Source: Family Grant Proximity Housing Grant (PHG)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/family-grant-proximity-housing-grant-phg/  (index: Family Grant Proximity Housing Grant (PHG))
aliases: How much can I get from the Family Grant Proximity Housing Grant|PHG|HFGPHG

term: an open house
definition: In real estate, an open house refers to a specific period set in advance, allowing prospective buyers to explore a house. It presents the ideal occasion to showcase your residence and attract potential buyers to encourage them to submit an offer. Additionally, it conveys to prospective homebuyers your earnest dedication to selling your property. During this time, property owners or tenants usually vacate the premises to facilitate the open house, which a real estate agent oversees.  Source: Open house  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/open-house/  (index: Open house)

term: Why is an open house important
definition: Hosting an open house holds paramount significance for both sellers and potential buyers. For sellers: • Maximising exposure: An open house provides an exceptional opportunity to showcase the property to many potential buyers. By allowing numerous individuals to visit and experience the property firsthand, sellers can attract more interest and increase the chances of finding the right buyer. • Creating competition: The sense of urgency created by an open house often leads to a competitive atmosphere among potential buyers. Multiple interested parties visiting the property simultaneously can result in a quicker sale and potentially higher offers. • Showcasing features: During an open house, sellers can emphasise the property’s unique features, layout, and amenities. This personal touch can help buyers envision themselves living in the space, making them more likely to form an emotional connection and consider making an offer. For buyers: • Convenience: Open houses typically occur during weekends or other convenient times, allowing potential buyers to explore properties without having to schedule individual appointments. This convenience encourages a larger pool of interested buyers to attend. • Immediate feedback: Attending an open house enables buyers to ask questions directly to the listing agent and gather important information about the property. This immediate feedback can help buyers make informed decisions about whether the property meets their needs. • Comparative analysis: Open houses often allow buyers to view multiple properties in a single day, facilitating direct comparisons. This process can assist buyers in narrowing down their choices and identifying the most suitable property.  Source: Open house  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/open-house/  (index: Open house)

term: Singapore National Day
definition: The National Day in Singapore commemorates the country’s establishment as an independent city-state. Its origins can be traced back to 1963 when Singapore and the Federations of Malaya, Sarawak, and Sabah merged to form Malaysia. However, due to significant challenges and circumstances, the merger proved to be unviable. As a result, in 1965, Singapore emerged as a sovereign state. Today, Singaporeans celebrate National Day on August 9th each year, to signify their unity, patriotism, and the nation’s progress. This is a public holiday in Singapore, with government institutions, schools, and businesses remaining closed.  Source: Singapore National Day  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/singapore-national-day/  (index: Singapore National Day)

term: What happens during Singapore National Day
definition: One of the highlights of the Singapore National Day is the grand parade, usually at Marina Bay, the National Stadium, or the Padang. The parade features the participation of various groups, including the Armed Forces, Police Force, Civil Defense Force, representatives from political parties, and members of labour unions. Students from uniformed organisations such as the Girl Guides, Scouts, and Cadet Corps also join in the procession. Adding to the spectacle, the Singapore Air Force presents a captivating flyover with a display of numerous military aircraft. Every year since 1966, the Prime Minister of Singapore records a National Day Message, which is delivered on the eve of National Day. The message covers domestic and global developments, economic performance and outlook, national priorities, and government plans. Following the address, a fireworks display accompanies the festivities, choir performances, school band shows, and other entertaining presentations. Although National Day is observed on August 9th annually, preparations and rehearsals start around 3 to 4 months ahead of time, with preview shows commencing approximately two weeks earlier.  Source: Singapore National Day  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/singapore-national-day/  (index: Singapore National Day)

term: property cooling measures
definition: In the realm of real estate, property cooling measures are policies that the government puts into action with an aim to preserve a stable and sustainable property market. Their main purpose is to thwart the creation of property bubbles, which can precipitate serious economic fallout if they burst. In the Singaporean context, the government frequently rolls out property cooling measures when the property market shows signs of overheating.  Source: Property cooling measures in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-property-cooling-measures-in-singapore/  (index: Property cooling measures in Singapore)

term: Factors influencing property cooling measures and the application process
definition: Several elements contribute to the decision to implement property cooling measures. These can range from sudden surges in property prices and high transaction volumes to low interest rates and a robust demand for property. The government keeps a close watch on these elements and may roll out cooling measures as required to maintain market equilibrium.  Source: Property cooling measures in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-property-cooling-measures-in-singapore/  (index: Property cooling measures in Singapore)

term: Comparing property cooling measures with other market regulations
definition: Property cooling measures are often juxtaposed with other market regulations like loan-to-value limits and stamp duties. Even though these regulations can also sway the property market, they serve different functions. For instance, loan-to-value limits are there to prevent borrowers from overcommitting, whereas stamp duties are taxes levied on property transactions.  Source: Property cooling measures in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-property-cooling-measures-in-singapore/  (index: Property cooling measures in Singapore)

term: Advantages and disadvantages of property cooling measures
definition: The primary benefit of property cooling measures lies in their ability to uphold a stable and sustainable property market. By averting the formation of property bubbles, they shield property buyers and the broader economy. On the downside, property cooling measures can pose challenges. They can make it tougher for first-time buyers to dip their toes in the market, and they may trigger a deceleration in the property market, potentially affecting developers and other stakeholders in the industry.  Source: Property cooling measures in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-property-cooling-measures-in-singapore/  (index: Property cooling measures in Singapore)

term: Types of property cooling measures
definition: Over the years, Singapore has enacted a range of property cooling measures such as increased stamp duties, reduced loan-to-value limits, and limitations on the number of properties individuals can possess. The precise measures that are implemented hinge on the market conditions at any given time. [HEADING-H3] Conclusion In a nutshell, even though property cooling measures can affect property buyers and sellers, they serve a pivotal role in fostering a stable and sustainable property market in Singapore.  Source: Property cooling measures in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/understanding-property-cooling-measures-in-singapore/  (index: Property cooling measures in Singapore)

term: a property title deed
definition: A property’s title deed is a legal document that contains a complete record of all transactions related to a specific piece of registered property in Singapore. This document is important as it provides the following details: • Description of the property • Type of ownership (leasehold or freehold) • Information about ownership interests and any encumbrances like mortgages on the property • Names of the property owners, serving as proof of ownership Before a sale and purchase agreement can be finalised, it is essential to establish proof of a clear title, which is provided by a valid title deed. The title deed verifies the rightful owner and ensures the property is free from encumbrances or other issues.  Source: Property title deed Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/property-title-deeds/  (index: Property title deed Singapore)
aliases: What is a property title deed?

term: types of property title deeds available
definition: In Singapore, there are several types of title deeds, including: • Certificate of Title for landed properties such as terrace houses or bungalows. • Subsidiary Strata Certificate of Title for condominiums and other apartment units. • Subsidiary Certificate of Title for Housing Development Board (HDB) flats.  Source: Property title deed Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/property-title-deeds/  (index: Property title deed Singapore)
aliases: What are the types of property title deeds available?

term: Where is the property title deed kept
definition: Your property title deed will be printed and sent to you for safekeeping under the following conditions: • When you purchase the property without a mortgage or CPF funds • Once you have fully paid off the mortgage and/or CPF funds  Source: Property title deed Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/property-title-deeds/  (index: Property title deed Singapore)

term: How to obtain or view a copy of your property title deeds
definition: If you have not received a printed and released title document, it is advisable to review your title deed before engaging in any transaction. For owners of private properties or digitised HDB flats, you can easily access your title deed online at no cost through MyProperty by SLA. This online service is always accessible 24/7 and requires logging in with your SingPass. However, you can only check title records for properties where you are the registered owner or have lodged a caveat as a purchaser. If your property is not listed on MyProperty, it may be caused by one of the following reasons: • No caveat lodged by you as the purchaser for the private property or HDB flat you have purchased. • The property was purchased under a trust arrangement, with you as the beneficiary rather than the trustee. • The identification number used during login differs from the records maintained by SLA.  Source: Property title deed Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/property-title-deeds/  (index: Property title deed Singapore)

term: a conveyancing lawyer
definition: Conveyancing involves the transfer of legal ownership of a property from one individual to another. Conveyancing lawyers can guide you throughout the property buying or selling transaction process. They possess expertise in various aspects, including negotiating purchase or sale agreements and managing the transfer of ownership following a successful transaction. Moreover, they are equipped to address any legal matters that may emerge throughout the process.  Source: Conveyancing lawyer  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/conveyancing-lawyer/  (index: Conveyancing lawyer)

term: What does a conveyancing lawyer do
definition: A conveyancing lawyer can support you by: • Creating the necessary conveyancing contracts, including the Option to Purchase (OTP) and the sale and purchase agreement. • Acting as a witness during the contract signing and engaging in negotiations with the other party’s lawyer. • Facilitating communication and coordination with relevant parties, such as banks and government authorities, including the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board, the Singapore Land Authority (SLA), the Housing Development Board (HDB), and the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS), among other responsibilities.  Source: Conveyancing lawyer  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/conveyancing-lawyer/  (index: Conveyancing lawyer)

term: Do I need a conveyancing lawyer
definition: However, HDB buyers with a bank loan to finance the flat purchase and private property buyers must engage a private law firm to act as their legal representatives for the conveyancing process.  Source: Conveyancing lawyer  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/conveyancing-lawyer/  (index: Conveyancing lawyer)

term: Defects Liability Period (DLP)
definition: The Defects Liability Period (DLP) is a designated timeframe specified in the property’s sale and purchase agreement. It holds the developer accountable for addressing and resolving any defects found within the individual units, the overall project, or communal spaces. These defects may include cracks, stains, or faulty power points. Therefore, it is important to thoroughly inspect your home for any damages, poor workmanship, or missing fixtures/appliances that were not part of the agreed-upon sale and purchase agreement. If you identify any defects and report them within this timeframe, the developer must cover the costs and undertake the required repairs or rectification works. It’s important to note that the DLP applies to issues arising from the construction process rather than normal wear and tear.  Source: Defects Liability Period (DLP)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/dlp-what-is-the-defects-liability-period-dlp/  (index: Defects Liability Period (DLP))
aliases: What is the Defects Liability Period (DLP)?|Defects Liability Period|DLP

term: How long does the Defects Liability Period (DLP) last
definition: The duration of the DLP varies based on the terms and conditions stated in your property’s sale and purchase agreement. Typically, the DLP lasts 12 months (1 year) starting from whichever comes first: • The day you receive your keys (vacant possession), or • The 15th day after the Temporary Occupation Permit (TOP) is issued. Example:  If your TOP was issued on 1 Jan but you only received keys on 1 April, your DLP starts on 15 Jan, not April It’s crucial to note that receiving the TOP does not necessarily mean immediate key collection, and there may be a delay of several months. As a result, you will have a shorter time frame to enter your new home, conduct inspections, and report any identified defects.  Source: Defects Liability Period (DLP)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/dlp-what-is-the-defects-liability-period-dlp/  (index: Defects Liability Period (DLP))

term: What should you do when you identify the defects
definition: If you come across any defects in your property, here are the steps you can take: To report defects in HDB properties, you have two options: Submit a rectification request online through the HDB website or visit the temporary Building Service Centre in person and file a rectification request. Following your request, the Building Service Centre will schedule a joint inspection. The reported defects will be verified during this inspection, and a contractor will be assigned to address them. Once the defects have been rectified, a subsequent inspection will be arranged for you to confirm that the necessary fixes have been implemented. For newly constructed condominium units or landed properties, follow these steps: • Obtain a defect reporting form from the developer and submit it to report the identified defects. • The developer should respond within one month and proceed with rectifying the defects. If the developer fails to take appropriate action, you can inform the developer of your intention to engage a contractor to fix the defects and provide an estimated cost if possible. In the case that the developer continues to neglect the defects for another 14 days, you have the right to hire a contractor to rectify the defects. Just be sure to keep photographic evidence and detailed notes of the defects as proof, and retain the receipts for the contract work to support your claim for reimbursement from the developer.  Source: Defects Liability Period (DLP)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/dlp-what-is-the-defects-liability-period-dlp/  (index: Defects Liability Period (DLP))

term: Singapore Interbank Offer Rate (SIBOR)
definition: Singapore Interbank Offer Rate, or SIBOR, is the estimated amount a bank predicts it will need to pay to borrow Singapore dollars from another bank. This estimation is determined by a panel of contributor banks through daily submissions. Soon, Swap Offer Rate (SOR) and SIBOR will no longer be used because financial markets worldwide are shifting to interest rate benchmarks that use real transaction data to calculate them. The 6-month SIBOR has already been phased down since March 31, 2022, while the commonly used 1-month and 3-month SIBOR will be discontinued right after December 31, 2024. As a result, SORA (Singapore Overnight Rate Average) will replace SOR and SIBOR as a new benchmark.  Source: Singapore Interbank Offer Rate (SIBOR)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/singapore-interbank-offer-rate-sibor/  (index: Singapore Interbank Offer Rate (SIBOR))
aliases: What is the Singapore Interbank Offer Rate (SIBOR)?|Singapore Interbank Offer Rate|SIBOR|SIOR

term: How is SIBOR calculated
definition: The Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS) determines SIBOR daily by collecting interest rate data from its 20 member banks. To calculate the SIBOR, at least 12 member banks must submit their daily interest rates. If more than 12 member banks submit their rates, the top and bottom 25% are discarded to derive an average SIBOR. If fewer than 12 banks report their rates, no SIBOR is calculated for that day.  Source: Singapore Interbank Offer Rate (SIBOR)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/singapore-interbank-offer-rate-sibor/  (index: Singapore Interbank Offer Rate (SIBOR))

term: What influences the SIBOR
definition: The following factors can affect the SIBOR: • The exchange rates and connected economies • The supply and demand of transferring funds among banks, borrowers, and equity funds in Singapore • The overnight funds market • The United States federal funds rates  Source: Singapore Interbank Offer Rate (SIBOR)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/singapore-interbank-offer-rate-sibor/  (index: Singapore Interbank Offer Rate (SIBOR))

term: What should SIBOR borrowers expect
definition: If you have loans that use the 6-month SIBOR as a reference rate, your bank should have contacted you about your options. If you haven’t been contacted, you should immediately get in touch with your bank, as the 6-month SIBOR is no longer used. For those who use 1-month or 3-month SIBOR, information on how to switch your loan will be provided later, as these reference rates will only be discontinued after December 31 2024. To make the transition easier for everyone, if you switch to a SORA package with the same bank, you won’t have to recalculate your Mortgage Servicing Ratio (MSR) and Total Debt Servicing Ratio (TDSR). If you want to refinance your property loan with another financial institution, you should check for any other TDSR exemptions. For example, owner-occupiers are exempt from TDSR when refinancing their property loans.  Source: Singapore Interbank Offer Rate (SIBOR)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/singapore-interbank-offer-rate-sibor/  (index: Singapore Interbank Offer Rate (SIBOR))

term: GST
definition: Goods and Services Tax (GST), also known as Value Added Tax (VAT) in many other countries, is a consumption tax paid on the supply of commodities and services in Singapore and the import of goods into Singapore. GST is an indirect tax that is applied to the selling price of products and services delivered by GST-registered business entities in Singapore. It is now 8% and will be raised to 9% in January 2024.  Source: GST in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/gst-singapore/  (index: GST in Singapore)

term: How does GST work
definition: For example, if you charge a customer in Singapore S$100 for your services, you must invoice your customer S$107 (S$100 for your service + 7% GST). This invoiced GST amount obtained from the client on behalf of the tax authorities must then be paid to the Singapore tax department quarterly via GST tax filing.  Source: GST in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/gst-singapore/  (index: GST in Singapore)

term: Why do we need GST
definition: It is viewed as a mechanism to reduce personal and corporate income tax rates while also providing a consistent cash flow to the Singapore government regardless of the status of the economy. Furthermore, because this is a consumption tax rather than an income tax, it is regarded as more equitable. It encourages individuals to save and invest in fostering a more stable economy. The GST rise funds government spending that benefits Singaporeans, by allocating the funds to improving healthcare, education, and security. These funds can be used to not only improve the infrastructure required in these fields, but also hire capable professionals, employ better technological solutions, and put in place more efficient processes. Ultimately, raising the GST is required to meet our country’s growing demands. In addition, the GST Voucher scheme assists lower and middle-income Singaporeans in offsetting a portion of their GST expenditures.  Source: GST in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/gst-singapore/  (index: GST in Singapore)

term: Should I register my company for GST
definition: You have to register your company for GST when; • Your company’s annual revenue exceeds S$1 million. This is known as the retrospective basis. • You are currently generating revenue and can predict that annual revenue will exceed S$1 million within the next 12 months. This is known as the prospective basis. Included in this are any contracts or agreements you have made in which your anticipated annual revenue exceeds S$1 million. You have 30 days to submit the GST application to IRAS once your income exceeds S$1 million. Penalties will apply if your company isn’t registered with IRAS within the allotted time frame.  Source: GST in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/gst-singapore/  (index: GST in Singapore)

term: Advantages and Disadvantages of GST in Singapore:
definition: Advantages Disadvantages:  Source: GST in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/gst-singapore/  (index: GST in Singapore)

term: World Gourmet Summit (WGS)
definition: The World Gourmet Summit (WGS), which began in 1997, is an annual event initially organised by the Singapore Tourism Board (STB) and later taken over by Peter Knipp Holdings (PKH) after the second edition. This summit attracts internationally acclaimed chefs who showcase their culinary expertise, making it a popular choice among locals and tourists. Since its debut in July 1997, the event has gained increasing global attention and response, expanding from one to two weeks in 2003.  Source: World Gourmet Summit (WGS)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/world-gourmet-summit-wgs/  (index: World Gourmet Summit (WGS))
aliases: What is the World Gourmet Summit (WGS)?|World Gourmet Summit|WGS

term: What happens during the World Gourmet Summit (WGS)
definition: The WGS is an annual celebration of culinary excellence held in Singapore. It attracts renowned master chefs and vintners worldwide, who showcase their gastronomic creations to trade professionals and the general public. Participants can immerse themselves in culinary experiences and wine appreciation with engaging activities such as Masterclasses, Masterchef Safaris, Epicurean Delights, and Vintner’s Dinners. The summit is more than just a financial endeavour for sponsors such as hotels and restaurants. They see it as an opportunity for their local staff to learn from talented chefs and elevate their brand reputation within the industry. In addition to the culinary showcases, the summit presents Awards of Excellence (AOE) to recognise and honour exceptional talent in Singapore’s food and beverage (F&B) industry.  Source: World Gourmet Summit (WGS)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/world-gourmet-summit-wgs/  (index: World Gourmet Summit (WGS))
aliases: What happens during the World Gourmet Summit|WGS|WWGS

term: What awards has the World Gourmet Summit (WGS) won
definition: Over the years, the summit has garnered multiple prestigious awards from the International Festivals & Events Association (IFEA) based in the United States. These awards recognise the summit’s exceptional creativity, innovation, and effort in solidifying Singapore’s reputation as a leading gourmet capital in Asia.  Source: World Gourmet Summit (WGS)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/world-gourmet-summit-wgs/  (index: World Gourmet Summit (WGS))

term: Fair Market Value (FMV)
definition: Fair Market Value (FMV) in real estate estimates the potential selling price of a property in the open market, such as HDB flats, private condos, landed houses, retail spaces, or factory units. Real estate agents commonly rely on FMV to determine an appropriate price range for a home when assisting sellers or buyers in developing a listing or offer strategy. It is important to note that FMV does not directly reflect a home’s actual value. Rather, it is more of a theoretical concept. It represents the approximate amount of money a buyer and seller would likely agree upon through negotiations, assuming normal market conditions. During home-buying, appraisers also consider FMV when preparing an appraisal report, particularly when financing or refinancing a property. While the appraised value provided by a single appraiser may not always align precisely with FMV, the appraisal report remains the prevalent method for estimating it. Beyond real estate transactions, FMV is considered by attorneys, government officials, and insurance companies in various situations, such as divorce, death, eminent domain, and loss caused by natural disasters.  Source: Fair Market Value (FMV)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/fair-market-value-fmv-definition/  (index: Fair Market Value (FMV))
aliases: What is Fair Market Value (FMV)?|Fair Market Value|FMV

term: How to determine Fair Market Value (FMV)
definition: There isn’t a single formula to calculate the FMV, but here are four approaches: It’s important to note that the FMV of a house can fluctuate based on the economy and local housing market conditions. To ensure accuracy, evaluate a property’s value as close to the intended transaction point (buying, selling, or refinancing) as possible.  Source: Fair Market Value (FMV)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/fair-market-value-fmv-definition/  (index: Fair Market Value (FMV))

term: bid in Singapore real estate
definition: A bid refers to the process of making an offer or proposal to purchase a property at an auction or through a competitive bidding process. Bidding allows potential buyers to compete with each other by offering different prices for the property they are interested in. The highest bidder typically wins the auction and secures the property by agreeing to pay the bid amount. Bidding is a common method used in property auctions to determine the final selling price of a property based on the competitive offers made by interested buyers.  Source: Bid  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/bid/  (index: Bid)
aliases: What is bid in Singapore real estate?

term: How to craft a competitive construction bid and stand out from the crowd
definition: The construction industry is highly competitive. When bidding on a new project, it’s important to submit an attractive and accurate bid to stand out from other contractors. Follow these tips to craft a construction bid that gives you the best chance of winning the job. Carefully review the project plans, specifications, and any other documents provided by the client. Make sure you fully understand the scope of work. Visit the job site to assess any access issues or other challenges. The more familiar you are with the project details, the more accurate your bid will be. Calculate your direct construction costs like materials, labour, and equipment rental. Don’t forget to factor in overhead costs like insurance, bonding, permits, and project management. Build in a reasonable profit margin as well. Underestimating costs is one of the biggest mistakes contractors make. Some clients award contracts purely based on lowest bid price. Others use a scored system that factors in things like experience, reputation, and project approach. Know what the client values most so you can tailor your bid accordingly. Even if the bid process is anonymous, find ways to showcase what makes your company qualified. Provide examples of similar projects you’ve completed successfully. Demonstrate knowledge of the latest methods and building codes. Promote awards your firm has won. Follow all instructions precisely. Use the required bid forms and format. Ensure all pricing and details are included. Double check for errors. Submit a neat, professional bid package that conveys competence. If possible, establish rapport with the client before bidding by asking questions and offering solutions. Follow up after submitting your bid as well. The more familiar the client is with you, the better your chances. With proper preparation, accurate estimating, and attention to what the client wants, you can submit competitive construction bids that get the results you want. Pay close attention to the details in the bidding process to stand out from the competition.  Source: Bid  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/bid/  (index: Bid)

term: What is tenancy-in-common?
definition: Tenancy-in-common refers to a situation where multiple individuals share ownership of land or property, with each co-owner holding a specific portion. This share can vary from 30% to 70% or even 1% to 99%. Other unequal share arrangements are also possible and usually explicitly outlined in the property’s title deed. This type of ownership arrangement is particularly suitable for property owners who are purchasing for investment purposes or for couples who plan to acquire another property in the near future.  Source: Tenancy-in-Common  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/tenancy-in-common/  (index: Tenancy-in-Common)

term: How does tenancy-in-common work
definition: Upon the co-owners demise, their ownership stake in the property is transferred to their beneficiaries. The transfer occurs either according to the provisions specified in the individual’s will or, in the absence of a will, under the Intestate Succession Act (Cap. 146). For instance, Tenant 1 may possess a 60% share, while Tenants 2 and 3 hold 20% each. In the event of Tenant 1’s passing, the 60% ownership share in the property would be transferred to their beneficiaries, while the ownership stakes of Tenants 2 and 3 would remain unchanged. This arrangement allows for a fair division of ownership interests and ensures that the property remains collectively owned even in the face of individual changes in ownership.  Source: Tenancy-in-Common  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/tenancy-in-common/  (index: Tenancy-in-Common)

term: How does Tenancy In Common differ from Joint Tenancy
definition: In Joint Tenancy, all co-owners have an equal interest in the property, and there exists a ‘right of survivorship.’ This means when one joint tenant dies, their share automatically passes to the surviving joint tenant(s). This is in stark contrast to TIC, where each owner’s stake may be unequal and does not have the right of survivorship.  Source: Tenancy-in-Common  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/tenancy-in-common/  (index: Tenancy-in-Common)

term: Popular Uses of Tenancy In Common in Singapore
definition: While not as commonly mentioned as Joint Tenancy, TIC is prevalent in various scenarios: Business Partnerships: Business partners might buy property as a joint investment but want flexibility in ownership based on their contribution. Inheritance Planning: Families might use TIC to ensure property shares are distributed among heirs in specific ways. Friends Buying Property Together: Friends who want to invest together but retain the freedom to sell or bequeath their share independently.  Source: Tenancy-in-Common  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/tenancy-in-common/  (index: Tenancy-in-Common)

term: Annual Value (AV) of the property
definition: A property’s Annual Value (AV) refers to the estimated annual rent that could be earned if the property was rented out, excluding maintenance costs and furniture. The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) determines a property’s AV. To make these estimates, IRAS considers various factors such as the property’s size, condition, location, other relevant physical characteristics, and the rentals of comparable properties nearby. It is worth noting that a property’s AV is determined by IRAS’ assessment criteria and not the actual rent earned by the property. The AV remains the same whether the property is vacant, rented, or owner-occupied.  Source: Annual Value of your property  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/annual-value-of-your-property/  (index: Annual Value of your property)
aliases: What is the Annual Value (AV) of the property?|AV

term: Why does IRAS use rentals rather than selling prices to calculate the Annual Value (AV)
definition: This is because there are usually more rental transactions than sales transactions, making it easier to obtain an accurate picture of market activity. Rental price changes are also more predictable than sale price changes, which helps keep the property tax system more stable for property owners. Malaysia and Hong Kong also use a similar method to determine AV. Additionally, it would be unfair to subsequent property owners to base AV on prior purchase prices, as costs of similar properties can change over time. This means newer property owners may have a higher AV if property prices rise.  Source: Annual Value of your property  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/annual-value-of-your-property/  (index: Annual Value of your property)

term: Why is the Annual Value (AV) important
definition: Essentially, AV helps to determine how much tax you need to pay for your property. If your property has a higher AV, you must pay more property tax. term: When will IRAS update my property’s Annual Value (AV)
definition: IRAS checks the AV of properties each year to see if there are changes in the rental values of similar properties in the market. The AV will be amended if the latest market rent data no longer supports your existing AV. If any changes are made to your property that could significantly affect its rental value, IRAS will adjust your AV from the change date. Property owners will receive a Valuation Notice from IRAS, informing them of any AV changes, whether it has gone up or down, and when it will take effect. term: EBITDA
definition: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortisation (EBITDA) is a measure of a company’s operating performance. In the context of real estate investment, it can provide insights into a property’s profitability before the influence of tax structure and financing  Source: EBITDA  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/ebitda/  (index: EBITDA)

term: Understanding EBITDA
definition: EBITDA is calculated by adding back interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation to net income. This metric is often used by investors to compare the financial performance of different companies by eliminating the effects of financing and accounting decisions. It’s a non-GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles) financial figure, meaning it does not adhere to standard accounting rules used for financial reporting. As such, it’s often used in conjunction with other financial metrics for a more complete understanding of a company’s or property’s performance.  Source: EBITDA  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/ebitda/  (index: EBITDA)

term: Importance of EBITDA in Real Estate
definition: In the real estate sector, EBITDA can be a useful tool for comparing the performance of different properties or real estate companies. It can provide a clearer picture of operational performance by focusing on earnings from core business operations, excluding interest, taxes, and non-cash expenses. For instance, a real estate investor might use EBITDA to compare the profitability of two properties before considering the impact of their different financing structures or tax situations. [HEADING-H3] Conclusion EBITDA is a valuable metric for real estate investors, offering a measure of a property’s or a real estate company’s operational profitability. However, it should be used in conjunction with other financial metrics to get a comprehensive view of financial performance. It’s important to note that while EBITDA can provide useful insights, it’s not a substitute for GAAP metrics and should not be used in isolation when making investment decisions.  Source: EBITDA  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/ebitda/  (index: EBITDA)

term: Is GST payable on the residential lease
definition: GST is not applicable on the sale and lease of residential properties. However, non-residential properties are subject to GST. In cases where a property has residential and non-residential parts, only the non-residential portion is subject to GST. When residential properties are furnished, GST should be charged on the supply of movable furniture and fittings. However, certain fixtures like built-in cabinets, wardrobes, kitchen and sanitary wares, and permanently attached wall-mounted air conditioners can be exempted from GST along with the property.  Source: GST Payable on Residential Lease  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/gst-payable-on-residential-lease/  (index: GST Payable on Residential Lease)

term: What residential properties are exempt from GST
definition: Buildings that have received URA approval for “residential use” are eligible for GST exemption. Some examples of URA-approved residential buildings include: • Condominium flats • Detached houses • Semi-detached houses • Terrace houses • Townhouses • Cluster housing • Strata landed houses • The upper floors of shophouse (if they are solely used for residential purposes) • Homes for senior citizens • Serviced apartments • Student hostels • Workers’ dormitories • Welfare homes  Source: GST Payable on Residential Lease  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/gst-payable-on-residential-lease/  (index: GST Payable on Residential Lease)

term: abandonment
definition: Abandonment is the act of giving up the right to a property with no intention of returning. In Singapore’s real estate market, abandonment can have significant legal implications.  Source: Abandonment  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/abandonment-definition-understanding-and-importance/  (index: Abandonment)

term: Understanding abandonment
definition: Abandonment involves the voluntary surrender of property, owned or rented, without naming a successor to own or rent it, and with the intention of not returning. In real estate, abandonment can refer to a homeowner who has left their property permanently and does not intend to return. It can also refer to a tenant who has left a rental property before the end of their lease without intending to return.  Source: Abandonment  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/abandonment-definition-understanding-and-importance/  (index: Abandonment)

term: Importance of abandonment in real estate and property
definition: In the context of real estate, abandonment can have significant legal implications. For instance, a tenant who abandons a rental property before the end of their lease may still be liable for the remaining rent. Similarly, a homeowner who abandons their property may still be liable for mortgage payments, property taxes, and other obligations. [HEADING-H3] Conclusion Abandonment can have significant implications in real estate, affecting both landlords and tenants, as well as homeowners and lenders. Understanding the concept of abandonment can help individuals navigate these issues more effectively. Nonetheless, dealing with abandonment can be complex, and it’s often advisable to seek legal advice.  Source: Abandonment  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/abandonment-definition-understanding-and-importance/  (index: Abandonment)

term: a property agent
definition: Also known as real estate salesperson (RES), property agents are licensed professionals who assist individuals in buying, selling, and renting real estate. Their primary responsibility is to connect buyers and sellers, and they receive payment in the form of a commission, typically a percentage of the property’s sale price. The RES can act on behalf of either the buyer or the seller.  Source: Property agent  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/property-agent/  (index: Property agent)

term: Should my property agent be registered with CEA
definition: The Council for Estate Agencies (CEA) requires all property agents in Singapore to be registered with their respective property agencies. If the RES operates without a licence, they can be fined up to S$75,000 and imprisoned for up to three years. The client may also be affected if an unregistered agent causes any trouble. You can easily verify if a property agent is CEA-registered by checking for their unique registration number. This would be a six-digit code with an alphabet at the front and back. It’s important to note that property agents are prohibited by law from representing both buyers and sellers in a transaction due to potential conflicts of interest that can arise.  Source: Property agent  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/property-agent/  (index: Property agent)

term: Key features of T-Bills
definition: Treasury Bills, commonly called T-Bills, are obtainable in two maturity periods: 6 months and one year. Unlike traditional bonds that make periodic interest payments, T-Bills are initially sold at a price lower than their face value and then redeemed at face value upon reaching maturity. The variance between the purchase price and the face value constitutes the interest earned. For instance, a 6-month T-Bill issued in August 2024 offered a cut-off yield of 3.34% per annum.  Source: T Bills (Treasury Bills) in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/t-bills-treasury-bills-in-singapore/  (index: T Bills (Treasury Bills) in Singapore)

term: Investment requirements and process
definition: T-Bills can be acquired through DBS, UOB, or OCBC bank platforms via online banking or in person at CPFIS agent bank branches. When participating in T-Bills auctions, investors have the option to submit either competitive or non-competitive bids. In a competitive bid, an investor specifies the yield they are willing to accept. In contrast, in a non-competitive bid, the investor only specifies the amount to be invested without regard to the yield. Non-competitive bids are typically prioritized, with up to 40% of the total issuance allotted.  Source: T Bills (Treasury Bills) in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/t-bills-treasury-bills-in-singapore/  (index: T Bills (Treasury Bills) in Singapore)

term: Benefits and considerations
definition: Treasury Bills (T-Bills) present an opportunity for risk-free returns as they are guaranteed by the Singapore Government, thus offering a secure investment avenue. Furthermore, the interest income derived from T-Bills is exempt from tax for individual investors, presenting an added financial advantage. Although T-Bills are not redeemable before maturity, their short tenors of 6 months or one year render them relatively liquid investments.  Source: T Bills (Treasury Bills) in Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/t-bills-treasury-bills-in-singapore/  (index: T Bills (Treasury Bills) in Singapore)

term: Comparison with other investment options
definition: Moreover, T-Bills offer analogous or marginally lower returns compared to fixed deposits. However, they boast lower minimum investment requirements and shorter lock-in durations. term: asset management in Singapore’s real estate
definition: Asset management in Singapore real estate involves the strategic management of properties and investments to optimise their value and performance. This includes overseeing the acquisition, operation, maintenance, and disposition of real estate assets to meet the owner’s objectives. How to maximise returns and mitigate risks with real estate asset management strategies? Implementing a strategic asset management plan is key to optimising the performance of rental properties and mitigating risk exposure:  Source: Asset management  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/asset-management/  (index: Asset management)
aliases: What is asset management in Singapore’s real estate?

term: 1. Conduct thorough tenant screening and underwriting
definition: One of the biggest risks landlords face is ending up with a bad tenant who causes property damage or fails to pay rent on time. Conducting thorough tenant screening and underwriting during the leasing process is critical to assessing applicant risk and avoiding delinquencies. Run background checks, credit checks, verify income and rental history, and call references to carefully evaluate prospective tenants. It’s also important to utilise tenant underwriting to confirm applicants meet minimum income and credit requirements. Setting appropriate occupancy standards minimises risk and helps attract responsible, reliable tenants.  Source: Asset management  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/asset-management/  (index: Asset management)

term: 2. Implement preventative maintenance programmes
definition: Preventative maintenance helps preserve the physical and financial integrity of investment properties over time. Schedule regular unit inspections and tackle minor repairs immediately to prevent bigger, costlier issues down the road. Well-maintained properties also command higher rents and retain tenants longer.  Source: Asset management  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/asset-management/  (index: Asset management)

term: 3. Maintain adequate property reserves
definition: Adequate cash reserves provide landlords with a financial safety net to handle unexpected vacancies, repairs, legal issues, and other unforeseen expenses that arise. The rule of thumb is to set aside 10-15% of gross rental income in a reserve account. This provides funds to smoothly handle crises without impacting cash flow. For newer investors, aim to build up to the full 10-15% over time. Park reserve funds in a separate high-yield savings account so the money is easily accessible when needed.  Source: Asset management  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/asset-management/  (index: Asset management)

term: 4. Diversify your real estate portfolio
definition: Concentrating investments in one geographic area or property type amplifies risk exposure. Economic shifts or natural disasters can devastate a concentrated portfolio. Diversifying real estate assets across different markets, building classes, and tenant demographics helps mitigate localised risks.  Source: Asset management  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/asset-management/  (index: Asset management)

term: 5. Work with a seasoned property management company
definition: Handling day-to-day rental property management yourself may save money upfront, but also amplifies risks. Working with an experienced property management company acts as a risk mitigation strategy. Professional property managers specialise in areas like tenant relations, maintenance, rent collection, compliance, and leasing – allowing landlords to take a hands-off approach. While fees do apply, the benefits gained from a property manager protecting your assets outweigh the costs. Their expertise also maximise operational efficiency. Implementing these 5 essential real estate asset management strategies will help investors optimise returns while minimising risk exposure. Proactively managing properties using smart tenant screening, preventative maintenance, ample reserves, portfolio diversification, and professional property management sets up rentals for success. With a strategic approach to asset management, real estate investors can maximise profits and mitigate risks over the long-term.  Source: Asset management  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/asset-management/  (index: Asset management)

term: boutique condos
definition: Boutique condo, or boutique condominium, is a smaller, exclusive development, offering privacy and unique features. These properties appeal to those who value privacy and serenity over large-scale living. While boutique condos have fewer amenities and smaller site areas than larger developments, they offer a unique living experience.  Source: Boutique Condos  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/boutique-condo-singapore/  (index: Boutique Condos)

term: Location
definition: These condos are often located in quieter, more private areas, making them ideal for couples, empty nesters, or anyone seeking a more intimate living environment. The smaller community fosters stronger connections between neighbours, creating a sense of belonging.  Source: Boutique Condos  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/boutique-condo-singapore/  (index: Boutique Condos)

term: Features
definition: A key feature of boutique condos is their flexibility in layout. Unlike larger condos built with prefabricated construction methods, boutique developments often allow for more freedom in interior design. This means homeowners can personalise their space more easily, whether by knocking down walls or opting for open-concept designs. Additionally, many boutique condos are freehold properties, which means they come with perpetual ownership. This makes them a valuable long-term investment for Singaporeans.  Source: Boutique Condos  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/boutique-condo-singapore/  (index: Boutique Condos)

term: Affordability
definition: Because these developments are on smaller plots of land, they are often more affordable than larger projects. The lower launch prices, however, do not necessarily mean lower future returns. While larger condos may experience faster price growth due to higher transaction volumes, boutique condos still offer solid investment potential.  Source: Boutique Condos  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/boutique-condo-singapore/  (index: Boutique Condos)

term: Pros of buying a boutique condo in Singapore
definition: The biggest value-add when buying boutique condos is freehold ownership. Freehold properties offer perpetual ownership, meaning they are not subject to lease decay. This makes them a rare commodity, particularly in Singapore, where land is limited. Freehold boutique condos can serve as valuable legacy assets, passing down wealth to future generations. This sense of security is attractive to those looking for a property that will retain its value over time and provide financial stability for their families. Furthermore, boutique condos often come with a lower entry price compared to larger developments. Due to their smaller size and fewer amenities, developers can offer these properties at more affordable rates. This makes boutique condos an attractive option for buyers who want to invest in property without the premium costs associated with larger, more luxurious developments. Last, but not the least, boutique condos offer privacy, exclusivity, and personalisation. With only a limited number of residents, these developments create a much more intimate and serene living environment. This exclusivity can be particularly appealing to individuals who prefer a quieter, more peaceful lifestyle. Homeowners have the opportunity to knock down walls, create open-concept spaces, or personalise their homes to suit their needs. This is particularly attractive for buyers who want to create a bespoke living environment that reflects their individual style. Larger developments, on the other hand, often come with stricter renovation rules due to the use of prefabricated construction methods.  Source: Boutique Condos  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/boutique-condo-singapore/  (index: Boutique Condos)

term: Cons of choosing a boutique condo
definition: One of the main disadvantages is the limited amenities offered. Larger developments often provide a wide range of facilities, such as gyms, pools, and communal spaces, which may be lacking in boutique condos. This can be a downside for residents who value these features or for families with young children who need access to recreational areas. Many boutique condos are located in more private, less accessible areas. While this offers a sense of tranquillity and exclusivity, it may also mean that residents are further away from key amenities such as public transport, schools, and shopping centres. The more secluded nature of these developments may also affect daily commuting and overall accessibility. Another potential concern is the lower liquidity of boutique condos. Smaller developments tend to have fewer buyers and lesser transaction volumes than larger developments, which may make it harder to sell a unit quickly. If you are looking for a property that can be easily resold, the limited number of units in boutique condos might pose a challenge.  Source: Boutique Condos  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/boutique-condo-singapore/  (index: Boutique Condos)

term: Annual Percentage Rate (APR)
definition: The APR, or Annual Percentage Rate, refers to the yearly interest rate a person or organisation must pay for the privilege of borrowing money. This rate is applied to various financial products, such as credit cards, car loans, and mortgages. In other words, the APR tells you the total expense of borrowing money as a percentage of the loan’s original principal amount. The purpose of the APR on a loan or credit card is to provide an exact idea of the borrowing cost. Hence, the APR is among the most important figures to consider when applying for new credit.  Source: Annual Percentage Rate (APR)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/annual-percentage-rate-apr/  (index: Annual Percentage Rate (APR))
aliases: What is the Annual Percentage Rate (APR)?|Annual Percentage Rate|APR

term: What factors influence the Annual Percentage Rate (APR)
definition: The lender or creditor determines your APR, but it can also be affected by your credit scores. For example, if you have a history of good credit behaviour and are viewed as a low-risk borrower by potential lenders and creditors, you may be offered a reduced interest rate, which typically leads to a lower APR.  Source: Annual Percentage Rate (APR)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/annual-percentage-rate-apr/  (index: Annual Percentage Rate (APR))
aliases: What factors influence the Annual Percentage Rate|APR|WAPR

term: difference between the Annual Percentage Rate (APR) and the interest rate
definition: APR and interest rate are similar in meaning, but they are not identical. Interest rates only cover the cost of borrowing money and do not include any other expenses associated with the loan. It is expressed as a percentage and can be paid annually, monthly, or daily. In contrast, the APR is the total interest rate charged for an entire year and includes additional costs associated with the loan. For example, a mortgage APR would typically reflect the interest rate and any closing costs, origination fees, broker fees, and other expenses related to obtaining a loan. When comparing different loans, the APR gives borrowers a more comprehensive idea of the total costs involved. Due to this, the APR is generally higher than the interest rate, but this may vary from case to case.  Source: Annual Percentage Rate (APR)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/annual-percentage-rate-apr/  (index: Annual Percentage Rate (APR))

term: appreciation in Singapore real estate
definition: Appreciation in Singapore real estate refers to the increase in the value of a property over time. Capital appreciation occurs when you sell your property for a higher price than when you purchased it. For example, if you buy an HDB 3-room for S$500,000 and sell it 5 years later for S$900,000, the capital appreciation is S$400,000. Similarly, if you buy a freehold condo at $800,000 and later sell it at S$1,000,000, the capital appreciation is S$200,000.  Source: Appreciation  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/appreciation/  (index: Appreciation)

term: What factors influence property appreciation in Singapore
definition: Factors that can contribute to capital appreciation in Singapore real estate include:  Source: Appreciation  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/appreciation/  (index: Appreciation)

term: Tips on growing your property’s appreciation
definition: If your objective is to transform real estate appreciation into lasting generational wealth, consider the following tips: Start early and be consistent Commence your real estate investment journey as early as possible to allow your properties ample time for appreciation. Initiate investments once you’ve accumulated sufficient savings for an initial rental property or flip. Consistency is crucial; continually augment your portfolio with new properties over the years, fostering equity growth and realising appreciation returns. Reinvest profits As your properties appreciate, reinvest a significant portion of your rental income and flip profits into acquiring new properties. The compounding effect in real estate can exponentially boost your portfolio and net worth over time. Purchase cash-flowing rentals While emphasising long-term property appreciation, acknowledge the importance of cash flow. Acquire rental properties in areas with robust tenant demand to minimise vacancy rates and enhance monthly cash flow, which can be reinvested. Cash flow acts as a financial cushion, especially during vacancies or necessary repairs. Improve and maintain properties Enhance your rental properties through upgrades and renovations. Initiating projects like kitchen and bathroom remodels, exterior facelifts, and system upgrades enables you to raise rents and boost property values. Consistent maintenance preserves curb appeal, retaining tenants for increased returns. Utilise leverage Optimise your purchasing power by leveraging rental property loans, lines of credit, and other financing tools. Although leveraging introduces risk, it enables the acquisition of more properties than feasible with personal capital alone, translating to greater appreciation potential over time. Hold properties long-term Resist the urge to sell properties prematurely. Prolonged ownership of real estate investments maximises appreciation potential. Holding onto properties over an extended period allows for optimal appreciation, facilitating the option to gift or sell at a reduced tax rate for intergenerational wealth transfer.  Source: Appreciation  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/appreciation/  (index: Appreciation)

term: discharge of the CPF charge

CPF Charge represents the withdrawn amount from your CPF savings used for property payment. Most Singaporeans have CPF Charges as they utilise CPF funds for their homes and are obligated to repay the CPF Charge upon selling the property. term: Key laws and regulations
definition: Joint ventures in Singapore are governed by a combination of contract law, company law, and specific real estate regulations. Let’s go over these in detail: 1. Contract Law: The foundation of a JV is the Joint Venture Agreement. This contract outlines the rights, obligations, and responsibilities of each party. Key aspects include profit and loss sharing, management roles, dispute resolution, and exit strategies. The Contract Act governs the enforceability of these agreements. 2. Company Law: Often, a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) – a separate company – is formed for the real estate joint venture. This is governed by the Companies Act, which dictates company registration, shareholder rights, and directors’ duties. This allows each party to maintain their individual corporate identity while still engaging in the venture. 3. Land Titles (Strata) Act: The Land Titles (Strata) Act in Singapore is a crucial piece of legislation that governs the ownership and management of strata-titled properties. These are properties where multiple owners share common areas, such as condominiums, apartments, and some commercial buildings. The Act’s primary purpose is to provide a legal framework for the subdivision of land and buildings into strata titles, enabling individual ownership of units within a larger development. It sets out the rights and responsibilities of strata title owners, the management of common property, and the resolution of disputes. It applies to all strata-titled developments in Singapore, both residential and commercial. 4. Planning Act: The Planning Act in Singapore is a cornerstone of the country’s urban development, providing the legal framework for land use planning and control. The Planning Act’s primary purpose is to regulate and control the development of land in Singapore, ensuring that it aligns with the country’s long-term planning objectives. The Act empowers the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) to formulate and implement land use plans, guiding the physical development of Singapore. In any real estate joint venture, all parties are expected to comply with zoning regulations and planning permissions obtained from the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA). Any deviations require approvals and may impact the project’s feasibility. 5. Building Control Act: This Act ensures building safety and standards. All joint ventures must adhere to regulations set by the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) for design, construction, and maintenance of buildings. This includes obtaining necessary building permits and certificates of statutory completion. 6. Stamp Duties Act: Stamp duties are payable on property transactions. JVs must account for stamp duties on land transfers, share transfers, and other relevant transactions. The amount payable varies depending on the type of property and the transaction value. 7. Foreign Ownership Restrictions: For any real estate joint ventures involving foreign entities, restrictions on foreign ownership of certain types of land (e.g., landed properties) apply. These are governed by the Residential Property Act and require approvals from the Singapore Land Authority (SLA). term: Basic Retirement Sum (BRS)
definition: The Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) represents the monthly payouts during retirement that cover essential living expenses. The BRS is one of three tiers within the CPF Retirement Sum framework, with the other two being the Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS) and the Full Retirement Sum (FRS). The BRS is the lowest tier compared to others, designed to provide a baseline level of financial security. When individuals turn 55, their CPF savings up to the BRS are set aside in their Retirement Account (RA). These savings are then utilised to generate monthly payouts through the CPF LIFE (Lifelong Income for the Elderly) scheme, starting at 65 or a chosen later age. If your CPF balance meets the BRS requirement at the age of 55 and you do not own any property, you can withdraw S$5,000 monthly. However, if an individual owns a property with sufficient lease remaining until the age of 95 or older, they have the flexibility to meet their BRS using a combination of property and cash. This enables them to withdraw a portion of their RA savings to the BRS using their property. Individuals can access a larger amount for withdrawal from their CPF accounts by opting to pledge their property. By adhering to the BRS, CPF guarantees that future retirees will get adequate monthly payouts to cover all their essential needs and maintain financial security.  Source: Basic Retirement Sum (BRS)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/basic-retirement-sum-brs/  (index: Basic Retirement Sum (BRS))

However, renting out individual rooms within the flat is still allowed. If you plan to wait for the 10-year MOP to expire and rent out the entire flat, expecting a favourable rental yield, we regret to inform you that this option is unavailable under the PLH model. Here is the comparison between HDB BTO and PLH flats: • Resale of flat: Permitted after 5-year MOP for BTO, 10-year MOP for PLH flats. • Buying another private property: Permitted after 5-year MOP for both BTO and 10-year MOP for PLH flats. • Renting out the whole flat: Permitted after 5-year MOP for BTO flats only; not allowed for PLH flats. • Renting out rooms: Permitted for both BTO and PLH flats. The information provided was accurate at the time of publication. For the latest changes and updates, you can check the official websites. term: Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS)
definition: Upon reaching age 55, Singaporean and Permanent Resident (PR) CPF members will have a Retirement Account (RA) established for them. The funds from their Ordinary Account (OA) and Special Account (SA) will be used to finance the RA, up to the Full Retirement Sum (FRS) limit. The balance in the RA will continue to accrue interest until it is transferred into the CPF Life Scheme at the age of 65. The savings in the RA play an essential role in determining the monthly CPF Life payment and overall CPF balances. CPF has established three target amounts, namely the Basic Retirement Sum (BRS), Full Retirement Sum (FRS), and Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS), to ensure that Singaporeans are saving sufficiently for their retirement.  Source: Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/enhanced-retirement-sum-ers/  (index: Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS))
aliases: What is the Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS)?|Enhanced Retirement Sum|ERS

term: How does the Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS) work
definition: The ERS is a little bit different from the BRS and FRS as it represents the upper limit for topping up your RA and determines the maximum CPF Life payouts you can receive. Upon reaching age 55, you become eligible to contribute funds to your RA up to the ERS, provided that you meet its threshold. In 2023, the ERS threshold is set at S$298,200, reflecting the target amount for a secure and comfortable retirement. According to CPF, the ERS is set at three times the BRS, resulting in significantly higher CPF Life payouts. For individuals with surplus funds intended for retirement, it can be advantageous to allocate these funds toward meeting the ERS in their RA.  Source: Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/enhanced-retirement-sum-ers/  (index: Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS))

term: Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) vs Full Retirement Sum (FRS) vs Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS) – Which is the best fit for you
definition: Achieving the FRS guarantees a reliable monthly income through CPF Life payouts, ensuring a comfortable standard of living during retirement. On the other side, meeting the BRS may require exploring options like downsizing one’s property to adequately fund retirement expenses. For those who desire a higher level of financial security and wish to enjoy a more luxurious retirement, aiming for the ERS is recommended. The information provided was accurate at the time of publication. For the newest changes and updates, head over to the official website.  Source: Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/enhanced-retirement-sum-ers/  (index: Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS))

term: a Tenancy Agreement in Singapore
definition: The Rental Tenancy Agreement is a contract that outlines the terms and conditions of a rental property, including clauses that protect the interests of both landlords and tenants. It covers key aspects of the tenancy, such as monthly rent, maintenance and repairs, and privacy. In case of disputes or disagreements, the Tenancy Agreement serves as a point of reference for both parties.  Source: Tenancy Agreement Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/tenancy-agreement-singapore/  (index: Tenancy Agreement Singapore)
aliases: What is a Tenancy Agreement in Singapore?|TAS

term: What should be included in a Tenancy Agreement in Singapore
definition: The agreement should clearly state the property being rented and the duration of the tenancy. It should also specify the payment of rent and utilities, including any additional charges, subscriptions, or license fees. The tenant may be required to provide a security deposit, which may be forfeited if the property is damaged or the tenant violates the terms of the agreement. The agreement should also outline the permitted use of the premises and require appropriate upkeep of the property. The tenant’s covenants, such as paying rent and keeping the property in good repair, should also be included, along with the landlord’s covenants, such as providing a habitable dwelling and ensuring quiet enjoyment of the property. Termination of the lease, suspension of rent, notices, anticipatory breach, and stamp fees are important clauses that should also be included in the agreement.  Source: Tenancy Agreement Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/tenancy-agreement-singapore/  (index: Tenancy Agreement Singapore)

term: process of the payment and signing of the Tenancy Agreement in Singapore
definition: To secure a rental property, tenants typically need to pay a deposit equal to one month’s rent for a one-year lease or two month’s rent for a two-year lease, along with the first month’s rent. It’s advisable not to pay more than one month’s rent as a deposit. A third-party witness, such as an agent, should witness the signing of the tenancy agreement. Both parties should agree on a fixed payment method, such as GIRO or internet banking, to ensure proper documentation of all financial transactions. It is also recommended to avoid making cash payments for the deposit or rent unless necessary. Instead, cheques should be used as proof of payment.  Source: Tenancy Agreement Singapore  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/tenancy-agreement-singapore/  (index: Tenancy Agreement Singapore)

term: an SG Arrival Card
definition: The SG Arrival Card (SGAC), also known as the white card or paper disembarkation/embarkation (DE) card, is the electronic equivalent of the paper form foreign visitors use to fill out upon arrival in Singapore for immigration clearance. On March 27, 2020, the Immigration & Checkpoints Authority (ICA) discontinued using the paper DE card, requiring all travellers to provide their arrival information through an “SG Arrival Card” e-Service instead. Every traveller must complete the SGAC declaration within a maximum of 3 days before their arrival. This ensures smooth immigration clearance without unnecessary delays. The only exception to this rule is for Singapore Citizens, Permanent Residents, and Long-Term Pass Holders who enter Singapore through land checkpoints, as they are not required to fill in the SGAC declaration.  Source: SG Arrival Card  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/sg-arrival-card/  (index: SG Arrival Card)

term: Don’t get burned: Why property insurance is a must-have for every homeowner
definition: As a homeowner, securing property insurance is one of the most crucial steps you can take. It may seem like an added expense at first, but the long-term benefits and protections it offers are invaluable. Let’s delve into why property insurance is essential for every homeowner. [HEADING-H3] Protect your investment Your home is likely the largest investment you’ll ever make. The time, money, and effort you’ve invested in acquiring your home can be jeopardised by unforeseen events. Fires, storms, floods, and theft can cause significant damage or total loss. Property insurance offers peace of mind, safeguarding your financial investment against these unpredictable calamities. [HEADING-H3] Avoid massive out-of-pocket expenses Damage to your property can lead to enormous repair costs. Simple repairs for water damage or replacing personal belongings can quickly amount to thousands of dollars. Without insurance, these expenses come out of your pocket. Property insurance covers the majority of these costs, preventing the need to drain your savings or incur debt.  Source: Property insurance  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/property-insurance/  (index: Property insurance)

term: Get replacement cost coverage
definition: Your policy must include replacement cost coverage. This coverage pays for rebuilding your home with similar quality materials if it’s destroyed. The land may retain some value, but the cost of rebuilding can be staggering. Replacement cost coverage ensures you can rebuild without suffering a major financial loss. [HEADING-H3] Protect yourself from liability Home insurance isn’t just about protecting your property; it’s also about protecting yourself. Liability coverage is crucial if someone gets injured on your property and decides to sue. This can include slip and fall incidents or injuries caused by defects in your home. Liability coverage provides a buffer against legal fees and damages, protecting your financial well-being. [HEADING-H3] Safeguard yourself against disasters Disasters like fires, storms, and floods might seem distant until they happen to you. Being unprepared for such events can lead to total loss. Property insurance is your primary defence against these disasters. Ensure your coverage limits are adequate to protect your home’s value. Property insurance provides essential financial security for homeowners. It’s a protective measure that shouldn’t be overlooked or delayed. By securing a comprehensive insurance policy, you protect your home, belongings, and financial stability. Don’t wait until disaster strikes – get insured now to avoid the potentially devastating consequences of being unprotected.  Source: Property insurance  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/property-insurance/  (index: Property insurance)

term: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)
definition: MAS was formed on January 1, 1971, following Parliament’s passing of the Monetary Authority of Singapore Act in 1970. As Singapore’s central bank and integrated financial regulator, MAS plays a pivotal role in shaping the country as a thriving global financial centre.  Source: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/monetary-authority-of-singapore-mas/  (index: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS))
aliases: What is the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)?|Monetary Authority of Singapore|MAS

term: What does the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) do
definition: Under the MAS Act, MAS is entrusted with various responsibilities to ensure the smooth functioning of the financial system. It acts as a trusted banker and financial agent for the Government, promotes monetary stability, and implements credit and exchange policies that foster economic growth. MAS’s broad range of responsibilities includes: • Conducting monetary policy • Issuing currency • Overseeing payment systems • Undertaking integrated supervision of financial services • Managing the nation’s official foreign reserves • Positioning Singapore as a highly sought-after international financial hub  Source: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/monetary-authority-of-singapore-mas/  (index: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS))

term: How does the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) fulfil its duties
definition: MAS implements several measures and initiatives to fulfil its duties, which include: MAS is responsible for developing and executing effective monetary policies that support sustainable and non-inflationary economic growth. As such, it closely monitors macroeconomic trends to ensure stability and favourable economic conditions. MAS also actively manages critical factors such as Singapore’s exchange rate, official foreign reserves, and banking sector liquidity. As an integrated financial supervisor, MAS exercises meticulous oversight over all financial institutions in Singapore. This includes banks, insurers, capital market intermediaries, financial advisors, and stock exchanges. The primary objective is to uphold the integrity and stability of the financial services sector, foster well-functioning financial markets, and promote ethical conduct among market participants. MAS seeks to empower investors by providing educational initiatives and promoting awareness of financial matters. By enhancing financial literacy and ensuring transparency, MAS aims to enable individuals to make informed investment decisions and safeguard their interests. MAS collaborates closely with the financial industry to drive Singapore’s position as a dynamic international financial centre. It actively supports the development of robust infrastructure, encourages the adoption of cutting-edge technology, and facilitates continuous skills enhancement within the financial industry workforce.  Source: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)  https://www.99.co/singapore/glossary/monetary-authority-of-singapore-mas/  (index: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS))

term: Can I appeal for my real estate agency examination results
